signals.title: Reject divergent same-named parts in parallel replicas coordinator
signals.text: The parallel replicas coordinator deduplicated parts purely by `MergeTreePartInfo` (name + version), so when two replicas announced a same-named part holding genuinely different data the second announcement was silently merged into the first. The coordinator then dispatched ranges from the first replica's snapshot to the second replica, whose local part was different, producing an exception `Trying to get non existing mark N, while size is M` inside `MergeTreeIndexGranularityConstant::getMarkRows` — or, when the layouts happened to line up, potentially incorrect results. This is reachable with `parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1` against a cluster whose members each have independent local `MergeTree` data: block numbers of a non-replicated `MergeTree` come from a node-local `SimpleIncrement`, so each member's local first part is named `all_1_1_0` but can store different data. The fix makes the coordinator validate the identity of same-named parts across announcements: - `RangesInDataPartDescription` now carries the underlying part's total mark count, a content fingerprint (`checksums.getTotalChecksumUInt128`), and a `part_name_identity` tri-state saying whether a part name identifies the same content on every cluster member. The fields are gated on a new parallel replicas protocol version (`DBMS_PARALLEL_REPLICAS_PROTOCOL_VERSION` bumped to 10). - `part_name_identity` is `ClusterWide` when the engine coordinates block numbers through Keeper (`ReplicatedMergeTree` and descendants) *or* when all of the table's disks keep their metadata in storage shared by every cluster member (`MetadataStorageType::Plain`, `PlainRewritable`, `StaticWeb`, `WebIndex`, `Keeper`) — there every member enumerates literally the same parts. It is `NodeLocal` for a plain `MergeTree` on ordinary local or per-node remote disks. - `InOrderCoordinator` and `DefaultCoordinator` snapshot these fields from the first announcement of each part and compare later announcements against the snapshot. A fingerprint mismatch raises `BAD_ARGUMENTS` naming the diverging part and pointing the user at `ReplicatedMergeTree` or at disabling `parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree`. - When the fingerprint is unavailable on either side (a replica running an older server version, or a part whose checksums are not loaded) and either side reports `NodeLocal` part names, the coordinator fails closed with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` instead of weakening the identity check — such same-named parts cannot be verified, and merging them blindly could return incorrect results. For `ClusterWide` part names the part name implies identical content, so a mark-count fallback keeps mixed-version clusters working during rolling upgrades. Only analyzed-view fields (`rows`, `ranges`) are deliberately NOT compared: per-replica PK and skip-index analysis can legitimately select different mark subsets from the same underlying part, and `ranges` is consumed in place as the coordinator dispatches work. The protocol bump also required pinning one existing consumer of the serializer. The `read_bucket` task parameter of a distributed read plan (`make_distributed_plan`) embeds a `RangesInDataPartsDescription` blob but travels as an opaque query parameter with no handshake to negotiate a version on, so producer and consumer both used the build's own `DBMS_PARALLEL_REPLICAS_PROTOCOL_VERSION` and would disagree about the field layout across a rolling upgrade. The blob is now pinned to `DBMS_PARALLEL_REPLICAS_DISTRIBUTED_READ_BUCKET_VERSION = 8`, the layout in effect when it was introduced. Surfaced by the AST fuzzer (STID `4920-51f2`) on PR #105706. The 5-replica `parallel_replicas` cluster used by `tests/queries/0_stateless/02275_full_sort_join_long.sql.j2` exposes the divergence whenever local `t2` parts differ in size across replicas. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105706&sha=84790f83ec78aee26b08ab6e0bc6712f6e4f1745&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105706 Coverage is via `gtest_parallel_replicas_coordinator`, which exercises both coordination modes and both announcement orderings: rejection on divergent mark counts and divergent fingerprints, acceptance of identical announcements and of divergent analyzed views over the same part, the fail-closed path for `NodeLocal` part names without a fingerprint, the mark-count fallback for `ClusterWide` part names in mixed-version clusters, and a serializer round trip across protocol versions 8, 9 and 10 that requires the reader to consume the whole buffer. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an exception `Trying to get non existing mark N, while size is M` and potential incorrect parallel-replica range assignment when `parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1` is used on divergent local `MergeTree` data: the parallel replicas coordinator now validates same-named parts by a content fingerprint of the underlying part instead of merging announcements blindly, and fails closed when the fingerprint is unavailable and part names are not guaranteed to identify the same content on every cluster member. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is unchanged

signals.title: Fix FREEZE permanent failure on empty shadow/increment.txt
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105719 ## Motivation A concurrent `ALTER TABLE ... FREEZE WITH NAME` and `ALTER TABLE ... UNFREEZE WITH NAME` race, or a writer killed between `truncate(0)` and the subsequent `writeIntText` inside `CounterInFile::add`, could leave the server-global `shadow/increment.txt` at size 0. Every subsequent FREEZE on the server then failed permanently with `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF` until an operator manually removed the file. Backup tools that issue FREEZE concurrently (clickhouse-backup, ad-hoc scripts, CI) were stuck in that broken state. Slach's deterministic reproducer (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105719): ```bash docker exec ch bash -c ': > /var/lib/clickhouse/shadow/increment.txt' docker exec ch clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t FREEZE" # Code: 32. DB::Exception: File ... is empty. (ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF) # Every subsequent FREEZE also fails. Server never recovers. ``` ## Fix 1. `CounterInFile::add` drops the TOCTOU-unsafe pre-lock `fs::exists` check, takes the exclusive `flock`, then uses `fstat` under the lock to determine state. A size-0 file is treated the same as a missing file: with `create_if_need` the counter is repaired in place; without it the call throws, a missing file is not created, and an existing empty file is left untouched. 2. `MergeTreeData::freezePartitionsByMatcher` walks `shadow/` on every configured disk for the maximum numeric subdirectory name and passes it as a lower bound for the recovered counter, so the next FREEZE without `WITH NAME` does not collide with an already-allocated `shadow/<N>/`. The scan is evaluated lazily, only on the recovery path and under the counter lock, so a healthy counter never pays for it. Healthy counter values found in a non-empty file are used as-is and are NOT clamped, so steady-state behavior is unchanged. The scan must observe every `shadow/<N>` that exists, because it is collision avoidance: a bound that is too low hands out an identifier a backup already holds. So a failure that could hide one fails the FREEZE rather than silently lowering the bound. There are two deliberate exceptions, both logged so an operator can raise the counter once: - a **broken** disk, which is a routine and possibly long-lived state that must not fail every FREEZE on the server; - a **read-only** disk whose inspection raises, i.e. one whose backing store is unreachable, such as a `web` disk whose endpoint is down. Without this, such a disk breaks every FREEZE that has to recover the counter, including the very first FREEZE on a server, where no counter file exists yet. Being read-only is deliberately NOT sufficient on its own. `DiskLocal` becomes read-only whenever write access is lost while staying fully readable and not broken, so such a disk can still hold `shadow/<N>` written while it was writable, and skipping it would hand out an identifier one of them already holds. Note that with an unreachable disk configured a recovery FREEZE now succeeds but pays that disk's connection-retry budget, rather than failing outright. ## What `FREEZE WITH NAME` does with the counter A named FREEZE takes its directory name from `WITH NAME`, never from the counter. Whether it has to touch the counter therefore depends on the name, and the two cases are split: **A numeric name is an identifier an unnamed FREEZE could allocate**, so it must be reserved or the two collide. It is taken with `create_if_need = true`, floored by the name, and recovered through the same all-disk scan. The counter ends up at or above the name: at it when the name is the highest id in play, higher when the scan found a larger existing backup. Either way the name is marked allocated, because an unnamed FREEZE hands out the stored value plus one. `shadow/0` is the one exception and needs no reservation, because a recovered counter is the bound plus one and zero is never allocated. If the scan refuses because an existing backup already holds the counter's maximum, the numeric named FREEZE fails, keeping the scan's message, which names the directory to remove. It is tempting to proceed unreserved instead, since there is no next id anyway, but that state is not durable: `SYSTEM UNFREEZE` removes a backup directory without taking the counter lock, and the named backup's own directory is created only after the lock is released. In that window an unnamed FREEZE allocates exactly the pending name and two tables silently share one backup directory. **Any other name cannot collide with an allocated id**, so it must not depend on the recovery scan: an unrelated disk whose `shadow` lookup throws would otherwise fail a query that never needs the counter to choose a name (reported by the review bot on this PR). It is taken with `create_if_need = false`, which keeps the one property it needs and drops the one it does not: - it still advances a **healthy** counter, because consuming the value is what keeps a later unnamed FREEZE from handing it out; - it never creates or repairs a **missing or empty** counter, and never runs the scan. Recovery stays pending for the next FREEZE without `WITH NAME`, the only operation that consumes the counter. Persisting a value no scan produced would instead let that FREEZE see a healthy counter, skip recovery, and reuse an existing `shadow/<N>/`; - it also proceeds when the counter is **exhausted**, i.e. parked at the value beyond which no next id exists. That state has no id for an unnamed FREEZE to allocate, so there is nothing to reserve against, and the overflow guard throws before writing, so the stored maximum is left intact (reported by the review bot on this PR: refusing here turned uniquely named backups into a permanent failure). Unlike the scan's refusal above, this state is durable, because only writing the counter file can leave it. A genuinely broken counter still fails the query: an unreadable one, a short read, content `readIntText` rejects outright, or any errno other than `ENOENT`. Content that `readIntText` accepts as a prefix (`abc`, `12x`, a value wider than `Int64`) is taken at face value here exactly as it is on master, so this PR neither improves nor regresses it; validating the committed counter format is a separate concern. The scan counts only entries an unnamed FREEZE could have produced: a directory (the iterator also yields plain files, and a numeric file is not a backup) whose name is the canonical decimal spelling within the counter's range: `09223372036854775807` is a different path from `9223372036854775807` and only `FREEZE WITH NAME` can create it, so folding it in would raise the bound over an identifier that is still free. The bound is the counter's maximum rather than one below it, because `shadow/<Int64 max>` is reachable (recovery from `max - 1` adds one) and must therefore be accounted for. That makes exhaustion reachable, where no next id exists at all, and recovery then fails with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` naming the directory instead of overflowing the counter and reusing it. ## Regression tests `tests/queries/0_stateless/04277_105719_freeze_recover_from_empty_increment.sh` covers thirteen scenarios: an empty counter with no prior backup (A) and with a prior non-numeric backup (B); recovery above a planted numeric directory (C); no reuse of a numeric `FREEZE WITH NAME` directory (D); an oversized numeric name ignored (E); a non-canonical numeric name such as `09223372036854775807` ignored (J); a non-numeric named FREEZE leaving recovery pending (G); a named FREEZE reserving its numeric name against a healthy counter (H) and against an empty one (N); the reservation happening before the directory is created (P); a non-numeric name leaving an empty counter alone (O); a numeric plain file ignored by the scan (M); and a numeric backup living on a non-default disk (F). Each assertion was mutation-tested: reverting the corresponding part of the fix makes exactly the matching scenario fail. `tests/integration/test_freeze_recover_broken_disk/test.py` covers what a stateless test cannot safely do: - a broken disk being skipped rather than failing every FREEZE; - a numeric backup on a nested `DiskEncrypted` still counting toward the bound; - the `Int64` boundary, where a backup named `max - 1` must still allow `max` to be allocated while a backup occupying `max` itself is refused with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, the directory and the empty counter both surviving, a non-numeric named FREEZE still succeeding, and a numeric one refused without creating its directory or writing the counter; - the counter states the named path must tolerate (exhausted, missing, empty) or propagate (unparsable, unopenable), that a numeric name is a floor rather than the final value, and that a healthy counter is advanced by a non-numeric name too; - on its own instance, that an unreachable read-only disk does not fail recovery while a local disk that turned read-only but is still readable does raise the bound. Those cases need either a directory name that cannot be varied, an unrecoverable state written into `shadow/increment.txt` itself, or a disk configuration of their own. The stateless server's counter is shared with every other test and is deliberately never restored on cleanup, so a run killed inside such a case would leave every later FREEZE on that server failing. Each integration instance owns its own `shadow/`. The read-only cases live on a separate instance because an unreachable disk also breaks the unrelated all-disk orphaned-parts scan that a non-default storage policy performs at table load, which the other cases here rely on. `src/Common/tests/gtest_counter_in_file.cpp` pins the `CounterInFile::add` contract directly: missing and empty files with and without `create_if_need`, the lower bound and the lazy provider each applying on recovery from a missing file as well as from an empty one and never on a healthy counter, and a throwing provider aborting without writing. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ALTER TABLE ... FREEZE` failing permanently with `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF` after `shadow/increment.txt` was left empty by a concurrent FREEZE/UNFREEZE race or an interrupted writer. The counter is now repaired in place from the maximum existing `shadow/<N>/` directory rather than requiring manual operator intervention. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is unchanged.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Use text index for LIKE/ILIKE with ESCAPE
signals.text: Follow-up to #99774 (qoega's LIKE ESCAPE clause). Before this change, a query like `... WHERE col LIKE pattern ESCAPE 'c'` silently bypassed the primary key (`KeyCondition`), the text index (`TYPE text`), and the bloom-filter text indexes (`ngrambf_v1`, `tokenbf_v1`, `sparse_grams`), falling back to a full scan even on tables with such an index defined or with `col` in the sorting key. Root cause: `LIKE pattern ESCAPE 'c'` is parsed into a 3-argument function call `like(col, pattern, escape_char)`. `MergeTreeIndexConditionText::traverseAtomNode`, `MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText::extractAtomFromTree`, and `KeyCondition::extractAtomFromTree` only accepted 2-argument forms; any 3-arg `like`/`ilike` was rejected without ever reaching the LIKE handler. The execution layer in `FunctionsStringSearch::executeImpl` already calls `likePatternWithCustomEscapeToLikePattern` to fold the custom escape into standard backslash escapes before matching, so result correctness was never affected, only performance. Apply the same fold at index-condition time: - Text index (`MergeTreeIndexConditionText`): handles 3-arg `like` and `ilike` (the same arities `isSupportedFunction` allows for the index). - Bloom-filter text indexes (`MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText`, for `ngrambf_v1` / `tokenbf_v1` / `sparse_grams`): handles 3-arg `like` and `notLike` (the like-family forms this index supports; `ilike` is not supported by this index type). - Primary key (`KeyCondition`): handles 3-arg `like` and `notLike` (the like-family forms present in `atom_map`). Case-insensitive `ilike`/`notILike` are not in `atom_map` and continue to fall back to row-level evaluation, same as the existing 2-arg behavior. In all paths the pattern must be a constant String and the escape argument a constant String of length 1; otherwise we bail out. Invalid escape sequences cause analysis to skip the index/key so row-level evaluation throws the same error the user would have seen before. The `nextInStringLike` tokenizer used by both text-index variants drops the backslash for an unknown escape `\c` while row-level matching keeps it, so an unknown/trailing backslash is declined (the `likePatternHasUnknownBackslashEscape` guard) and falls back to row-level matching to avoid wrongly pruning a matching granule. In the bloom-filter path this guard is placed in the shared `traverseTreeEquals`, so it protects both the folded 3-argument form and the pre-existing 2-argument `like` / `notLike` / `mapContainsKeyLike` / `mapContainsValueLike` paths. Regression tests use `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` to assert that pruning now happens: - `04277_text_index_function_like_escape.sql` covers the `TYPE text` index for `LIKE`/`ILIKE`, both `splitByNonAlpha` and `array` tokenizers, and both the operator form and the functional form `like(a, p, 'c')`. - `04292_105885_primary_key_like_escape.sql` covers the primary key for `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE` (with a remaining wildcard so the perfect-prefix extraction succeeds) and the functional form. - `04351_bloom_filter_text_index_like_escape.sql` covers the `ngrambf_v1` / `tokenbf_v1` / `sparse_grams` text indexes for `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE` ESCAPE and the functional form, including a consumed escape character, `force_data_skipping_indices`, and the unknown/trailing-backslash decline for both the 2-argument and 3-argument forms. The tests FAIL on master without this change and PASS with it. Closes #105885 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` and `ILIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` predicates (added in #99774) now use `TYPE text` skip indexes to prune granules; `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` and `NOT LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` additionally use the `ngrambf_v1`, `tokenbf_v1`, and `sparse_grams` skip indexes, and the primary key when the column is in the sorting key, instead of falling back to a full scan. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is unchanged (the existing text-index docs already describe LIKE-based pruning; this change only fills a coverage gap for the recently added ESCAPE clause).

signals.title: Fix EXECUTE AS for LDAP-backed users not yet logged in
signals.text: Fixes #99574. `EXECUTE AS <user>` failed with `UNKNOWN_USER` for users provided by an external LDAP user directory whenever the target had not yet authenticated against this server since the last restart. The LDAP storage materializes its in-memory entry on first successful login, so `AccessControl::getID` (which iterates `findImpl` over the nested storages) saw nothing. ### Approach Per @ pufit's review direction on this PR, the fix adds a `force_external_lookup` overload on `IAccessStorage::find` and `findImpl`. `MultipleAccessStorage` propagates the flag to nested storages; `LDAPAccessStorage::findImpl(..., force_external_lookup=true)` performs the upstream lookup against the LDAP server using a configured service-bind account, verifies the user via `user_dn_detection`, and materializes the in-memory entry with the resolved role mapping. `InterpreterExecuteAsQuery` resolves the target user through a two-pass lookup that preserves the existing `user_directories` precedence: first a normal `find<User>` (so a target already cached locally wins over an LDAP entry that has not yet been materialized), then the forced lookup if pass 1 missed. ### LDAP service-bind The forced lookup needs to confirm a user exists in the directory without their password. `LDAPClient` is extended with a service-bind mode (`BindMode::Service` on `openConnection`) that binds with two new configuration fields: ```xml <ldap_servers> <my_ldap_server> <host>...</host> <bind_dn>cn={user_name},ou=users,dc=example,dc=org</bind_dn> <!-- Required for force_external_lookup, optional otherwise --> <lookup_bind_dn>cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org</lookup_bind_dn> <lookup_password>...</lookup_password> <user_dn_detection> <base_dn>ou=users,dc=example,dc=org</base_dn> <search_filter>(&(objectClass=person)(cn={user_name}))</search_filter> </user_dn_detection> </my_ldap_server> </ldap_servers> ``` When `lookup_bind_dn` is empty the forced lookup is a no-op for that server, so existing deployments are unaffected. ### Why not `AlwaysAllowCredentials` The earlier commit on this branch routed the lookup through `IAccessStorage::authenticate` with `AlwaysAllowCredentials`. As @ pufit and the LLVM Coverage review flagged, `LDAPAccessStorage::areLDAPCredentialsValidNoLock` short-circuits to `true` for that credential type before any LDAP bind or search; the storage would have materialized a phantom user for any name reachable to a holder of `IMPERSONATE ON *`, and role mappings would have been empty. This redesign fixes both: nonexistent names are rejected at the `user_dn_detection` search, and resolved users get their proper role mapping. ### Reviewer-driven follow-ups * `parseLDAPServer` errors are remembered keyed by server name. `findLDAPUser` rethrows the saved error so a misconfigured server (e.g. `lookup_bind_dn` set without `user_dn_detection`) surfaces as a query-time `BAD_ARGUMENTS` instead of degrading to `UNKNOWN_USER`. Per @ tiandiwonder. * `LDAPAccessStorage::findImpl(..., force_external_lookup=true)` refreshes a cached entry whose `users_external_roles[name]` is shorter than `role_search_params`. This catches the cache-poisoning shape that distributed `EXECUTE AS` over an interserver `<secret>` cluster otherwise produces: the `AlwaysAllowCredentials` short-circuit on the receiving shard materializes the user with empty role mapping, and a subsequent local `EXECUTE AS` on that shard otherwise inherits only the common roles. Per @ tiandiwonder. * `findLDAPUser` re-validates the server and `params_hash` after the LDAP round-trip, mirroring the existing post-check in `checkLDAPCredentials`, so a concurrent `SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG` cannot publish a result against stale lookup semantics. * `parseLDAPServer` rejects an empty `lookup_password` when `lookup_bind_dn` is set, blocking the LDAP unauthenticated simple bind path. ### Tests `tests/integration/test_ldap_execute_as/` covers eleven cases: * `test_execute_as_ldap_user_without_prior_login` -- the issue reproducer; fails on master, passes here. * `test_execute_as_ldap_user_after_login_still_works` -- regression coverage for the previously-working path. * `test_execute_as_requires_impersonate_grant` -- the `IMPERSONATE` access check still fires before any LDAP work. * `test_execute_as_unknown_ldap_user_throws` -- proves a nonexistent LDAP name returns `UNKNOWN_USER` instead of being silently materialized. * `test_execute_as_ldap_user_with_role_mapping_without_prior_login` -- the forced-lookup path applies role mapping. * `test_execute_as_local_user_takes_precedence_over_ldap` -- two-pass lookup keeps a local user from being shadowed by the forced LDAP lookup on a global normal-lookup miss. * `test_execute_as_already_materialized_ldap_user_when_ldap_first` -- when the LDAP storage is ordered first AND already has the same name cached, pass 1 returns the LDAP entry. Pins the resolution order; matches pre-PR `getID<User>` behavior. * `test_execute_as_misconfigured_lookup_throws_config_error` -- a misconfigured LDAP server surfaces a query-time error instead of `UNKNOWN_USER`. * `test_execute_as_role_mapping_user_dn_filter` -- AD-style `{user_dn}` substitution through the forced lookup. * `test_execute_as_refreshes_distributed_cache_poisoned_entry` -- two-shard cluster with `<secret>`. After a remote query under `EXECUTE AS` poisons shard2's cache via `AlwaysAllowCredentials`, a local `EXECUTE AS` on shard2 still receives the mapped role. * `test_execute_as_wrong_lookup_password_throws_ldap_error` -- invalid service-bind credentials surface as an LDAP error, not `UNKNOWN_USER`. Local run: 11/11 passed. The cache-poisoning test was verified to fail on a binary built without the refresh logic in `InterpreterExecuteAsQuery::resolveImpersonationTargetUser` (confirms both directions). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `EXECUTE AS <user>` failing with `UNKNOWN_USER` for users from an LDAP user directory that had not yet authenticated against the server since the last restart. The LDAP server definition now accepts optional `lookup_bind_dn` and `lookup_password` for the service account used by `EXECUTE AS` to resolve the target user without the user's own password; `user_dn_detection` is required when the new fields are set. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Parquet: map TIME logical type to Time64
signals.text: The native Parquet reader currently maps both `logical.TIMESTAMP` and `logical.TIME` (and the deprecated converted types `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`/`TIMESTAMP_MICROS`/`TIME_MILLIS`/`TIME_MICROS`) to `DataTypeDateTime64`. That was fine before ClickHouse 25.6, when there was no time-of-day type, but it now produces the Parquet analogue of #104038: when the target column is `Time64` and `session_timezone` is non-UTC, the `DateTime64 -> Time64` cast (PR #90310) shifts the value by the timezone — silent data corruption for a value that has no date/timezone to begin with. This PR splits the schema-converter branch so that: - `logical.TIME` / `TIME_MILLIS` / `TIME_MICROS` → `DataTypeTime64(scale)` (timezone-unaware). - `logical.TIMESTAMP` → `DataTypeDateTime64(scale, timezone)` (unchanged). It also extends `is_output_type_decimal` to recognize `Time64` so min/max stats stay enabled when the output column is `Time64`, and removes the stale comment that claimed ClickHouse has no time-of-day type. While covering explicit type hints in the test (`SELECT * FROM file(..., 'Parquet', 't Time')`), I hit a second pre-existing gap from 25.6: `Time64 -> Time` was never registered as a cast — it threw `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` because `IsDataTypeNumber<DataTypeTime>` is `false` (it inherits `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>`, not `DataTypeNumber<Int32>`). Before this PR the path went `DateTime64 -> Time` and returned a wrong, timezone-shifted value; after the Parquet fix it would have thrown. The second commit adds an inline `Time64 -> Time` branch in `ConvertImpl` that divides by the scale multiplier — no timezone offset, because both Time64 and Time are timezone-unaware seconds-of-day. A new stateless test `04277_parquet_time_of_day` covers: - Schema-less inference (Parquet `time32[ms]`/`time64[us]`/`time64[ns]` → `Nullable(Time64(3/6/9))`; `TIMESTAMP` stays `Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC'))`). - Import into `Time64(scale)` columns under `session_timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai'` (values must not shift). - Explicit type hints under non-UTC session: `Time64(3)` / `Time` / `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')` / `Int64`. Review follow-up: making `Time64 -> DateTime` legal also exposed that `ToDateTimeMonotonicity` treated `Time64` sources as monotonic, while the cast wraps negative time-of-day values with the default `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'ignore'` (`-00:00:01` -> `2106-02-07 06:28:15`), i.e. it drops at zero. `toDateTime` now reports non-monotonic for `Time`/`Time64` sources; the regression test `04828_time64_to_datetime_not_monotonic` shows that without the guard the key condition prunes every granule and range/point queries over a `Time64` key silently return empty results. The Parquet docs (`docs/reference/formats/Parquet/Parquet.mdx`) are updated for the new `TIME` -> `Time64` mapping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Parquet `time32`/`time64` columns being read as `DateTime64` and then silently shifted by `session_timezone` when inserted into a `Time64` target column. Parquet `TIME` logical types now map directly to `Time64`, and a previously-missing `Time64 -> Time` cast is added. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106019&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106019](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106019+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix SummingMergeTree FINAL dropping rows when column pruning hides non-zero summing columns
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106125 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `SELECT FINAL` on a `SummingMergeTree` table silently dropping a physically-present row when column pruning narrowed the read set to a subset of the summing columns and the only visible summing column was zero for that row. The "drop the group's row when all summing columns are zero" rule is now evaluated over the full set of physical summing columns from the table metadata, matching real on-disk merge semantics. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Description `SELECT FINAL` on a `SummingMergeTree` could silently drop a physically-present row when column pruning narrowed the read set to a strict subset of the summing columns and the only visible summing column was `0` for that row. A real on-disk merge keeps the row because another (pruned) summing column has a non-zero value. Root cause: `SummingSortedAlgorithm` applies a "drop the group's row if all summing columns are zero" rule over the summing columns present in its input header. That header is the table sample block, i.e. every physical column (ordinary plus materialized). `ReadFromMergeTree` already pins `sign_column` / `version_column` / `is_deleted_column` for `Collapsing` / `Replacing` / `VersionedCollapsing` so those algorithms see complete row state under `FINAL`; the `Summing` branch was missing the same treatment. The same gap existed in `getColumnsRequiredForMergingFinal`, used by the `removeUnusedColumns` query-plan optimization. Both read-set paths now share one helper that mirrors `SummingSortedAlgorithm::defineColumns`' membership exactly, so the on-the-fly `FINAL` path and a real merge keep/drop the same rows: - All physical columns via `getAllPhysical()`, so a materialized non-key numeric column is preserved. (An earlier revision used `getOrdinary()`, which omits materialized columns and could still drop a row whose only non-zero value lives in one.) - An explicit `columns_to_sum` entry that names a `Nested` table, e.g. `SummingMergeTree(SomeMap)` whose stored columns are `SomeMap.ID` / `SomeMap.Num`, is expanded to its physical subcolumns the way the engine matches `columns_to_sum`. A `*Map` Nested member is kept regardless of `columns_to_sum`, because the algorithm discovers and sums maps independently of the scalar `columns_to_sum` filter. - A non-summable scalar (e.g. a `String` column) is pruned: the algorithm copies it last-value and it never affects the zero-row decision, so it is not read from disk. - With `allow_tuple_element_aggregation`, the algorithm flattens `Tuple` columns (`Nested::flattenTupleRecursive`) and sums the leaves, so a `Tuple` column is kept when any flattened leaf is summable. The whole physical column is read, which gives the merge every leaf. The tuple recursion mirrors `defineColumns`' flattened-leaf gates: a `*Map`-suffixed array leaf is a summed-map candidate only when its synthesized parent is a real tuple ancestor and, with an explicit `columns_to_sum`, the leaf or an ancestor is named; otherwise it is copied last-value and not pinned, so an unlisted tuple `*Map` is not over-read. Reproducer from issue #106125: ```sql CREATE TABLE s (c0 UInt32, v_keep Int32, v_zero UInt32) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY c0; INSERT INTO s VALUES (0,1,0),(1,1,1),(2,1,2); INSERT INTO s VALUES (3,1,3),(4,1,4),(5,1,5); SELECT c0 FROM s FINAL WHERE v_zero >= 0 ORDER BY c0; -- before: 1,2,3,4,5 (c0=0 incorrectly dropped) -- after: 0,1,2,3,4,5 ``` Tuple-leaf reproducer (`allow_tuple_element_aggregation`): ```sql CREATE TABLE s (k UInt64, metrics Tuple(a Int64, b Int64)) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS allow_tuple_element_aggregation = 1; INSERT INTO s VALUES (0,(0,1)),(1,(5,5)); INSERT INTO s VALUES (0,(0,0)),(2,(7,7)); SELECT k FROM s FINAL WHERE metrics.a >= 0 ORDER BY k; -- before: 1,2 (k=0 dropped though metrics.b=1) -- after: 0,1,2 ``` Validation: - New stateless test `04301_106125_summing_final_column_pruning_drops_row.sql` covers implicit, explicit, materialized, explicit-Nested-map, explicit-multi-column, non-summable-String, tuple-leaf, nested-tuple and explicit-excluded-tuple cases under `FINAL` with column pruning. It fails on the unfixed binary and passes with the fix. - Existing `SummingMergeTree`, `Coalescing`, `AggregatingMergeTree`, `allow_tuple_element_aggregation` and remove-unused-columns-under-`FINAL` stateless tests pass. - Semantic check: a row whose summing columns are all zero is still dropped by `FINAL`; the fix only restores rows whose full stored form has a non-zero summing column. Verified the on-the-fly `FINAL` result matches a real `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` merge for the tuple case. Closes #106125
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Allow ON CLUSTER `<db_name>` pass-through on Replicated / Shared databases for RENAME and EXCHANGE
signals.text: Closes: #106087 For non-`Replicated` databases, users can run DDL on a cluster via `ON CLUSTER`. `Replicated` and `Shared` databases already propagate DDL across the cluster themselves, so `ON CLUSTER` is redundant when the cluster name in `ON CLUSTER` matches the database's automatic cluster name (the database name itself). Today this only works for `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE`, `UNDROP TABLE`, `TRUNCATE` and `DETACH / ATTACH TABLE` because `maybeRemoveOnCluster` in `executeDDLQueryOnCluster.cpp` requires the AST to derive from `ASTQueryWithTableAndOutput`. `RENAME` and `EXCHANGE TABLES` use `ASTRenameQuery` which derives from `ASTQueryWithOutput`, so the helper bailed out early and the query was sent to the DDL worker, where it then failed inside `DatabaseReplicated::tryEnqueueReplicatedDDL` with `"It's not initial query. ON CLUSTER is not allowed for Replicated database."`. This PR extends `maybeRemoveOnCluster` to handle `ASTRenameQuery`. For `RENAME` and `EXCHANGE TABLES`, every element's `from`/`to` database must be the same database, otherwise the helper conservatively bails out and the original `ON CLUSTER` path runs unchanged. `OPTIMIZE` is intentionally left out. Routing it through the `Replicated` database DDL queue throws `NOT_A_LEADER` on a non-leader initiator, because `DDLWorker` rethrows the initial-task exception instead of handing off to another replica. The existing `executeDDLQueryOnCluster` path already selects a leader correctly for `OPTIMIZE ... ON CLUSTER`, so it is kept unchanged. Behavior matrix on a `Replicated` database `db`: | Query | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | `CREATE TABLE db.t ON CLUSTER db ...` | works | works | | `ALTER TABLE db.t ON CLUSTER db ...` | works | works | | `DROP TABLE db.t ON CLUSTER db` | works | works | | `RENAME TABLE db.x TO db.y ON CLUSTER db` | rejected | works | | `EXCHANGE TABLES db.a AND db.b ON CLUSTER db` | rejected | works | | `RENAME TABLE db.a TO other.b ON CLUSTER db` (cross-database) | rejected | rejected | | `RENAME ... ON CLUSTER 'other_cluster'` | rejected | rejected | | `ignore_on_cluster_for_replicated_database=1` for the above | already worked for some | now works for `RENAME` too | For `Shared` databases (Cloud), the same code path is used via `IDatabase::shouldReplicateQuery`, so the fix extends transparently to them. Motivation: scripts written against non-`Replicated` databases (often with a literal cluster name baked in) can be ported to `Replicated` and to ClickHouse Cloud `Shared` databases without rewriting the `ON CLUSTER` clauses, as long as the cluster name matches the database name. See the SigNoz case referenced in #106087. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow `ON CLUSTER` clause for `RENAME TABLE` and `EXCHANGE TABLES` on a `Replicated` (or `Shared`) database when the cluster name matches the database's automatic cluster name (i.e. the database name itself). The clause is treated as a no-op and the database engine propagates the DDL as usual. This already worked for `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP` and similar queries, and lets scripts written for non-`Replicated` databases be ported to `Replicated` and Cloud `Shared` databases without rewriting `ON CLUSTER` clauses. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Push down volume-reducing functions in query plan
signals.text: Adds a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, so those steps carry the fixed-size result instead of the original `String` / `FixedString` argument. The rewrite is done with `ActionsDAG::split`: the function nodes form the first part, which becomes a new step below the child, and the second part becomes the parent step's `ActionsDAG` and reads the results as inputs. It only fires when the wide argument column really stops flowing through the child step — the column is removed from the child's output, and unless the child reads it itself it is not even produced below the child. `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` and `trySplitFilter` keep the pushed functions where they are, so the optimizations do not move the same nodes in opposite directions. For the shape from the issue below, `SELECT avg(length(s)) FROM test WHERE notEmpty(s)`, the filter still needs `s` to evaluate its condition, but `length(s)` is now computed before the filter, so the wide column is not copied for the surviving rows. Enabled by default; can be turned off with `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions = 0`. An earlier attempt at the same optimization was https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 by @talmawash, credited as a co-author. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82378 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, replacing the wide `String` / `FixedString` argument with the fixed-size result, so it is neither buffered by a sort nor copied by a filter. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions`, enabled by default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106199&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106199](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106199+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix vacuous truth for x op ALL (empty subquery)
signals.text: `x op ALL (empty set)` should return TRUE per SQL standard (vacuous truth). ClickHouse was returning FALSE because the `= ALL` rewrite uses `singleValueOrNull`, which returns NULL for empty sets, making `x IN (NULL) = FALSE` incorrectly. The `min` / `max` rewrites used for the other comparison operators have the same problem, because they return the default value of the type for an empty set. Fixed in `modifyAST` by also selecting `count` from the right-hand side, so the empty case can be recognized. To keep the right-hand side evaluated exactly once - evaluating it twice is observable when it is non-deterministic - `count` and the aggregate are computed by a single `SELECT` returning a tuple, and the two values are taken apart with `tupleElement`: ``` x op ALL (S) --> tupleElement(SQ, 1) = 0 OR x op tupleElement(SQ, 2) where SQ = (SELECT (count(*), aggregate_function(*)) FROM S) ``` Both occurrences of `SQ` are textually identical, and scalar subqueries are cached by the hash of the subquery (`ExecuteScalarSubqueriesVisitor` for the old analyzer, `evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded` for the new one), so `S` is scanned once and both `tupleElement` calls observe the same evaluation. This preserves all existing behavior for a non-empty right-hand side and only fixes the empty-set case. `04759_all_subquery_single_evaluation` is a regression test that fails if the right-hand side is evaluated twice. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105957 ### Changelog category : - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description): Fixed `x op ALL (empty subquery)` incorrectly returning FALSE instead of TRUE (vacuous truth). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106373&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106373](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106373+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Break symlink loops in StorageFile glob expansion
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106676 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `Too many levels of symbolic links` errors and duplicate or missing rows when the `file()` table function expands a recursive glob (`**`) over a directory tree containing a symlink to an ancestor directory. Such a walk is now pruned per (directory, remaining pattern) frame, and matches are deduplicated by resolved parent directory, so a symlinked ancestor neither loops nor yields a file twice while a symlink to a file is still reported under its own name. ### Description Recursive glob expansion in `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingImpl` did not protect against directory symlinks that target an ancestor. `fs::directory_iterator` does not follow symlinks for iteration, but `directory_entry::is_directory` does, so the recursion descended a loop until the kernel hit `ELOOP` and surfaced a raw `std::filesystem::filesystem_error: Too many levels of symbolic links` (`STD_EXCEPTION`). The depth cap added in #106676 does not catch this because the kernel error fires first. The walk now enters each frame at most once, where a frame is the canonical directory together with the pattern still to be matched there. That pair is the whole state of the walk, so a frame repeating it can only redo what another frame already did, whether that is an enclosing frame (a cycle) or a finished sibling (an alias). Keying on the directory alone is wrong, because `**` matches zero levels: the re-application enters the current directory with a shorter suffix while the enclosing frame is still there, and directory-only keying dropped it, so `file('root/*/**/top.txt')` with `root/x/back -> ..` returned 0 rows instead of 1. Because a `**` walk can now reach one file through two frames, its match deduplication resolves the parent directory of each match; lexical forms do not resolve symlinks. The final component is deliberately left as written, so a symlink to a file and its target stay two rows, which is what the pattern selected. This is scoped to `**` expansions, since a finite glob can also name one file twice through two ancestor aliases sharing a filename, and master reports both. Deduplication only filters results, so it cannot stop the walk re-descending; a dense graph of aliased directories previously returned 109600 rows for eight real files, and now returns 8. `04325_test_storage_file_glob_symlink_loop` covers the loop, aliasing, finite-glob and write-refusal shapes above; each assertion is mutation-tested. <details> <summary>Canonicalization cost on large symlink-free trees</summary> Deduplicating by canonical path needs the canonical parent of each match. Every entry one invocation emits shares that parent, so a glob suffix resolves once per directory rather than once per file. A purely finite glob resolves nothing. Counting `readlink` against master: | pattern, tree | master | here | rows | |---|---|---|---| | `**/*.tsv`, 20 000 files in one directory | 26 | 34 | 20 000 | | `**/*.tsv`, 10 000 files in 100 dirs at depth 3 | 26 | 1 702 | 10 000 | | `**/file.txt`, 251 files in 500 dirs | 4 033 | 7 038 | 251 | A literal suffix costs more: the globstar frame resolves its directory, then applies the suffix in a fresh call that resolves the match's own parent, which for a multi-component suffix is a deeper directory. Both are bounded by directories walked, not by rows. Latency on the 10 000-file tree is 329 ms against 417 ms. Pruning cost on dense alias graphs, where every one of N sibling directories links to every other and none links to an ancestor: | aliases | frames remembered while descending only | frames remembered once walked | |---|---|---| | 6 | 0.46 s | 0.10 s | | 8 | 30.2 s | 0.10 s | | 10 | over 700 s | 0.11 s | </details>

signals.title: Fix signed integer overflow in condition_variable::wait_for with huge timeouts
signals.text: A wait-timeout setting that reaches `std::condition_variable::wait_for` unchecked overflows the chrono conversion inside it. libc++ evaluates `wait_for(d)` as `steady_clock::now() + d` in nanoseconds, multiplying a millisecond duration by 1000000: a timeout above ~9.2e12 ms overflows Int64, and one above the Int64 millisecond range even turns into a negative duration, so the wait returns at once and the caller busy-loops instead of waiting. UBSan aborts the server; a release build silently wraps. The setting that reaches it in practice is `interactive_delay`, a plain unbounded `UInt64` of microseconds: the server waits `interactive_delay / 1000` milliseconds for the next result chunk in `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::popImpl`, through the lazy output format, on both the `TCPHandler` and the `clickhouse-local` path. Found by serverfuzz on master, and again in the stress test of an unrelated pull request — https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112177&sha=e601607e228ad5d736ad491220ebf4b62d531d51&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112177): ``` /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__chrono/duration.h:93:79: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 18584892780430 * 1000000 cannot be represented in type '_Ct' (aka 'long long') ... #6 ConcurrentBoundedQueue<DB::Chunk>::popImpl<true>(...) src/Common/ConcurrentBoundedQueue.h:73 #8 DB::LazyOutputFormat::getChunk(unsigned long) src/Processors/Formats/LazyOutputFormat.cpp:25 #11 DB::TCPHandler::processOrdinaryQuery(DB::QueryState&) src/Server/TCPHandler.cpp:1540 SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior ``` Reproduces deterministically: ``` clickhouse-local --query "SELECT 1 SETTINGS interactive_delay = 100000000000000000" ``` Fix: clamp the timeout to one year before constructing the chrono duration, via a small shared helper `saturatedMilliseconds`. The same cap is already used for `CancellationChecker` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96450); it is applied here to the remaining `wait_for` sites that take a user-controlled millisecond timeout, and `saturatedSeconds`/`saturatedSecondsFrom` cover the seconds-typed timeouts and the query cache expiry built as `now() + seconds(query_cache_ttl)`. A `Milliseconds`- or `Seconds`-typed setting can no longer carry such a value in the first place: `SettingFieldTimespan` rejects a value that does not fit into Int64 microseconds, so the clamp there is only defence in depth. That check landed on master after this branch was cut and supersedes the saturating conversion this pull request originally added to `SettingsFields`, which is dropped along with its unit tests in favour of master's stricter ones. What is left for the clamp is every setting that is not a timespan — above all `interactive_delay`. Keeper has its own coordination waits with a different bound; they are handled separately in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112088. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112088 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112177 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a signed integer overflow when a wait-timeout setting, such as `interactive_delay`, was set to a huge value: the wait could time out immediately instead of waiting, and the server could abort under the Undefined Behavior Sanitizer.

signals.title: Fix crash on skip index over a column with pending ALTER MODIFY COLUMN type change
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112213 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112484 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception ("Sizes of nested column and null map ... are not equal after deserialization") when querying a table with a skip index over a column that has a pending `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN` type change while `apply_mutations_on_fly` and `apply_patch_parts` are both disabled. ### Description A pending `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` leaves old parts with skip-index data serialized using the old column type. `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::canUseIndex` skips such an index for a part by checking the column against `AlterConversions::getAllUpdatedColumns()`, populated from the read snapshot's `READ_COLUMN` mutations. `createStorageSnapshot` built that snapshot with `need_alter_mutations = apply_mutations_on_fly || apply_patch_parts`. With both off the pending mutation is dropped, the incompatible index is not excluded, and `filterMarksUsingIndex` deserializes an old granule with the new type. For `String` to `Nullable(UInt64)` that raises `Sizes of nested column and null map of Nullable column are not equal after deserialization` (an exception in release builds; debug and sanitizer builds abort). The implicit `count()` projection reaches the index read during planning, so a plain `SELECT count()` is enough. Neither setting relates to column type changes, so the snapshot now requests alter mutations whenever one is pending. The request is `need_alter_mutations_if_pending`, resolved against `num_alter` inside `getMutationsSnapshot`, which already holds the lock guarding the counters and already reads them for its fast-path condition. A read with no pending alter still returns the empty snapshot without scanning `current_mutations_by_version`, and adds no lock acquisition. Column data reads were already correct: `IMergeTreeReader` converts from the part's own stored type. The `supportsSkipIndexesOnDataRead` guard covers the data-read phase but not this planning-time path; both are pinned by the tests. Found by serverfuzz running `03702_alter_column_modify_secondary_index_rebuild.sh`. Repro: ```sql CREATE TABLE tg (id UInt64, value String, INDEX idx_set (value) TYPE set(0) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY id PARTITION BY id SETTINGS add_minmax_index_for_numeric_columns = 0, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO tg VALUES (1, '10'), (2, '20'), (3, '300'); SYSTEM STOP MERGES tg; ALTER TABLE tg MODIFY COLUMN value Nullable(UInt64) SETTINGS alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0; SELECT count() FROM tg WHERE value = 300 SETTINGS apply_mutations_on_fly = 0, apply_patch_parts = 0; ``` Related: #112213 (this fixes the pending-mutation half; the killed-mutation half is #112484).

signals.title: Retry tests on the "Coordination error:" rendering of transient Keeper errors
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/80416 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The functional test runner (`tests/clickhouse-test`) retries a test when its output matches an entry in `MESSAGES_TO_RETRY`. The two transient-Keeper entries only match the socket-layer rendering `Coordination::Exception: Session expired` / `Coordination::Exception: Connection loss`. Generic Keeper operations (`exists`/`get`/`getChildren`) throw via the `Coordination::Exception(code)` / `fromPath(code, path)` constructors, which format the message as `"Coordination error: {}"`. The client then prints: ``` Code: 999. Coordination::Exception: Coordination error: Session expired, path /zookeeper/.../replicas/1/is_active. (KEEPER_EXCEPTION) ``` That string is not a substring of the existing retry entries, so the runner never retried it and the test failed instead. This is the OPTIMIZE wait path in `StorageReplicatedMergeTree` (`tryWaitForReplicaToProcessLogEntry` -> `getZooKeeper()->exists(.../is_active)`), which surfaced as a flaky failure of `03100_lwu_29_concurrent_merges` on amd_tsan during `OPTIMIZE TABLE` (reported on #80416). The same `Coordination error:` rendering also hit `test_drop_database_replica` and `test_distributed_ddl_parallel`. Fix: add the `Coordination error: ...` variants so both renderings are retried. The existing entries are kept so the socket-layer rendering stays covered. No test reference file contains these strings, so there is no false-positive risk.

signals.title: Do not connect to MySQL during startup metadata loading
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed slow server startup when a `MySQL` database engine points at a host that black-holes the connection. The MySQL database engine no longer connects to the server during startup metadata loading; tables are fetched lazily on first access, matching the `PostgreSQL` database engine. ### Description `DatabaseMySQL` connected to the MySQL server synchronously in its constructor (`empty()` -> `fetchTablesIntoLocalCache()`). The constructor runs during startup metadata loading and on `ATTACH DATABASE`, both of which happen before the server binds its listen ports. A `MySQL` database engine pointing at a host that drops connection attempts (so the connect blocks until timeout, rather than failing fast) then stalls startup for `connect_timeout * connection_max_tries` before the ports come up. `DatabasePostgreSQL` already does the right thing: its constructor does not connect, and tables are fetched lazily on access. This change makes `DatabaseMySQL` match by skipping the constructor connect when `attach` is true (server startup / `ATTACH DATABASE`). Tables are still fetched lazily by every accessor (`empty` / `getTablesIterator` / `tryGetTable`), so behavior on access is unchanged. The non-attach `CREATE DATABASE` path keeps its original probe and error semantics. The integration test in this PR (`test_restart_server_with_unreachable_mysql`) demonstrates the behavior: with the host partitioned away, without this change the server does not come up within the start window; with it, the server starts and the database is fetched lazily on first access.

signals.title: Fix minmax skip index and partition pruning skipping NaN under negated float ranges
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106533 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106948 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110266 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106568 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a `MergeTree` query filters a `Float`/`Nullable(Float)` column with a negated comparison range such as `NOT ((val >= a) AND (val <= b))`. Partition pruning and the `minmax` skip index previously dropped partitions or granules containing `NaN`, even though `NaN` rows satisfy the negated predicate (since `NaN >= a` is false). Regression since v26.3. ### Description Supersedes #106568, which fixed only the partition-pruning half of #106533, and fixes the skip-index half (#106948). One root cause: range analysis over floats ignores `NaN` under a negated comparison. **1. `KeyCondition` negation rewrite (#106533).** `cloneDAGWithInversionPushDown` rewrites `not(greater(x, c))` into `lessOrEquals(x, c)`. That is invalid when an operand can be `NaN`: `not(NaN > c)` is true while `NaN <= c` is false, so pruning dropped the partition holding the `NaN`. The rewrite is now skipped for the six comparison ops when an operand is a non-constant float column or a `NaN` constant. Finite constants and non-float types are unaffected. **2. `minmax` loses `NaN` in mixed granules (#106948).** Granule extremes come from `getExtremes`, which skips `NaN`, so `[1.0, nan, 3.0]` stored a clean `[1, 3]`. Since `NaN` sorts after `+inf`, the true upper bound is `NaN`: it is now stored as the max, tripping the `NaN` guard in `checkInHyperrectangle`. Widening a range only causes conservative keeps, never wrong skips, so positive-range pruning is intact. Covers the skip index and the part-level minmax. **3. Single-sided comparison (#110266).** Same cause for `NOT(f > c)` over an all-`NaN` granule; fix 1 covers it and `04327` asserts it. **Upgrade behavior.** Both fixes are on the write path, and neither on-disk format (`.idx2`, `minmax_<col>.idx`) carries a version marker, so a reader cannot tell a pre-fix granule from a good one. Parts written before the upgrade keep the old result until rewritten via `ALTER TABLE ... REWRITE PARTS`. `MATERIALIZE INDEX` does **not** help (the mutation hardlinks an index file already present); `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` repairs skip indexes but not the part-level minmax, which a non-row-reducing merge unions from its sources. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106533 Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106948 Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110266 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107074&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107074](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107074+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not leak a correlated subquery's `TOTALS` into the outer query
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106920 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a spurious `TOTALS` block returned for a non-aggregate `SELECT` whose `WHERE` contains a correlated subquery using `GROUP BY ... WITH TOTALS`. The subquery's totals are no longer propagated as the outer query's totals. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106920 A non-aggregate `SELECT` returned an extra totals row when its `WHERE` contained a correlated scalar or `EXISTS` subquery producing a totals stream: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32, val Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, number * 7 FROM numbers(3); SELECT id FROM t WHERE id >= (SELECT 0 GROUP BY 1 WITH TOTALS HAVING isNull(val) = 0); -- returned 0, 1, 2 and then a spurious totals row ``` **Root cause.** A subquery's totals are not part of the value it returns; the non-correlated scalar evaluator consumes data chunks only. Decorrelation replaces the subquery with a `JOIN`, and `joinPipelinesRightLeft` propagates totals from whichever input has them. **The change.** `buildLogicalJoin` is the only place where the join's two inputs are unambiguous, so it records there which input carries the subquery (after the `correlated_subqueries_default_join_kind` swap, so one expression covers both values). `JoinStep::updatePipeline` drops that input's totals and extremes at the top, before the `swap_streams` swap and before algorithm dispatch, the only point where the pipelines still match the step's declared inputs. Only the carrier input is touched, so a legitimate totals stream on the other input still propagates (guarded by `03808_correlated_subquery_with_totals`). That side is only meaningful while the join has two inputs, so the existing swap-only `query_graph_size_limit = 2` clamp is extended to cover it, and the side is re-derived after reconstruction, reversing it when the optimizer flips the children. **Validation.** New test `04327_correlated_subquery_with_totals`, 26 assertions covering scalar and `EXISTS`, nested totals, both values of `correlated_subqueries_default_join_kind` and `correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer`, an aggregating outer query, `extremes = 1`, `WITH ROLLUP`, a cached subquery, a distributed plan. Fails on master, passes here, 50 randomized runs green. The existing correlated suite shows no reference churn: the only `.reference` this PR changes is the new one. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107075&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107075](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107075+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix mapKeys bloom_filter index over-pruning for FixedString default equality
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106924 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong query results and spurious errors when a `bloom_filter` index on `mapKeys(map)` or `mapValues(map)` is used with a `map[key] = const` comparison. Index analysis compared the constant against the wrong default and hashed it without converting it to the indexed type, so `map[k] = toFixedString('', N)` returned no rows, a `mapValues` index dropped a matching granule for a constant storing a different representation of the indexed string type, and a valid predicate such as `map[k] = 1.0` over a `Map(String, UInt64)` failed with `BAD_GET`. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106924 Three defects in `MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter::traverseTreeEquals`, all reachable from `map[key] = const`. **1. The absent-key default was compared against the wrong type.** An absent key makes `map[key]` return the map value type default, so a granule lacking the key still matches when `default = const`. The check compared the constant byte-wise against the *constant's* own type default: for `toFixedString('', 3)` that is 3 NUL bytes against an empty `String`, so every granule without the key was pruned although `'' = toFixedString('', 3)` is true at runtime. The real `equals` now runs on a default column of the map value type. A NULL result is not a match, so a `Nullable` value type stays prunable. **2. `mapValues` hashed a constant storing a different representation.** Equality ignores trailing NUL padding, and an `Enum` constant carries its number while equality compares the name, so one constant can equal several stored values or hash to what none of them produces, dropping a matching granule. The index is now used only when the constant's primitive type equals the indexed string type. Wrappers are ignored, since a `LowCardinality(String)` constant stores the same `String`. **3. `mapValues` hashed the raw constant.** `hashWithField` reads the `Field` via `Field::safeGet`, which tolerates only `UInt64 <-> Int64`, so any other constant type threw `BAD_GET` and failed a valid query. It is converted first, as the ordinary column path and the sibling `mapContainsValue` and `IN` paths already did, and the index is declined when the constant is not representable. A resource limit, stack overflow, cancellation or internal error still reaches the caller rather than quietly disabling the index. The test asserts both directions per case: granules-read < granules-total where pruning must survive, `INDEX_NOT_USED` where it must decline. <details> <summary>Measured carriers</summary> `BAD_GET` on a valid predicate (defect 3), all on master before this change: | indexed `mapValues` type | constant type | |---|---| | `UInt64` | `Float64`, `Int128`, `Decimal64` | | `Float64` | `UInt64` | | `Date`, `Enum8` | `String` | | `Int128` | `Int64` | A matching granule dropped (defect 2), against an indexed `String`: a `FixedString` of a different width, `Enum8`, `LowCardinality(FixedString(3))`, `Variant(FixedString(3), UInt64)`. The last two also predate this PR. A resource limit, a stack overflow, a cancellation or an internal error is not a statement about the constant, so it still reaches the caller rather than quietly disabling the index. `mapKeys` needs no conversion, since `arrayElement` resolves the key constant to the map key type first. Heterogeneous integers were already sound: both signednesses share one `Field` slot and `getNumberTypeHash` casts to the indexed type. </details>

signals.title: Do not terminate the server on retryable errors while loading outdated parts
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106736 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Do not terminate the server when a transient retryable error (such as `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` or a network error) occurs while loading outdated or unexpected data parts in the background. Such errors are not a sign of an inconsistent on-disk set of parts, so the loading task is now retried instead of aborting the whole server. The existing fail-fast behaviour is preserved for genuinely inconsistent state. ### Description Closes #106736 `MergeTreeData::loadOutdatedDataParts()` and the sibling `loadUnexpectedDataParts()` wrap their whole body in a `catch (...)` that calls `std::terminate()`, to fail fast on a genuinely inconsistent on-disk set of parts. The same `catch` also fires for transient runtime errors such as `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (including the stress test memory fault injector) or network errors, which are not on-disk corruption. This takes the whole server down in the experimental `serverfuzz` stress jobs. `loadDataPartWithRetries()` already classifies and retries such exceptions via `isRetryableException()`, but only around `loadDataPart()` itself; an exception thrown elsewhere in the loader (part removal, ZooKeeper cleanup, rename, the runner machinery, or newly memory-tracked allocations) escapes straight to the terminating `catch`. The fix reuses `isRetryableException()` in both `catch` blocks: for a retryable error in the asynchronous background loader, it logs a warning and reschedules the loading task instead of terminating, so the server stays up and retries once the transient condition clears. Non-retryable errors and the synchronous drop-table path keep the existing fail-fast behaviour. The unexpected-parts loop is made idempotent so a rescheduled retry skips already-loaded parts. A `REGULAR` failpoint `mergetree_load_outdated_parts_inject_retryable_exception` and an integration test (`test_load_outdated_parts_retryable`) inject a retryable error into the outdated-parts loader and verify the server survives and finishes loading. The retry must not requeue a part whose retryable error happened after it was already published. `loadDataPartWithRetries()` inserts a normal Outdated part into `data_parts_indexes` before its post-load cleanup (`preparePartForRemoval` writes the removal TID and can throw retryably); requeueing it as-is made the retry reload the same directory as a fresh part, hit the duplicate-part path, and `remove()` could delete the directory while the published part still referenced it. The published part is now rolled back out of the index before requeueing so the retry reloads it cleanly. The unexpected-parts loop has the same shape (its optional `broken-on-start` detach runs after the part is set), so it now uses a separate `finished` marker set only after the detach succeeds. Two more failpoints exercise these post-load paths and the integration test gains a third case asserting nothing is wrongly detached. The broken-part detach in both loaders no longer hides its errors. It used to call `renameToDetached("broken-on-start", /*ignore_error=*/ replicated)`, and `renameToDetached` swallows `ErrnoException` and `fs::filesystem_error` when `ignore_error` is set - exactly the exception types a failing rename raises, and exactly the class `isRetryableException` treats as transient. On a replicated table a transient detach failure therefore never reached the new classification: the worker continued as if the cleanup had succeeded, leaving the broken outdated part on its original path with its ZooKeeper entry already removed, or setting the unexpected part's `finished` marker so the retry skipped it. Both call sites now pass `ignore_error = false` and classify the error themselves; the tolerance `ignore_error` gave replicated tables is preserved, but only for a permanent failure and only after the retryable case has been handled. A failpoint that throws the swallowed exception type and a regression case per loader cover it. #### Provenance Surfaced on master as the `'px != 0' failed` family whose actual fatal is the `loadOutdatedDataParts` terminate. Latest master hit: `Stress test (experimental, serverfuzz, arm_release)`, commit `81a8bcef7e8ba2dae3dfdc762dde87a853f40070`, STID 3782-2f00. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=81a8bcef7e8ba2dae3dfdc762dde87a853f40070&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28experimental%2C%20serverfuzz%2C%20arm_release%29

signals.title: Support group_by_use_nulls in WITH TOTALS
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39574 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `GROUP BY ... WITH TOTALS` now respects the `group_by_use_nulls` setting when the analyzer is enabled (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default): the GROUP BY keys in the TOTALS summary row are reported as `NULL` instead of their default values, consistent with `GROUPING SETS`, `ROLLUP` and `CUBE`. Keys whose types cannot be wrapped in `Nullable` (for example `Array` or `Map`) keep their default value. With the old query analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 0`) the keys keep their default value as before. ### Description Rebase and port of #39574 (original author @ novikd) on top of current master. With `group_by_use_nulls = 1`, GROUP BY keys are already reported as `Nullable` for `GROUPING SETS`, `ROLLUP` and `CUBE`, but plain `GROUP BY ... WITH TOTALS` was left out: the keys stayed non-nullable and the TOTALS summary row showed `0` (the default value) instead of `NULL`. The original PR fixed this in the old interpreter by converting the keys inside `AggregatingStep`. The analyzer is now the default, so this ports the fix to the analyzer planner: - `PlannerExpressionAnalysis`: include `WITH TOTALS` in the `group_by_use_nulls` condition so the result type of the keys is analyzed as `Nullable`. - `Planner`: insert a `toNullable` conversion for the GROUP BY keys right before the `TotalsHaving` step. The TOTALS row is filled from default values, so a `Nullable` key column yields `NULL` there. This also covers `CUBE`/`ROLLUP WITH TOTALS`, whose own nullable conversion happens after `TotalsHaving` and would otherwise leave the TOTALS row non-NULL. Keys that cannot be made `Nullable` are skipped. Example (before this change the last row was `0`): ```sql SELECT number FROM numbers(10) GROUP BY number WITH TOTALS ORDER BY number SETTINGS group_by_use_nulls = 1; -- 0 .. 9 -- -- \N ``` The behavior is analyzer-only, so the affected tests set `enable_analyzer = 1`, and the documentation/changelog qualify the behavior as applying only with the analyzer. Updated tests: `02343_group_by_use_nulls`, `02535_analyzer_group_by_use_nulls`, `03912_tuple_comparison_group_by_use_nulls`, and the new `02373_group_by_use_nulls_with_totals` (from the original PR).
