signals.title: Enable fractional RANGE OFFSET for Decimal ORDER BY columns
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/56101 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow fractional offsets in a `RANGE` window frame when the `ORDER BY` column is a `Decimal`. For example, subsecond `RANGE` frames over a `DateTime64` cast to `Decimal64(3)`: `range between 0.5 preceding and 0.5 following`. Fractional `RANGE` offsets are standard SQL. ### Description Continuation of #56101 (original author @garcher22, who asked us to carry it forward). Rebased onto current master and addressing the reviewer feedback that had stalled the original PR. Fractional offsets in a `RANGE` window frame were disabled for `Decimal` `ORDER BY` columns. This PR re-enables them, which lets users look at rows within a fractional distance of the current row when ordering by e.g. a subsecond timestamp cast to `Decimal64(3)`. What changed: - `QueryAnalyzer` / `WindowDescription`: accept non-native-integer numeric (Decimal) frame offsets. The integer bound check still applies to `ROWS` and `GROUPS` frames; `RANGE` offsets are coerced to the `ORDER BY` column type and validated in the window transform. - `WindowTransform`: register `ColumnDecimal<Decimal32/64>` comparators and use `NativeType<>` for the offset cast so the `DecimalField` is unwrapped to its underlying integer. - Reject a NaN `RANGE` offset explicitly in the transform constructor. The original PR relied on comparison-visitor semantics for this, which @alexey-milovidov objected to (it made the shared `FieldAccurateComparison` visitors inconsistent). Checking NaN locally keeps those shared visitors untouched and fixes an abort: with the shared-visitor change reverted, a NaN offset slipped past validation and hit `chassert(offset >= 0)` downstream (this is the `02833_window_func_range_offset` failure on the original PR). Tests: `02892_decimal_window_fractional_range` (new, the feature), and `02833_window_func_range_offset` updated (`0.0` offset is now valid; NaN still rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`).

signals.title: Reset adopted part level to 0 on ATTACH PART/PARTITION for non-Ordinary engines
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109674 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109674 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `SELECT ... FINAL` and `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` returning duplicate rows after `ALTER TABLE ... ATTACH PART`/`ATTACH PARTITION` (and `FETCH PART`, restore from backup) adopted a merged part with duplicate sorting keys into a `ReplacingMergeTree`, `SummingMergeTree`, `AggregatingMergeTree` (or other `FINAL`-relying engine). The adopted part's merge level is now reset to 0 so the destination deduplicates/collapses it on the next merge and during `FINAL`. ### Description A part attached from `detached/` (via `ALTER TABLE ... ATTACH PART`/`ATTACH PARTITION`, `FETCH PART`, or restore from backup) has unknown provenance. Since commit `20e5dfc789f` the ATTACH path kept such a part's merge level clamped to 1 for non-Ordinary engines. But a level greater than 0 does not guarantee unique/collapsed ORDER BY keys when the part was merged elsewhere (for example a plain `MergeTree`, which does not collapse rows on merge). `SELECT ... FINAL`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` and the `PartsSplitter` FINAL optimization treat a lone level greater than 0 part as already merged and skip the row-collapsing transform, so duplicate keys survived `FINAL` on `ReplacingMergeTree`/`SummingMergeTree`/`AggregatingMergeTree`/`VersionedCollapsingMergeTree`/`GraphiteMergeTree`/`CoalescingMergeTree`, returning wrong results silently. The fix resets the adopted part's level to 0 at both part-adoption sites: `StorageMergeTree::fillNewPartNameAndResetLevel` (ATTACH PART/PARTITION) and `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink::writeExistingPart` (replicated ATTACH and restore). The destination then re-merges the part under its own semantics. This restores the pre-`20e5dfc` behavior for these paths. The cross-table adoption path (`getLevelForAdoptedPart`) is unaffected: it already has a `hasSameMergeSemantics` uniqueness check and keeps its own level logic. This implements the approach requested by @ den-crane in the issue (mirroring PR #107481, which fixed the cross-engine CLONE/ATTACH-PARTITION-FROM/MOVE path). Test `03283_optimize_on_insert_level` asserted the old level-1 outcome after a same-table DETACH/ATTACH round-trip; that assertion encoded the bug, so its reference is updated to level 0. Reproduction (returns 3 with the fix, returned 6 before): ```sql CREATE TABLE src (a UInt32, b UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO src VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,30),(2,40),(3,50),(3,60); OPTIMIZE TABLE src FINAL; -- produces a lone level-1 part with duplicate keys CREATE TABLE dst (a UInt32, b UInt32) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY a; -- copy src's part directory into dst's detached/ folder, then: ALTER TABLE dst ATTACH PART 'all_1_1_1'; SELECT count() FROM dst FINAL; -- 3 (was 6) ```

signals.title: Preserve execution limits and resources in derived QueryPlans
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Preserve execution limits and resource lifetimes when deriving `QueryPlan` instances for internal query execution. ### Description The non-destructive in-place set-build fix from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 is already on `master`; this follow-up fixes the remaining `QueryPlan` propagation and lifetime invariants. `QueryPlan::clone` and `QueryPlan::extractSubplan` previously copied or moved only the node tree. The derived plan consequently lost its `max_threads`, `concurrency_control`, and `QueryPlanResourceHolder` state. `QueryPlan::unitePlans` also discarded `concurrency_control` when joining child plans. This change preserves those plan-level execution caps and shared resource handles, and adds focused unit coverage for `clone`, `extractSubplan`, and both child orders of `unitePlans`. The HTTP `make_distributed_plan` set-build behavior described in the remaining review thread is intentionally out of scope: it is a pre-existing `QueryPlan::convertToDistributed` boundary unrelated to this follow-up, and the native protocol re-applies concurrency control after pipeline construction. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109722&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109722](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109722+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Retry reference-binary download in bugfix validation
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105139 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The `Bugfix validation (functional tests)` job downloads the master reference ClickHouse binary via a single `wget ... strict=True` with no retry (`ci/jobs/functional_tests.py`). A transient S3 5xx (e.g. `ERROR 503: Service Unavailable`, wget exit code 8) aborts the whole job before any test runs. This is a broad transient class that reddens finish ledgers across unrelated PRs; the `aarch64` variant passing on the same head while `amd64` errors on the download is the tell that it is not code-related. Fix: use praktika's native `Shell.run` retry (`retries=5`, exponential backoff, 1s->2s->4s->... capped at 60s) around the reference-binary `wget`. It stays `strict`, so a persistently-missing artifact still fails closed and errors clearly after all attempts. Download-robustness only; `aarch64` behavior is unaffected. Same team-approved pattern as #105139 (wget retry for `.deb`/`.tgz`) and #108675 (keeper S3 retry). Verified both directions locally against `praktika.utils.Shell.run`: a command failing twice then succeeding returns 0 after retries; a persistently-failing command still raises `RuntimeError` under `strict=True` after exhausting all attempts.

signals.title: Fix Arrow flattened Tuple subcolumn read from a nullable struct
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109726 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading a flattened `Tuple` subcolumn (e.g. `` `s.v` ``) from an `Arrow`/`ArrowStream` file whose column is a nullable struct returning column defaults instead of the actual data when `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` is enabled. ### Description Since #101272 the Arrow reader wraps a nullable struct into `Nullable(Tuple(...))`. `NestedColumnExtractHelper` reaches a subcolumn by calling `Nested::flatten` on the parent column, but `flatten` only descends into a plain `Tuple`, not `Nullable(Tuple)`, so the subcolumn was never produced and the read silently fell back to type defaults. The fix unwraps `Nullable(Tuple)` into `Tuple(Nullable(...))` (propagating the struct null map to each element via the existing `unwrapNullableTuple`) before flattening. It is a no-op for non-nullable tuples, so plain-`Tuple` reads (ORC fast decoder, Hive) are unchanged. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101272 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109185

signals.title: Avoid server abort on type mismatch during partial result evaluation
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110048 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97411 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Constant folding during query planning no longer executes a function whose argument type differs from the type the function was resolved for during analysis. Such a mismatch used to raise a `LOGICAL_ERROR` while the output header was being computed, which is an assertion failure in debug and sanitizer builds. Folding is now skipped instead, and a genuinely invalid query still reports a recoverable `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` error from the normal execution path. ### Description `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` matches header columns to DAG input nodes **by name only**, then runs `evaluatePartialResult` to compute the output header. A function node, by contrast, is resolved once during analysis: the overload is picked and the return type computed for a fixed set of argument types. If partial evaluation is handed an input column whose type differs from the one the function was resolved for, `executeActionForPartialResult` used to execute the function anyway. That trips a `LOGICAL_ERROR` inside the function body (for example `FunctionUnaryArithmetic`: "`negate`'s argument does not match the expected data type"), and because `handle_error_code` routes `LOGICAL_ERROR` to `abortOnFailedAssertion`, a debug or sanitizer build aborts the whole server process during planning rather than failing the one query. **Fix.** Before executing a `FUNCTION` node in partial evaluation, compare each argument column's type against the type recorded in `function_base->getArgumentTypes()`. If any of them differs, skip the fold: it is only an optimization, and the node's declared result type is already known from analysis. - With `input_rows_count == 0` (header computation) an empty column of the declared result type is produced, so header computation proceeds. - With `input_rows_count == 1` (the callers reached from JOIN rewrites, shard skipping and virtual-column path extraction) the column is left null. Those callers treat any non-null output as a definitive folded value, so a fabricated one could silently change a JOIN rewrite or skip the wrong shards; a null routes them through their existing "unknown value" path. The comparison is exact rather than wrapper-stripped, because `isNullable` derives its value from the argument type alone: its result type is `UInt8` either way, so a wrapper-only difference would produce a definitive but wrong value that no result-type check can catch. `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` need the same treatment, because both used to pass a value through while keeping the declared type computed during analysis. That hid the mismatch from the check above and let a downstream function execute on an incompatible column anyway. Both now carry the argument's actual type, which is what `ExpressionActions::executeAction` already does in its own `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` cases. One result type cannot be instantiated: `DataTypeFunction`, the result type of a captured lambda, inherits `IDataTypeDummy::createColumn`, which throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. The column is left null in that one case. Since a capture is normally a child of the higher-order function consuming it, that function then reports a recoverable `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, whereas executing the stale capture raises `Cannot capture column N because it has incompatible type`, another `LOGICAL_ERROR` abort. (`DataTypeNothing` and `DataTypeSet` derive from the same base but do override `createColumn`, so they are built normally.) **Scope.** In production the mismatch was produced by a concurrent `EXCHANGE TABLES`. The query does hold its table object, lock and metadata snapshot for its whole lifetime (`InterpreterSelectQuery.cpp:635-656`), so the held storage is never swapped. What drifts is that the old analyzer resolves the table name a second time for the analyzed column types (`getTableExpressions.cpp:118`, reached from `joined_tables.resolveTables()`), and an exchange changes what that second resolution returns. The per-query storage cache from #97411 is what keeps those two resolutions consistent; #108728 defeated it and #110048 restored it, which is what `03915_exchange_tables_race` races for. This change is therefore no longer the fix for that race; it hardens the planning path itself so that any argument-type mismatch degrades to "do not fold" instead of aborting the server. I left the changelog category as `Bug Fix` because the abort was user-visible on released builds before #110048, but I am happy to move it to `Not for changelog` if you prefer, given that the root cause is now fixed upstream. **Testing.** Coverage is a unit test rather than a functional one, because the race is an inherent TOCTOU and cannot be reproduced deterministically. Since `updateHeader` binds header columns by name only, the mismatch can be injected directly, single-threaded, with no race at all. `src/Interpreters/tests/gtest_actions_dag_partial_result_type_drift.cpp` covers a strict function (`Float64` resolved, `Int256` supplied), a wrapper-only difference through `materialize`, the same mismatch behind an `ALIAS` and behind an `ARRAY_JOIN`, the wrong-value hazard via `isNullable` at `input_rows_count == 1`, a captured lambda both as a terminal output and consumed by `arrayMap`, and a non-mismatched constant that must still be folded. Verified in both directions on a debug build. Against master's `executeActionForPartialResult` the first case aborts the test binary with `Logical error: 'Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Int256'` through `updateHeader` -> `evaluatePartialResult` -> `executeActionForPartialResult`; with the fix all eight cases pass. Each hunk was also reverted individually and fails only its own case, and forcing the guard to fire unconditionally fails only the still-folds-a-constant case. Full unit suite: 22357 tests pass. `03915_exchange_tables_race` passes 10 out of 10 runs. **Known residuals, both pre-existing on `master` and deliberately not addressed here.** I measured each one against a build with this branch's `ActionsDAG.cpp` replaced by master's, and the behaviour is identical, so neither is caused or widened by this change: - The add-time fold in `tryFoldFunctionToConstant` does not perform this check. Handing `addFunction` a `function_base` resolved for one type together with a differently typed constant child raises `Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Const(Int256)`. This diff does not touch that path, and adding the check there would alter DAG construction for every query on a scenario I could not reach from SQL. - At `input_rows_count == 1` with `allow_unknown_function_arguments`, a type-sensitive folder above a node whose column is unknown can still fold from the type alone. Two shapes: `identity -> isNullable` over a `Nullable(String)` yields `0` where the real chain would yield `1` (unchanged from `master`), and an `ARRAY_JOIN` whose argument stopped being an array leaves the declared nested type in place, so `isNullable` above it also folds to `0`. Closing this properly needs an explicit "unknown" marker propagated through descendants, which changes the `evaluatePartialResult` contract for every caller. I tried the two local shortcuts and neither works: clearing the type outright makes the unit-test binary abort and then segfault, because a null type in a `ColumnWithTypeAndName` breaks downstream consumers; handing up the argument's own type does not help, because the parent compares against the type it was itself resolved for. So this is a separate design decision rather than part of an abort-avoidance fix. Happy to follow up on any of these if you would like them in scope. This branch also takes master's version of `03915_exchange_tables_race` verbatim: master rewrote that test after this branch forked it (pinning `enable_analyzer` and capping concurrent clients so the flaky check does not run out of memory), and those changes belong with #110048's coverage rather than here.

signals.title: Supply `_sample_factor` to the per-part read path used by mutations and merges
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78465 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78465 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a mutation that references the `_sample_factor` virtual column failing mid-execution with `Unexpected const virtual column: _sample_factor` and leaving the mutation stuck. A mutation now reads it as `1`, the same value a query without `SAMPLE` returns. ### Description `_sample_factor` is registered with `VirtualsMaterializationPlace::Reader`, so a reader is expected to supply its value. `ReadFromMergeTree` publishes it into `shared_virtual_fields` and the normal read pool copies that map into every read task, which is why `SELECT` resolves it. The per-part path used by mutations and merges does not: `createMergeTreeSequentialSource` seeds only `_part_index` and `_part_starting_offset`, so `fillVirtualColumns` falls through to a throw. `ALTER TABLE t UPDATE u = _sample_factor WHERE ...` therefore starts, then fails per part with `Code 341` wrapping `Code 16`, and the mutation entry stays stuck. The fix seeds the field where the sibling already does. The value is `1` because no `SAMPLE` clause reaches this path: `used_sample_factor` is declared `1.0` and is overwritten only for an actual `SAMPLE` clause, which a mutation predicate cannot carry. It is a literal constant, identical on every replica, so it is safe on ReplicatedMergeTree and SharedMergeTree. The net change against master is 3 lines of source plus one test. This replaces the analysis-time rejection this PR previously carried, so the guard it added earlier is gone and `MutationsInterpreter.cpp` is now untouched. That guard decided column identity from raw AST identifier names, which cannot distinguish an `ALIAS` over a virtual column from an `ALIAS` over a real `Tuple`, because `ColumnsDescription` deliberately omits alias subcolumns. One of the six holes measured rejected `a Tuple(_table UInt8) ALIAS tup` over a real `tup`, which master and 26.7.2 both accept, so dropping the guard also removes that regression. Scope is `_sample_factor` only, which is what the issue reports. `_table` and `_database` derive from the local storage id, and a mutation persists what it reads, so seeding them could diverge replicas, while rejecting them for every MergeTree would be a new restriction. That design is filed separately, and their current mid-execution failure is unchanged here.

signals.title: Fix Iceberg insert out-of-bounds abort on schema column-count mismatch
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109835 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server abort (out-of-bounds read) when inserting into an `Iceberg` table whose cached ClickHouse structure has more columns than the table's current on-disk Iceberg schema. This can happen when a materialized view (whose output block is fixed at creation time) writes into an Iceberg target whose schema was shrunk out-of-band. The mismatch is now rejected with a clear `BAD_ARGUMENTS` error instead of crashing the server. Also rejects stale writes whose column names or partition layout no longer match the current schema, and no longer rejects writes whose column types only differ by an Iceberg-equivalent mapping (`UInt32`/`Int32`, `UInt64`/`Int64`, `Date`/`Date32`). ### Description Closes: #109835 `IcebergStorageSink` maps the input block's columns positionally onto the table's current schema fields when it writes per-column statistics (`DataFileStatistics`) and per-column value dumps. `DataFileStatistics::getColumnSizes()` (and the sibling getters) index `field_ids[i]`, where `field_ids` is sized from the current on-disk schema while `column_sizes` is sized from the written chunk. When the input block is wider than the current schema, these getters read past the end of `field_ids` and the server aborts (libc++ hardening `vector[] index out of bounds`). This is reachable from SQL: an Avro `IcebergLocal` table `t(3 cols)` fed by a materialized view `MV(3 cols)`; a sibling table on the same on-disk path drops a column so `t`'s current schema shrinks to 2 fields, while `t`'s cached ClickHouse structure and the MV output block stay at 3 columns. The MV pushes a 3-column block into the 2-field sink and the server aborts (AVRO data files also bypass the Parquet-only write-time field-id guard). The fix validates the column count against the current schema in the sink constructor, at the point where both the input block and the resolved current schema are available, and rejects the impossible mapping with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` rather than reading out of bounds. Reproduced frame-for-frame against the reported stack (`DataFileStatistics.cpp:97` -> `generateManifestFile` -> `IcebergStorageSink::initializeMetadata`): without the fix the `INSERT` aborts the server; with the fix it is a clean query error and the server stays alive. Fixed while reviewing this change: - A count-only check still let a same-width `RENAME`/`MODIFY COLUMN` drift through, so the guard compares names and types positionally, and it now runs for every mutation rather than only `UPDATE`. - `UPDATE`/`DELETE` are unsafe only when the partition layout changed, so the partition-spec guard resolves the manifest's embedded layout instead of rejecting on a differing spec id alone. - The name/type comparison itself was too strict. `getIcebergType` deliberately maps several ClickHouse types onto one Iceberg primitive (`UInt32`/`Int32` -> `int`, `UInt64`/`Int64` -> `long`, `Date`/`Date32` -> `date`) and the read side reconstructs the signed or wider member, so an unsigned or `Date` column with no drift at all was rejected. A materialized view is the reachable shape, because it hands the target its own unmapped header; a prior direct `INSERT` into the target refreshes the cached metadata and hides it. Types are now compared after that same mapping, so genuine drift is still rejected while an equivalent mapping is accepted. Report: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109835 (stack: signal 6, `DataFileStatistics::getColumnSizes()` OOB, build 26.7.1.644 / git 0633b44).

signals.title: Fix data race in shared format init exception rethrow
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a data race (and rare crash) when a parsing/analysis error is reported while reading a file/object storage table. A parse error raised during lazy `KeyCondition` initialization was shared as a single exception object across reader threads, and two threads could concurrently append `(in file/uri ...)` to its message, racing on the exception message string. ### Description The race is in the lazy, `std::call_once`-guarded init of the shared format filter, not in `ParallelParsingInputFormat` (that class has a single reader thread per its header and the `IProcessor` no-parallel-work rule). `FormatFilterInfo::initKeyConditionOnce` builds a `KeyCondition` under `call_once`; if that throws (e.g. `convertFieldToType` failing to parse a `DateTime64` literal, `readDateTimeTextFallback`), the exception is stored in `init_exception` and rethrown to every later reader via `std::rethrow_exception(init_exception)`. `std::rethrow_exception` hands out the SAME managed `DB::Exception` object. Up the stack, `IInputFormat::generate()` mutates it in place in its catch block via `e.addMessage(...)` -> `Poco::Exception::extendedMessage()`, which appends to the exception's `_msg` `std::string`. Two `StorageObjectStorageSource::generate()` readers therefore race on `_msg` (TSan report STID 2427-2c05, allocation stack in `FormatFilterInfo::initKeyConditionOnce`; the same class was seen as a segfault). Fix both `call_once` init sites (`FormatFilterInfo::initKeyConditionOnce` and the symmetric `FormatParserSharedResources::initOnce`): keep the stored `init_exception` an immutable template that is only ever read, and hand each caller - the first thrower and every later rethrower - a private copy via `copyMutableException()`. Both reads of the stored `exception_ptr` happen inside `call_once`, so the copies are race-free. `Common/Exception.h` documents that returning a reference to a mutable `DB::Exception` is unsafe for exactly this reason; @ azat applied the same helper to the Parquet reader in f6025e3. The earlier `ParallelParsingInputFormat` change is reverted - it was not the racing path. CI report (STID 2427-2c05, Stress test (amd_tsan)): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108469&sha=aef76155cf7a0af8fe890077cbea2598f0a521d9&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29

signals.title: Accept fractional unix timestamp for DateTime64 in containers and JSON
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109884 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed parsing of `DateTime64` values written as an unquoted fractional unix timestamp (e.g. `1783585473.954`) when they appear as elements of `Array`, `Tuple`, `Map`, or in JSON. Previously only scalar `DateTime64` columns accepted this form; inside containers the value failed with `CANNOT_READ_ARRAY_FROM_TEXT`. A bare integer is still interpreted as a scaled tick count, unchanged. ### Description Closes #109884. Parsing CSV/TSV/JSON/Values into a container of `DateTime64(N)` (e.g. `Array(DateTime64(3))`) rejected an element written as an unquoted fractional unix timestamp such as `1783585473.954`, failing with `Cannot read array from text, expected comma or end of array, found '.'` (`CANNOT_READ_ARRAY_FROM_TEXT`). The same instant written as integer ticks (`1783585473954`) worked, and a scalar `DateTime64` column accepted both forms. Root cause: container/JSON elements go through `SerializationDateTime64::deserializeTextQuoted` / `deserializeTextJSON`, whose unquoted branch used `readIntText`, which stops at the `.`. The leftover `.` then broke the array reader. Scalar CSV/Escaped columns use `readText` (`readDateTime64Text`), which already handles the fractional form. Fix: the unquoted numeric branch now reads the integer and, if a `.` follows, treats the integer part as whole seconds and the fraction as subseconds (mirroring the scalar `readDateTimeTextImpl` logic, including negative-timestamp handling and scale truncation/padding). A bare integer with no `.` keeps its existing raw-tick interpretation, so behavior is unchanged for every previously-accepted input (no backward-incompatible change).
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Use token skip indexes for LowCardinality(String) constants
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110010 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110010 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `text`, `tokenbf_v1` and `ngrambf_v1` skip indexes not being used when the searched constant has type `LowCardinality(String)` (e.g. `hasToken(s, toLowCardinality('rare'))` or `s = toLowCardinality('rare')`), which caused a silent full scan. Such predicates now prune granules like their plain `String` counterparts, matching the primary key and `bloom_filter` index behavior. ### Description The token-search index conditions checked the constant's type with `isStringOrFixedString()` before stripping wrappers. A `Const(LowCardinality(String))` needle kept its `LowCardinality` wrapper, failed the gate, produced no index condition, and the query degraded to a full scan. Since `hasToken`/text-search predicates have no fallback index type, an LC-typed needle guaranteed a full scan. `KeyCondition` (primary key) and the plain `bloom_filter` index already strip the wrapper and prune correctly. This aligns the token indexes with them: strip `LowCardinality`, then `Nullable` (only for a non-null value, mirroring `RPNBuilderTreeNode::tryGetConstant`, so a NULL needle stays rejected), before the string-type gate. The constant Field is already a plain value, so only the type wrapper needs stripping. Covers all three families (`text`, `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1`) and the shapes `LowCardinality(String)`, `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))`, `Nullable(String)`, plus derived-LC constants (scalar subquery over an LC column). Regression test asserts pruning is preserved via `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Decide parallel replicas eligibility with the subquery's own context
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100815 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallel replicas now honor a `SETTINGS` clause that changes table eligibility when it is written inside a subquery or a view body. Such a clause was ignored, so a query over a view whose body sets `parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 0` returned too many rows, and a `UNION` over a view overriding `parallel_replicas_allow_view_over_mergetree` per subquery could throw `Can't determine table for parallel replicas`. ### Description One root cause in three traversals: parallel-replicas table eligibility was decided with the OUTER query's context, while the read executes with the per-(sub)query context that `SETTINGS` applies to. Two symptoms. **Wrong results.** `StorageView::getUnderlyingMergeTreeStorageForParallelReplicas` walked a view's resolved inner query tree with a single captured outer context, so a `SETTINGS` clause in the view body was ignored and the view was still judged eligible. Each follower then read the whole table locally (its own view-body context has the setting disabled) and the initiator concatenated those results, so `SELECT count()` silently returned `max_parallel_replicas` times too many rows. Reported by an automated review comment here (3696132546). **Logical error.** In a `UNION` whose subqueries read a view over MergeTree, `getSupportingParallelReplicasQueries` decided eligibility with the outer context while `findTableForParallelReplicas` re-decided it while descending. With a per-subquery override the two disagreed: a subquery was chosen but no eligible table found, so the logical error was thrown (server abort in debug and sanitizer builds). Found by the AST fuzzer, `Stress test (amd_debug)` on master, STID 3634-4123: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=06136dac55ba4fb8544dc1697cd28b2ef769eb17&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_debug%29 The fix tracks the enclosing (sub)query context while descending, in all three traversals. Both halves ship together because neither is correct alone: with only the planner half a view whose body opts out still returns inflated counts, and with only the storage half the `UNION`-in-a-view shape reaches the pre-existing logical error the buggy helper had been suppressing. Some queries will stop using parallel replicas where they previously did; those were returning wrong answers. No new setting or default change, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry. Validated on a 3-replica cluster with `index_granularity = 1`, which makes the inflation deterministic: the new test `04728` fails on master on six rows and passes with the fix, over 100 randomized runs.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Text index looks through positive boolean wrappers
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110012 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110012 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The text (full-text) skip index now prunes granules for a supported search predicate even when it is wrapped in a positive boolean comparison, so `hasToken(s, 'x') = true`, `hasToken(s, 'x') != false`, `hasToken(s, 'x') IN (true)` and `hasToken(s, 'x') IS TRUE` use the index like the bare `hasToken(s, 'x')` instead of scanning every granule. Such wrappers are common in SQL generated by BI tools and ORMs. ### Description The text skip-index condition builder recognized a supported atom (`hasToken`, `equals`, `LIKE`, ...) as prunable only as a bare conjunct. When the same atom was wrapped in a semantically-equivalent positive boolean comparison the inner atom node was treated as the index column, `header.has()` failed, no index condition was built, and the query read every granule. Results were always correct; only pruning was lost. `traverseAtomNode` now looks through positive boolean wrappers by recursing into the atom: - `atom = true` / `true = atom` - `atom != false` - `isNotDistinctFrom(atom, true)` (this is also the desugaring of `atom IS TRUE`) - `atom IN (only-truthy-consts)` Only positive wrappers are handled. A positive wrapper selects a row exactly when the atom is true (under WHERE three-valued logic NULL and false rows are excluded in every case, so this holds for Nullable atoms too), hence the atom's granule mask remains a necessary condition and pruning stays sound. Negative wrappers (`= false`, `!= true`) map to the negated atom, whose NOT-of-a-granule-mask is always can-be-true and gives no pruning benefit, so they are declined. Non-boolean right-hand sides such as `= 5` are left to row-level evaluation. The recursed atom's direct-read mode is forced to `None`: the wrapper node is not shaped `[haystack, needles]`, so the direct-read / preprocessor rewrite (which assumes that shape) must not run on it. Granule pruning is mode-independent (driven by the RPN function type), so pruning is fully restored, and the bare inner atom node is still optimized for direct read independently. Regression test `04365_text_index_positive_boolean_wrapper` asserts via `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that every positive wrapper prunes to the same single granule as the bare atom, that negative and non-boolean wrappers do not prune, and that results are unchanged. Repro from the issue: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/33bc89bf-a740-450a-a1c8-26e7c3c59ba5

signals.title: Use text index on map element with Nullable constant key
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110018 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A text index defined on `mapKeys(m)` / `mapValues(m)` is now used for `m[key] = value` when the constant map key is wrapped in `Nullable` (e.g. `m[CAST('key' AS Nullable(String))]`), instead of falling back to a full scan. ### Description Closes #110018. A text index on `mapKeys(m)` / `mapValues(m)` was used for `WHERE m['key'] = 'value'` but not for the semantically equivalent `WHERE m[CAST('key' AS Nullable(String))] = 'value'`. The `Nullable` wrapper makes `arrayElement` return `Nullable(String)` and the comparison return `Nullable(UInt8)`, and the map-element analysis in the text index condition rejected both types. Fix: strip the `Nullable` wrapper in the map-element key/value analysis (`MergeTreeIndexConditionText`), mirroring what the JSON-subcolumn path already does. This is safe for a non-NULL constant key: `arrayElement(m, key)` returns the value-type default (empty string) for an absent key, not `NULL`, so the "predicate is false on the default value" invariant the map-element optimization relies on still holds. A `NULL` constant key still declines the `mapKeys` path (it would break the invariant); the value index remains a safe over-approximation there. Verified with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: both the `mapKeys` and `mapValues` indexes now prune granules (2/128) for a Nullable (and `LowCardinality(Nullable)`) constant key, matching the plain-key behaviour. Regression test: `02346_text_index_bug110018`.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Eliminate min/max/any/anyLast of LowCardinality GROUP BY keys
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110041 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `optimize_aggregators_of_group_by_keys` not eliminating `min`/`max`/`any`/`anyLast` of a `LowCardinality` `GROUP BY` key. The optimization was silently dead for `LowCardinality` columns, so a `HAVING` predicate on the key (e.g. `HAVING min(s) = 'x'`) was not pushed down to storage and could not use skip indexes, unlike the same query on a plain column. ### Description `optimize_aggregators_of_group_by_keys` (on by default) rewrites `min`/`max`/`any`/`anyLast` of a `GROUP BY` key to the key expression itself, so a `HAVING` predicate on the key can be pushed below the aggregation and prune granules via skip indexes. It never fired for `LowCardinality` keys: the pass required the aggregate's result type to be exactly equal to the argument type, but aggregate functions strip `LowCardinality` from their result (`min(LowCardinality(String))` returns `String`), so the check always failed. Fix: - Compare the aggregate result type and the argument type up to `LowCardinality` (`recursiveRemoveLowCardinality`) before deciding the aggregate can be replaced by the key. - Replacing the aggregate with its argument changes the node type (`String` -> `LowCardinality(String)`), which would break the enclosing function whose resolution was cached against the aggregate's type (and abort with a `LOGICAL_ERROR` in debug/sanitizer builds). So re-resolve the parent ordinary functions in `leaveImpl` when an argument type changed; this cascades upward and keeps predicates like `key = 'x'` operating directly on the key column, so `HAVING` pushes down and skip indexes prune as for a plain key. Verified locally (issue reproducer): `min(s)` / `any(s = 'x')` of a `LowCardinality(String)` key now eliminate the aggregate, push the `HAVING` predicate down, and prune the text index (8/128 granules, matching the plain-key behavior). Results are unchanged with the optimization on vs off across `LowCardinality(String)`, `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))`, and `LowCardinality(UInt8)`.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Apply Iceberg schema evolution when compacting (OPTIMIZE)
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `OPTIMIZE` (compaction) of Iceberg tables after schema evolution (e.g. `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN`). Data files written under an older schema were read by the current-schema column names, so the compacted file could get `DEFAULT`/`NULL` values instead of the original data, and the regenerated metadata could fail with `ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION`. Requires `allow_experimental_iceberg_compaction`. ### Description `IcebergMetadata::optimize` builds the compaction reader header from the table's current schema (`getSampleBlock()`), and `Compaction.cpp` read/regenerated everything against the current schema, ignoring per-file schema ids. After schema evolution this had three consequences: 1. **Data read**: old data files were read by the current column names. The normal read path (`StorageObjectStorageSource`) handles this via `getInitialSchemaByPath` + `getSchemaTransformer`; compaction did not, so a renamed column was compacted into `DEFAULT`/`NULL`. 2. **Metadata regeneration**: `createEmptyMetadataFile` always synthesizes `schema-id 0` from the current column names with fresh field ids, rebinding `schema-id 0` to different fields (`ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION` on the next read) and losing the field ids the data files reference. 3. **Snapshots**: regenerated snapshots were stamped with the current schema id while reusing the original snapshot ids, which are bound to their committed schema id on read (`snapshot already registered with schema id ...`). Fix: - `writeDataFiles` reads each data file by its own schema (`getClickhouseTableSchemaById`) and remaps it to the current schema via `getSchemaTransformationDagByIds`, mirroring the normal read path. Position deletes are applied first (they reference original file row positions), then surviving rows are remapped. - `writeMetadataFiles` carries the real `schemas`, `current-schema-id` and `last-column-id` from the source metadata, and preserves each snapshot's originally committed schema id. Added an integration regression (`test_storage_iceberg_no_spark/test_writes_optimize_after_rename.py`): INSERT, DELETE (positional delete so compaction has work), `RENAME COLUMN`, `OPTIMIZE` — asserts the renamed column keeps its original values (no `NULL`/`DEFAULT`) and the deleted row stays deleted. It fails before this change (`ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION`) and passes after. Verified locally on `IcebergLocal` (format-version 2): before the fix `OPTIMIZE` leaves the table unreadable (`ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION`); after the fix the renamed column reads back `hello`/`foo`, 0 NULLs, correct row count. A control run without rename confirms no change to the existing compaction path.

signals.title: Allow creating a Distributed table over a table function
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106189 Allow creating a `Distributed` table over a table function, in the same way the `remote`/`cluster` table functions already accept an arbitrary table expression. Previously `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Distributed(...)` only accepted `Distributed(cluster, database, table[, sharding_key[, policy_name]])`, where `database` and `table` had to be string literals or identifiers. `StorageDistributed` itself already supported being backed by a table function (`remote_table_function_ptr`), but that capability was only reachable through the `remote`/`cluster`/`clusterAllReplicas` table functions. This change lets the engine take a table function directly: ```sql CREATE TABLE t ENGINE = Distributed(cluster, table_function()[, sharding_key[, policy_name]]); -- e.g. CREATE TABLE distributed_numbers ENGINE = Distributed(test_cluster_two_shards, numbers(100)); ``` mirroring the `cluster('cluster_name', table_function())` signature. The second engine argument is treated as a table function only when it is a call to a registered table function; any other expression is still interpreted as a database name, so the existing `Distributed(cluster, database, table, ...)` form is unaffected. The structure is inferred from the table function when the columns are omitted. `INSERT` into a table-function-backed `Distributed` table is rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, since there is no concrete remote table to route rows to. As a side effect, `INSERT INTO FUNCTION cluster('cluster', table_function())` now fails with this clear error instead of silently building a broken `INSERT INTO <empty>` query for the shards. ### Relationship to #106189 This is complementary to #106189 (`Remote`/`RemoteSecure` storage engines): that PR adds address-based engines over an ad-hoc cluster, while this one lets the configured-cluster `Distributed` engine take a table function. The table-function `INSERT` guard in `StorageDistributed::write` is aligned with #106189 (identical exception message, guard placed only in `write`). The `read` path here additionally handles the case where the remote database/table names are empty (a table-function-backed `Distributed` stores empty names rather than the `system.one` placeholder that #106189's engines inherit from the `remote` table function); this also makes the shared `read` path robust for #106189's engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow creating a `Distributed` table over a table function, e.g. `CREATE TABLE t ENGINE = Distributed(cluster, numbers(100))`, in the same way as the `cluster`/`remote` table functions accept a table function. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110073&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110073](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110073+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add UUID2 data type with correct sorting
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110066 Introduces `UUID2`, a variant of the `UUID` data type with correct (lexicographic) sorting. ## Motivation For historical reasons, the `UUID` data type sorts by the *second half* of the value. This is unexpected and, in particular, hurts the performance of primary indexes built on `UUIDv7` columns, whose most significant bits are a timestamp: with sorting by the second half, primary-key analysis cannot prune granules by the timestamp. ## What this does `UUID2` stores the 128-bit value as a plain big-endian integer of the 16 canonical bytes, so that natural integer comparison of the underlying value matches the textual (lexicographic) order and the canonical byte order used by most other systems. It reuses the `UUID` column and `Field` representation (like `DateTime` reuses `UInt32`), so sorting is correct with no extra comparison code, and its binary/interchange serialization is the canonical big-endian byte order. - `UUID1` is an alias of the current `UUID` type. - A new setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) controls whether the bare name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` (`1`) or `UUID2` (`2`) at `CREATE`/`ALTER` time. The resolved concrete type is materialized into the stored table definition (including nested types such as `Array(UUID)`), so reads never depend on the session setting and existing tables are never rewritten. The default will be flipped to `2` in a later, separate change. - Conversions to/from `String`, `UInt128`, `FixedString(16)` and `UUID`, plus `toUUID2` / `toUUID2OrZero` / `toUUID2OrNull`. - Parity across functions (`hex`/`bin`, `reinterpretAs*`, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `UUIDToNum`, `empty`/`notEmpty`, `min`/`max`, hashing, `uniq`), formats (`RowBinary`, `Native`, `JSON`, `CSV`, `TSV`, `Arrow`, `Parquet`, `Avro`, `BSON`, `MsgPack`, `Protobuf`, `CapnProto`, `JSONExtract`) and storage (`generateRandom`, `bloom_filter` skip index). The `UUID` type is unchanged (verified: still sorts by second half, identical conversions, default `uuid_type_version = 1`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new data type `UUID2`, a variant of `UUID` that sorts by its textual (lexicographic) representation instead of by the second half of the value. The setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) selects whether the type name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` or `UUID2`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110084&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110084](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110084+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Parallelize aggregation-in-order via key-hash reshuffle (aggregation_in_order_shuffle)
signals.text: ## Description `optimize_aggregation_in_order` is not enabled by default because it is often slower than the default hash aggregation. The reason is structural: for a multi-stream read the whole aggregation is funneled through a single `FinishAggregatingInOrderTransform`, so it runs on ~2–6 cores regardless of `max_threads` and is 8–16× slower than the default parallel hash path for high-cardinality `GROUP BY` (it does *less* total CPU work, but cannot parallelize it). This PR adds an experimental setting **`aggregation_in_order_shuffle`** (default `0`) that removes that funnel by repartitioning, reusing the shuffle primitive introduced for the sharded aggregator (`BufferedShardByHashTransform`): ``` read N sorted streams -> scatter each stream by hash(GROUP BY keys) into num_shards (BufferedShardByHashTransform) -> per shard: MergingSortedTransform(N -> 1) -- groups are disjoint by key -> per shard: streaming AggregatingInOrderTransform + FinalizeAggregatedTransform ``` Each shard aggregates a disjoint set of keys, so there is no cross-shard coordination and no single-threaded merge, while each shard still streams out completed key groups (bounded, O(1) memory). It is only used when the `GROUP BY` order is not relied upon downstream (`!memoryBoundMergingWillBeUsed()`, no bucket-order requirement, no `LIMIT` push-down), and the output is therefore not ordered by the keys. ### Making the shuffle deadlock-free and bounded-memory The M per-shard merges share the N scatters, so a naive scatter deadlocks: a slow/exhausted lane blocks the shared scatter from feeding the others, and a per-shard *sorted* merge is a selective consumer. Two fixes in `BufferedShardByHashTransform` (unbounded mode, used only by this path): - **Demand-driven scheduling**: push to every ready lane first, and pull a new input chunk only to feed an output that is ready *and* starving (empty queue). The shared scatter never stalls on a slow lane (its data is just buffered), so there is no cross-lane cycle, and read-ahead — hence memory — is bounded by how far the fastest consumer runs ahead of the slowest. - **Per-output drain on EOF**: when the input is exhausted, finish each output whose queue is already empty, so a sorted merge gets EOF on exhausted inputs instead of waiting forever (this hung deterministically for non-overlapping parts). Verified: 0 deadlocks over 120+ runs across all cardinalities, overlapping and non-overlapping parts, and `max_threads` 8..128; results are byte-identical to the default for order-independent aggregates. ### Results (200M rows, 50M keys, 96 threads; median of 5) | GROUP BY | default | in-order (funnel) | **shuffle** | |---|---|---|---| | `sum`, 50M groups | 870 ms / 23 GB / 42 cores | 5779 ms / 0.8 GB / 4 cores | **1341 ms / 0.83 GB / 20 cores** | | `uniqExact`, 50M groups | 12040 ms / 56 GB | 5744 ms / 1.5 GB | **1049 ms / 2.0 GB / 22 cores** | For high-cardinality `GROUP BY` the shuffle is **4–11× faster than the current aggregation-in-order at the same O(1) memory**, and for `uniqExact` it is faster than the default while using ~28× less memory. ### Known limitation (why it stays off by default) It scatters raw rows, so it regresses for low/medium cardinality (where in-order is already fast and the shuffle gives no benefit, and long key-runs make the scatter buffer more). Gating it to high cardinality (e.g. from the primary-key granule estimate) is a natural follow-up. `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` is also fixed to render the scatter/merge stage of the in-order pipeline (it was previously omitted). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `aggregation_in_order_shuffle` that parallelizes `optimize_aggregation_in_order` by repartitioning the sorted input by the hash of the `GROUP BY` keys into independent shards, removing the single-threaded merge bottleneck while keeping the bounded memory of aggregation-in-order. For high-cardinality `GROUP BY` it is several times faster than the ordinary aggregation-in-order. Disabled by default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (the new setting is documented in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110102&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110102](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110102+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Prune partitions through identity ifNull/coalesce nested in a key expression
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110117 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109998 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110117 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109998 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed partition/primary key pruning being lost when an identity `ifNull(x, c)` or `coalesce(x, c)` over a non-Nullable column is nested inside a key expression (for example `PARTITION BY sipHash64(p)` with `WHERE sipHash64(ifNull(p, 0)) = ...` now prunes parts instead of scanning them all). Applies with the analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default). ### Description `ifNull(x, c)` and `coalesce(x, c)` are pure identities on `x` when `x` cannot be NULL: the fallback is unreachable and the result type equals `x`. Both functions already fold their return type to the first argument, but the `FunctionNode` remained in the query tree, so `KeyCondition`'s syntactic key-expression matching failed whenever the wrapper was nested inside another key function. `WHERE sipHash64(ifNull(p, 0)) = sipHash64(3)` against `PARTITION BY sipHash64(p)` therefore scanned all parts instead of pruning to one. This adds a query tree pass (`RemoveRedundantIfNullCoalescePass`) replacing such identity calls with their first argument. It fires only when the argument cannot be NULL, the result type is unchanged, and every discarded fallback is a constant (`ifNull`/`coalesce` are not short-circuit, so a non-constant fallback must still be evaluated). It is gated on `allow_key_condition_coalesce_rewrite`, the same knob as the top-level rewrite. Pruning then sees the bare argument inside any key expression: partition key, primary key or skip index. **Scope:** being a query tree pass, this applies under the analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default). The legacy `enable_analyzer = 0` path is unchanged and still scans all parts for the nested form. That path is being retired, and duplicating the rewrite plus its three correctness guards in `ExpressionAnalyzer` would mean keeping two implementations in sync, which is the reasoning applied in a8fd36400c95f4cf331b6f6f5644b032e57cb850 when `optimize_or_like_chain` was made analyzer-only. Regression test `03891_ifnull_coalesce_identity_nested_key_pruning` pins `enable_analyzer = 1` and covers the non-Nullable (prunes), Nullable (not simplified, correct results), setting-off and side-effect-fallback cases.

signals.title: Push filter above INTERSECT/EXCEPT into input branches
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110113 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110113 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Push a filter above `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` (both `ALL` and `DISTINCT`) into the input branches, so each input can prune with its own primary key, as already happens for `UNION ALL`. ### Description A filter above `UNION ALL` is pushed into every branch. The same filter above `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` stayed above the set operation, so both inputs were read in full. `IntersectOrExceptStep` shares the properties the `UnionStep` case relies on (header unchanged, branches positionally aligned), so `filterPushDown` now applies the same transformation: clone the deterministic filter into each branch and remove the original. Equivalence-preserving for all set operators: values failing the predicate cannot appear in the output (INTERSECT ALL multiplicity = min(left, right); EXCEPT ALL = max(0, left - right); DISTINCT variants by the same argument on sets), so dropping them from every input is safe. The pass's existing global guard already rejects stateful/non-deterministic filters. Regression test `04401_filter_push_down_intersect_except` asserts via `EXPLAIN indexes=1` that the key condition reaches both branches for INTERSECT ALL/DISTINCT and EXCEPT ALL/DISTINCT, plus a correctness check preserving multiplicity. Reproducer from the issue: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/4d1403c5-2a56-41dd-9401-4a84f1c52b24

signals.title: Preserve parameters in aggregate functions that dropped them, fixing the `-Array` combinator assert
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104812 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds) when the `-Array` combinator is applied with parameters to `argMin`, `argMax`, `argAndMin`, `argAndMax`, `min_by`, `max_by`, `groupArrayMovingSum`, `groupArrayMovingAvg`, `kolmogorovSmirnovTest`, `mannWhitneyUTest` or `intervalLengthSum`, for example `argMaxArray(2)([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])`. These functions dropped the parameters they were given; they now preserve them, so a state type name also keeps them, e.g. `AggregateFunction(groupArrayMovingSum(42), UInt64)` instead of dropping the window size. ### Description Found by the AST fuzzer. Example abort: ``` Logical error: 'AggregateFunctionArray: parameters mismatch between Array wrapper 'groupArrayMovingSumArray' and nested function 'groupArrayMovingSum'. Wrapper has 1 parameter(s): [UInt64_42], nested function has 0 parameter(s): []'. ``` Reproducers, one per affected family: ```sql SELECT groupArrayMovingSumArray(42)([1, 2, 3]); SELECT argMaxArray(2)([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]); SELECT intervalLengthSumArray('two-sided', 1)([0., 1], [10., 3]); SELECT mannWhitneyUTestArray('two-sided', 1)([1., 2, 3, 4], [0., 0, 1, 1]); ``` Root cause: each of these functions built its `IAggregateFunctionDataHelper` base with an empty parameter array instead of the parameters it was passed, so `getParameters` returned `[]`. The `-Array` combinator does not transform parameters and asserts that the wrapper's parameters equal the nested function's; with the wrapper carrying `[42]` and the nested function returning `[]`, the invariant fired. `groupArrayMovingSum`/`groupArrayMovingAvg` and `kolmogorovSmirnovTest`/`mannWhitneyUTest` are the set listed in the TODO added by #104812. `intervalLengthSum` and the `argMin`/`argMax` family instead accepted parameters and silently ignored them, so hard-rejecting them would make existing `AggregateFunction(argMin(...), ...)` metadata unreadable on upgrade; for those the parameters are preserved and normalized away in the state type via `getNormalizedStateType`, keeping legacy parameterless state columns `Merge`- and `CAST`-compatible. No performance impact: the change only forwards an already-constructed parameter array to a base constructor, with no work added on any aggregation hot path. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104812

signals.title: Support per-authentication-method GRANTS clause in CREATE USER and ALTER USER
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117 Implements per-authentication-method grant limits, the first part of the linked issue: ```sql ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY 'WYmdFyas8PftrHbHQQo8' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table) ``` When a user logs in with such a method, the access rights of the session are the intersection of the user's access rights (including granted roles) with the listed elements. The clause never adds rights: a listed privilege that is not granted to the user stays unavailable. This provides a way to create tokens for applications: an additional credential with an expiration date and a limited set of grants, which is tied to the user — it is displayed in `query_log` and `processlist` as the user, stops working if the user is deleted, and is narrowed when the user loses grants. Details: - The clause is parsed after the per-method `VALID UNTIL`, works with `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER [ADD] IDENTIFIED`, and `NOT IDENTIFIED`, is shown by `SHOW CREATE USER`, and persists through the SQL serialization of access entities (and therefore backups). Elements without a database name are bound to the current database when the query is interpreted. - The intersection erases all grant options (the clause cannot express them), so such sessions cannot `GRANT` anything. Role administration is denied entirely (fail-close), including per-role admin option. `EXECUTE AS`, `ALTER USER`, `CREATE USER` and similar escapes require the corresponding rights to be listed explicitly and granted to the user. - Reattaching to a named session (`session_id`) with a different credential re-applies the limit of the credential used by the new connection, so a limited credential cannot pick up the full rights of a session created by an unrestricted one. - The limit is captured at login: `ALTER USER` affects new sessions, not established ones (same as `VALID UNTIL`). - A new `auth_grants` column in `system.users` exposes the limit of each authentication method. - `ContextData`'s copy constructor now preserves `external_roles` and the new field: previously a recalculation of access rights on a copied context silently dropped external roles; for the new field that would mean silently widening the rights. - `EXECUTE AS <user> <statement>` now keeps the current database of the caller's session. `Context::setUser` sets the current database from the target user's `DEFAULT DATABASE`, so the wrapped statement used to be re-scoped and an unqualified table name resolved in a different database; the session form (`EXECUTE AS <user>` without a statement) already preserved it. Test `04907_execute_as_preserves_current_database` covers both forms. Known limitations (consistent with `VALID UNTIL` and external roles): the limit is not propagated to other nodes of a cluster in distributed queries or `ON CLUSTER` DDL (the query is checked on the initiator), and the clause is not available in `users.xml`. The `CREATE TOKEN` syntactic sugar and the separate grant for self-service `ADD IDENTIFIED` mentioned in the issue are left for a follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Authentication methods in `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER ... ADD IDENTIFIED` support a `GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table, ...)` clause which limits the access rights of sessions authenticated with that method to the intersection with the listed grants. This allows using additional credentials as tokens for applications: `ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY '...' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table)`. Closes [#109117](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110144&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110144](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110144+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add VALID FOR clause for users and credentials
signals.text: We support `VALID UNTIL` for users and credentials. This adds `VALID FOR <interval>` as a convenience shorthand. Instead of an absolute date and time, `VALID FOR` accepts an interval, and the expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus that interval at the moment the query is executed. The result is stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form, so `SHOW CREATE USER` always displays the resolved absolute deadline. It can be used everywhere `VALID UNTIL` can - at the user level and per authentication method, in both `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER`. Examples: ```sql CREATE USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY; CREATE USER u2 IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x' VALID FOR INTERVAL 3 MONTH; ALTER USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY + INTERVAL 12 HOUR; ``` Implementation notes: the current time is injected as a literal (rather than using `now`, which is non-deterministic and would not fold to a constant expression), and the deadline is computed with `toDateTime64` so that large intervals saturate at the `DateTime64` upper bound instead of overflowing the year-2106 boundary of `DateTime`. Note on the system table schema: to represent deadlines beyond the year 2106 exactly, the `valid_until` column of `system.users` changes from `Array(DateTime)` to `Array(DateTime64(0))`. This is a backward-incompatible change of a documented system table for tooling that introspects the column type; the values themselves keep second precision. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `VALID FOR <interval>` clause to `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER` as a shorthand for `VALID UNTIL`. The expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus the given interval at query execution time and stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form. The `valid_until` column of the `system.users` table now has the type `Array(DateTime64(0))` instead of `Array(DateTime)`, so that deadlines beyond the year 2106 are represented exactly; tooling that reads this column should handle the new type. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110171&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110171](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110171+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix use-of-uninitialized-value in WITH FILL suffix over a merge
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107074 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a use-of-uninitialized-value in `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL ... STALENESS` when the fill suffix generates no rows (for example when the staleness window leaves nothing to fill) and the result is read through a merge of sorted streams (such as a two-shard `Distributed` table). ### Description Found by the AST fuzzer under MSan on top of #107074. `FillingTransform`, when all input chunks are processed, may run the suffix path. If the fill constraints are satisfied but no fill rows are produced (e.g. `WITH FILL ... STALENESS` with an exhausted staleness window), `generateSuffixIfNeeded` returns `true` while the result columns are freshly `cloneEmpty()`'d and carry no data. Previously the transform still emitted a 0-row chunk built from those empty columns. A downstream `MergingSortedTransform` (as used when reading from a two-shard `Distributed` table) then built a sort cursor over that empty chunk and compared row 0, reading past the end of the empty column. Fix: do not emit the suffix chunk when it has no rows. Minimal reproducer (needs a two-shard merge on the initiator): ```sql CREATE TABLE m (key Int) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO m VALUES (100); CREATE TABLE d2 AS m ENGINE = Distributed(test_cluster_two_shards_localhost, currentDatabase(), m); SELECT _shard_num FROM d2 ORDER BY _shard_num ASC WITH FILL TO 46 STALENESS 1; ``` CI finding: `AST fuzzer (amd_msan)`, report https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107074&sha=3ec54c88d4eb535a5d644fc1ab91af31d717f9a5&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29 MSan use-of-uninitialized-value in `ColumnVector<UInt32>::doCompareAt` (`MergingSortedAlgorithm::consume`), origin `FillingTransform::initColumns` (`cloneEmpty`) via the suffix path. Verified on a local `amd_msan` build: reproduces before the fix (server aborts), clean after; the new regression test returns `1\n2`.

signals.title: Use fewer stateful-prepare insert threads for regular sanitizer runs
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110152 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The stateful data prepare step runs `INSERT INTO test.hits_s3 SELECT * FROM test.hits` with `max_insert_threads=16`. On regular sanitizer Stateless jobs this single INSERT tracks ~24 GiB and pushes ASan RSS to ~42 GiB, which memcg-OOM-kills the server (`Server died` + `OOM in dmesg`). #109954 already reduced this to 4 threads on sanitizer builds, but only for the bugfix-validation path, because `build_type` is only passed there. On regular runs `build_type` is `None`, so `is_sanitizer` was always `False` and the INSERT still used 16 threads. Fix: when `build_type` is not passed, fall back to `Info().job_name` to detect the sanitizer, mirroring the existing `limit_source` pattern in `functional_tests.py::run_tests` (which already does `build_type if build_type is not None else Info().job_name`). Same data is loaded, just a smaller peak. Example failure (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel): peak server MemoryTracking 24.2 GiB at 17:47:14 from the single hits_s3 INSERT; server OOM-killed at 42 GiB anon-rss. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110152&sha=729886a3f8576eae108e6bd09bc29c4922a39212&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%29

signals.title: Read database metadata files synchronously to avoid file-offset assertion
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104692 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104692 `readMetadataFile()` reads a table/database `.sql` metadata file with `getReadSettingsForMetadata()`, which forces `RemoteFSReadMethod::threadpool`. On object-storage-backed metadata that produces an `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer`, which caches the file size at construction and asserts `file_offset_of_buffer_end <= getFileSize()` in `nextImpl()`. Metadata `.sql` files are mutable: `ALTER`/`RENAME` rewrite them in place. A concurrent rewrite that grows the object under an already-open reader makes the inner reader return bytes past the cached size, tripping the assert and aborting the server in debug/sanitizer builds. The read is a single full-file read of a tiny file, so none of the size-snapshotting stages buy anything here. The fix pins the metadata read to the plain synchronous `ReadBufferFromRemoteFSGather`, which has no cached-size assertion, by disabling the three stages the pipeline may otherwise pick: the async prefetch buffer (`RemoteFSReadMethod::read`), the reader executor, and the in-memory page cache. The fix is in the single `readMetadataFile()` free function, so it covers all metadata read sites (`DatabaseOrdinary`, `DatabaseOnDisk`, `DatabaseReplicated`, startup load). Found by the BuzzHouse (amd_msan) and stateless flaky-check fuzzers. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110127&sha=1f4a1b8f87ea4ec3270939654c508b009bde65da&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29 Reproduced deterministically on an object-storage metadata disk under ThreadFuzzer (`ENGINE = Buffer` table + concurrent `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COMMENT` with varying comment lengths + `SELECT FROM system.tables`): server aborts within ~90s without the fix; survives a 35-minute run with it.
