signal.title: Promote exponentialTimeDecayed window-functions to aggregate-functions
signal.text: ## Motivation `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` already exist and are documented as aggregate functions, but their current implementation is a special window-function implementation in `WindowTransform`. They do not provide mergeable aggregate states that can be persisted and combined with aggregate combinators such as `-State` and `-Merge`. This prevents incremental time-decayed aggregation in engines such as `AggregatingMergeTree`: data has to be evaluated through the window path instead of being aggregated independently in multiple batches and merged later. This PR adds regular, mergeable aggregate implementations for those three names while preserving the existing window implementation and its behavior. ## What changes For the regular aggregate form, each state keeps the weighted sum and sum of weights at the greatest timestamp observed by that state, plus that timestamp. When a row or another state has an older anchor, it is moved to the newer anchor with: `exp((older_time - newer_time) / decay_length)` The existing semantics are unchanged: `decay_length` is the interval after which a contribution has weight `1/e`. It is not a half-life. With the default `exponential_time_decay_aggregate_function_calculation_budget = 0`, the state representation makes independently built states mergeable with the same calculation. Input rows do not need to be timestamp ordered, and different row orders and batch distributions produce the same mathematical result subject to normal `Float64` rounding. A positive calculation budget opts into approximate aggregation: it is the maximum contribution age measured in decay lengths. Older rows or states are discarded before evaluating `exp`, improving performance when their remaining weight is not useful. Approximate results near the cutoff can depend on row order or merge grouping. The aggregate forms accept numeric timestamps, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64`. ### Finalized decaying values The sum and count aggregate forms return the experimental parameterized type: `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` The decay length is part of the type. Its tuple-compatible storage is canonicalized as `(sign, signed_unit_time, decay_length)`, where `unit_time = anchor_time + decay_length * ln(abs(value))` is the timestamp at which the curve has unit magnitude and `signed_unit_time = sign * unit_time`. Zero has the canonical form `(0, 0, decay_length)`. This representation makes native sorting and relative comparisons match the curve values at any common timestamp for values with the same decay length. Comparisons across different decay lengths are rejected. The redundant decay-length marker is checked against the type parameter when a value is evaluated or combined, preventing incompatible values from being silently mixed through layout-compatible custom-tuple paths. Values can be constructed/aggregated with: `exponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)(value, time)` A finalized decaying value can be aggregated again without repeating the decay length: `exponentialTimeDecayedSum(decaying_value)` When the input is `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)`, the decay length is inferred from its type and the result has the same parameterized type. This gives the closure property required by `SimpleAggregateFunction`, so it can be stored directly in `AggregatingMergeTree`: ```sql CREATE TABLE decaying ( key UInt64, value SimpleAggregateFunction( exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(60)) ) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree ORDER BY key; ``` The scalar helpers are: - `exponentialTimeDecayingValueAt(value, target_time)` — evaluate the same exponential curve before, at, or after its anchor, including at `now()` / `now64()`; - `exponentialTimeDecayingDecayLength(value)` — read the decay length encoded in the type; - `exponentialTimeDecayingAdd(a, b)` — combine two values at their greatest anchor. The `+` operator uses the same addition logic for two decaying values. Different decay lengths are rejected. `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg` continues to return `Float64`. All new regular-aggregate and decaying-value behavior is experimental and disabled by default behind `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. ## Effect on the existing window functions The existing window-function implementation remains in place. Window calls continue to use the previous frame-based implementation, retain their `Float64` result, and do not require `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. This PR also corrects the function documentation to consistently call the parameter `decay_length` and describe the existing `1/e` decay semantics. ## Correctness and tests Stateless tests cover: - regular aggregation and `-State` / `-Merge`; - direct aggregation of finalized `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` values; - direct `SimpleAggregateFunction(exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length))` storage and merging in `AggregatingMergeTree`; - different input orders and batch distributions, including reproducibly generated randomized inputs; - numeric, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` time arguments; - the experimental setting in enabled and disabled forms; - forward and backward value evaluation, addition, decay-length lookup, and rejection of inconsistent/mixed decay lengths; - native sorting and all relative comparison operators, including negative, zero, and positive values; - exact-default, bounded-cutoff, and state-merge calculation-budget behavior; - signed values, empty input, nullable paths, canonical reconstruction, and large-time decay/underflow cases. The implementation uses `Float64` accumulation. As with other floating-point reductions, large signed values that nearly cancel can expose order/grouping-dependent rounding. Stronger reproducibility for that case is intentionally left for a separate improvement if feedback shows it is important in practice. ## Benchmark status There are no end-to-end ClickHouse benchmark results yet. The benchmark already posted in the PR discussion is a standalone C++ microbenchmark of the decay formulas. It showed the expected benefit from avoiding redundant `exp` evaluations in the merge/value paths, but it excludes ClickHouse aggregation, column access, serialization, scheduling, and `AggregatingMergeTree` overhead and therefore is not evidence of end-to-end query throughput. An end-to-end benchmark, preferably a ClickHouse performance test covering state creation and state merging, is still pending. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental mergeable `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` aggregate forms, including a parameterized decaying-value type that can be stored directly with `SimpleAggregateFunction` in `AggregatingMergeTree`, while preserving the existing window-function behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110934&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110934](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110934+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Revert "Revert "NATS: add inline credentials setting""
signal.text: Reverts https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178, restoring the `nats_credentials` setting of the `NATS` table engine (originally added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733), and fixes the reason of the original revert: the possibility of referencing arbitrary server paths through `nats_credential_file`. `nats_credential_file` is a path on the server filesystem: the server opens it with its own privileges, and during authentication the credentials are sent to `nats_url`, which comes from the same query. So a path taken from SQL lets anyone who can define a `NATS` source probe the local filesystem (the error text distinguishes a missing file, a permission error, and a file without a seed), and exfiltrate files the server can read to a NATS server they control (the part of the file before the seed line is sent verbatim in the `CONNECT` frame's `jwt` field). See the analysis in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733#discussion_r3750203599. This hole predates #110733 (`nats_credential_file` exists since 24.2), but with the inline `nats_credentials` setting restored, the path form is no longer needed in SQL at all. The restriction, modelled on `StorageMySQL::getSSLParams` (`e700bbec4c84c585`): `nats_credential_file` is accepted only from a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. Every SQL spelling — the `SETTINGS` clause, an engine-argument override `NATS(collection, nats_credential_file = ...)`, or a named collection created by `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` — throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with a message directing to `nats_credentials`. It is rejected on provenance, whether the query assigned the key at all, rather than on the resulting value, so an override with the empty string cannot silently drop the credentials the operator configured. Loading from previously-validated metadata (server startup, force-restore, and short-syntax `ATTACH`) is exempt via `isLoadingFromExistingMetadata`, so existing tables keep working after an upgrade; a user-issued full `ATTACH TABLE` query is still checked. `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` is not a bypass: the `NATS` engine does not support settings alter. Replacing a configured path with inline `nats_credentials` from the query remains allowed — the path itself is not used then — as long as the named collection permits it. Because the contents are the only spelling a query has, `nats_credentials` inherits the override permission of the path key it replaces, the same way `ssl_ca_pem` does for `ssl_ca` in `findOverrideForbiddingKey`: credentials the operator pinned with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">` cannot be replaced through the contents form either, in either spelling, while the contents form stays usable when `allow_named_collection_override_by_default` is disabled (it is not a new key, it replaces one the collection defines). The `SETTINGS` clause is applied on top of the collection values without passing through the named-collection override check, so `resolveCredentialSource` enforces the same permission for both spellings. An empty `nats_credentials` is refused as well: it can only drop the credentials a collection carries, in either form, never replace them with other ones. Tests: a new stateless test `04891_nats_credential_file_path_restriction` covers all rejected SQL spellings and the accepted configuration-file sources, using `NATS` named collections added to the stateless-test server configuration (`tests/config/config.d/named_collection.xml`, with `nats_url = '127.0.0.1:1'`, so passing the validation surfaces as `CANNOT_CONNECT_NATS`) — one with a plain `nats_credential_file`, one where it is locked with `overridable="false"`, and one without credentials at all; `04665_nats_credentials_named_collection` is updated — the `nats_credential_file` query-override direction is now rejected. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85213 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `NATS` table engine accepts credentials inline in the new `nats_credentials` setting (the same payload as a `.creds` file), and no longer accepts `nats_credential_file` from SQL: the path is a reference to a file on the server filesystem, which the server opens with its own privileges, so it can only be specified in a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. A query may replace such a configured path with inline `nats_credentials`, unless the operator pinned it with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">`. Tables created before this restriction keep working after an upgrade. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114644&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114644](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114644+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Parallelize listing of globbed `s3` table function paths
signal.text: Speeds up listing files for the `s3` table function over globbed paths, in two complementary ways. The listing was a single serial stream of `ListObjectsV2` requests paginated by a continuation token, bound by the per-request latency of S3 (~75 ms measured against `clickhouse-public-datasets`); this dominates queries over buckets with many objects. An earlier attempt (#66504) used speculative keyspace splitting with fixed split points assuming a uniform key distribution and a fixed character set, and was closed as fragile. Controlled by the new setting `s3_list_object_parallelism` (default `1` = the previous serial behavior). **1. Hierarchical layouts** — walk the "directory" tree formed by the `/` delimiter with several worker threads in parallel, pruning subtrees that cannot contain a matching key (so for partitioned layouts like `year=*/month=*/` fewer objects are fetched, not merely listed in parallel). Recursive globs (`**`) keep serial listing. **2. Big flat directories** (e.g. files named by hash/UUID — `musicbrainz/mlhdplus-complete/<uuid>.txt.zst`, ~600k files in one prefix) — when a listed prefix is truncated but has no sub-directories, split it by keyspace: tile the remaining range into contiguous `(start_after, end]` sub-ranges listed concurrently, with boundaries derived from the byte alphabet observed in the listed page. Because the sub-ranges are contiguous they tile the interval **with no gaps** — a key whose byte is absent from the sampled alphabet still falls into the range that brackets it — so the split is complete regardless of the key distribution or character set. The split is a single level and is **probe-gated**: before splitting, one cheap `ListObjectsV2` checks whether any key exists beyond the current bucket; if not (keys share a common prefix, e.g. `pageviews-YYYYMMDD-HH`), the directory is paginated serially instead of issuing a fan of empty boundary probes. This is the robust counterpart to #66504 — it never regresses for clustered keys. On S3 Express / directory buckets — which reject `StartAfter` and only allow the `/` delimiter — keyspace splitting is disabled automatically (detected via `isS3ExpressBucket`), so flat ranges are paginated serially while hierarchical layouts are still listed in parallel. Correctness of glob matching is guaranteed by the existing per-file `RE2::FullMatch`, so the directory pruning only needs to be conservative. **Measured against real S3** (`clickhouse-public-datasets`, ~75 ms/list-request) across ~16 datasets — all return identical results (same count, no duplicates, identical path checksum), serial vs parallel: - Big flat, uniform keys — `musicbrainz/mlhdplus-complete` (594415 files): **37s → 3.7s (~10x)**. - Big flat, clustered keys — `wikistat` (97529) / `gharchive` (100091): probe sends them serial; parallel matches serial (no regression). - Hierarchical — `web/store`: ~2.5x (bounded by its small directory count; scales toward the parallelism factor for larger trees). - Small/medium directories (`nyc-taxi`, `ontime`, `hits/native`, `sensors`, `tranco`, `youtube`, `adsblol`, `bluesky`, …): correct, no regression. A unit test (`gtest_object_storage_parallel_listing`) asserts every key is produced exactly once across parallelism 1–64, including adversarial cases (bytes outside the sampled alphabet, shared long prefixes, boundary keys, mixed hierarchical+flat). Stateless tests (`04339_s3_parallel_glob_listing`, `04340_s3_parallel_flat_listing`) verify parallel and serial listing return identical results. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/65572 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66504 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a setting `s3_list_object_parallelism` to list the files of the `s3` table function over a globbed path in parallel. Hierarchically partitioned layouts are listed by walking the tree of common prefixes concurrently; a single big flat directory is listed by splitting its keyspace into contiguous sub-ranges. This speeds up queries over buckets with many objects (e.g. ~10x for a directory of 600k files). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107567&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107567](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107567+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not pop hints on a line displayed programmatically
signal.text: When a query is displayed at once rather than typed — recalled from the history with Up/Down/Ctrl-P/Ctrl-N, found by the incremental (Ctrl-T) or fuzzy (Ctrl-R) history search, pasted, brought back from the external editor, or preloaded — the as-you-type hints no longer appear at its end. With hints visible, the next Up/Down press would navigate the hints instead of the history, so navigating the history quickly was impossible. The hints are shown again as soon as the line is edited. The suppression is armed before the navigation action because replxx repaints (and regenerates the hints) inside `history_move` itself, and the displayed text is additionally pinned afterwards because replxx may throttle that repaint and replay it after the key handler returns (its "rapid refresh" of e.g. a held-down Up key). Verified with a new pty regression test (`04909_client_hints_history_navigation`, 6 cases), including duplicate-history and unchanged-editor same-text redisplays; the existing `04402_clickhouse_client_autocomplete_inline_hints` (11 cases) and the hint-related expect tests still pass. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114043 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The command line client no longer shows the as-you-type hints on a query recalled from the history (or otherwise displayed at once, e.g. pasted), so pressing Up/Down continues to navigate the history instead of the hint list. signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption when `max_untracked_memory` for those workers does not exceed this setting; operators that permit a larger per-query value must raise the server setting accordingly. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. The reservation itself does not alter query-level or user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`); however, every pipeline worker flushes its pending real allocation reports before releasing its outermost reservation, so those counters and memory-based heuristics can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. When it is at least the workers' `max_untracked_memory`, it makes server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reduces the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. The reservation does not alter query-level or user-level accounting, but workers flush pending real allocation reports before releasing their outermost reservation, so those counters can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Reserve memory for merges up front
signal.text: Add proactive memory reservation for background merges, enhancing the existing `merges_mutations_memory_usage_soft_limit` mechanism. `background_memory_tracker` measures memory that background tasks have *already* allocated, so `canEnqueueBackgroundTask` is purely reactive: when many merges are scheduled at the same time — for example right after a mutation produces many parts — their IO buffers are not allocated yet, all of them pass the gate, and only then grow their memory usage and collide. Every merge now estimates the memory of its input and output IO buffers (`CompactionStatistics::estimateNeededMemoryForMerge`) as the number of input column streams (over all source parts) times the read IO buffer size, plus the number of output column streams (of the result part) times the write IO buffer size. Object storage (S3) write buffers are large and double-buffered, so they are accounted separately. Since IO buffers only ever hold data that flows through them, the estimate is capped by the data volume of the merge (beyond the eagerly allocated per-stream compressor and file buffers, which honor adaptive write buffers): without this cap, a merge of tiny parts in a many-column table on object storage would reserve gigabytes it can never touch, and concurrent merges would saturate the soft limit and starve each other. The merge reserves this amount at start (`MergeMemoryReservation`) and releases it when it finishes. A merge that will certainly run the vertical algorithm is priced by the streams that are alive at once (the merging columns, one gathering column at a time, and up to `max_merge_delayed_streams_for_parallel_write` delayed streams) rather than all output streams concurrently, and a stream whose data volume is not derivable from the source parts (a rebuilt projection, a `DEFAULT`-filled column of variable size) is priced at the buffers its writer allocates before any data flows through it (its compressor block and file buffer) plus a projected-volume bound, rather than at any multipart upload size - a multipart writer starts from the buffer size its caller passes and grows it only with the data written into it, leaving further growth to the reactive tracker — over-reservation starves all merges, while under-reservation merely degrades to the reactive behavior of the current code for that stream. `canEnqueueBackgroundTask` now consults both the actual usage and the reservation: - a non-replicated background merge reserves at selection and is not scheduled when the reservation would exceed the limit (it retries later); once `CurrentlyMergingPartsTagger` chooses the actual destination disk, the reservation is corrected if the pre-selection guess made from the source parts was wrong, and a merge that waited in the background queue re-prices its reservation at task start against the destination disk's live multipart upload settings (a config reload could have raised them), as the replicated path does. Whether a background merge runs as a `ReplacingMergeTree` cleanup merge is decided at selection and carried to the scheduler, so a row-reducing cleanup merge is priced as one; - a replicated merge, already committed to run locally, reserves unconditionally at execution so the reservation still throttles selection of further merges; - a user-initiated merge (`OPTIMIZE`) also reserves unconditionally, so it is throttled by the gate for other merges but can never be silently skipped by it. A single merge whose estimate exceeds the whole limit is always allowed to proceed alone, so progress is never blocked. Adds the `MergesMutationsMemoryReservation` metric for observability, a `gtest` for the reservation accounting, and stateless tests: a smoke test and a regression test that `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` merges everything down to a single part under a pathologically small soft limit instead of silently doing nothing. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Background merges now reserve the memory of their input/output IO buffers up front against `merges_mutations_memory_usage_soft_limit`, so that scheduling many merges at once (for example right after a mutation) can no longer oversubscribe memory as they all start. A user-initiated `OPTIMIZE` is never silently skipped by this mechanism. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109433&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109433](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109433+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Randomize tests with DETACH/ATTACH table before query execution
signal.text: Add `reattach_tables_before_query_execution` and `reattach_tables_before_query_execution_probability` settings that enable randomly detaching and reattaching tables used in a query before its execution. This is a testing-only feature designed to find bugs related to table reattachment. Before executing a query, the system collects all tables referenced in the AST, and for each eligible table (stores data on disk, supports detaching, has no action locks or dependencies), it performs a `DETACH` followed by `ATTACH`. Changes: - Add `supportsDetachingTables` virtual method to `IDatabase` (overridden to `false` for engines that do not support non-permanent `DETACH TABLE`: `DatabaseDictionary`, `DatabaseReplicated`, `DatabaseSQLite`, `DatabaseBackup`, `DatabaseFilesystem`, `DatabaseHDFS`, `DatabaseS3`, `DatabaseURL`, `DatabaseRemote`, `DatabaseDataLake`, `DatabaseMaterializedPostgreSQL`) - Add `has`/`hasAny` methods to `ActionLocksManager` for checking existing locks (skipping expired `weak_ptr` entries) - Add table collection visitor and reattach logic in `executeQuery` (runs after AST validations, process list admission, and external tables initialization; skips `EXPLAIN`, transactions, internal/non-initial queries, and CTE name collisions) - Fix off-by-one in `MergeTreeDeduplicationLog::dropOutdatedLogs` (don't drop the active log) and add `sync` call in shutdown - Add `no-random-detach` tag to tests incompatible with this feature - Add `--no-random-detach` and `--reattach-tables-probability` options to `clickhouse-test` - Add `02461_reattach_tables` test Continuation of #55943. signal.title: Convert the JOIN keys to the type of the values that they have in common
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 There is no type that is able to hold all the values of both `UInt64` and `Int64`, so a JOIN on such keys was rejected: ``` SELECT * FROM (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS a INNER JOIN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS b ON a.number = b.number - 1 Code: 386. DB::Exception: There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64 ... ``` But a JOIN does not need the least supertype. It is enough to convert both keys to the type of the values that they have in common - the most subtype, which is `UInt64` for this pair, holding the values from `0` to `9223372036854775807`. A value outside of this range is not equal to any value from the other side, so `accurateCastOrNull` converts it to NULL, and it does not match anything. This is applied to the equality conditions in the `ON` section, and to the `USING` section of an `INNER JOIN` or a `SEMI JOIN`, where the result contains only the matched values. It is not applied to: - the kinds of JOIN with `USING` that can emit unmatched rows (`LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, `ANTI`), where the key is also a column of the result and can hold the unmatched values; - null-safe comparisons (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`), where NULL matches NULL, so the values converted to NULL would match each other; - the ASOF inequality (the last column in the `USING` list), which needs the order of the values, not only their equality; - a `Join` table engine whose stored key is not itself the common type, because its hash table is prebuilt over the original key values and cannot be converted - the opposite direction, where only the probe key has to be converted, is supported. A runtime filter is not built for such a JOIN, because a `NOT IN` filter over a set with NULLs would drop the rows that have to be preserved. Only the queries that were failing before are affected - the type inference is unchanged whenever the least supertype exists. It is implemented in the analyzer, which is enabled by default; with `enable_analyzer = 0` the old `TableJoin::inferJoinKeyCommonType` path still rejects such a JOIN, exactly as before. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow a JOIN on keys that have no common supertype, such as `UInt64` and `Int64`. Previously such a query was rejected with `There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64`. Now the keys are converted to the type of the values that they have in common, and a value outside of this range does not match anything. This requires the analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112951&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112951](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112951+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Sync `BackupImpl` lock-file handling and the Cloud-only resume state
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 This is the public side of the private pull request above, and most of it is that sync. The shared files both touch -- `BackupImpl.h`, `BackupImpl.cpp`, `BackupFactory.h` -- are identical here and there, down to the blank lines, so `Check public build` can overlay the private ones unchanged and later syncs have nothing to reconcile in them. What stays private is where the resume path lives, because nothing outside ClickHouse Cloud resumes a backup. The part that changes this build is the lock-file handling. `createLockFile` creates the lock with `writeFileIfNotExists`, so two backups racing for the same destination cannot both believe they own it. When the create fails it compares what is there against what it would have written: its own contents mean a concurrent backup, a completed `.backup` means the backup already exists, and a lock that has since disappeared rethrows the original failure rather than guessing. `removeLockFile` now reports whether the destination still holds the lock. `checkLockFile(false)` is false both for a foreign lock and for one it could not read, so a caller could not tell "not ours" from "unknown" while the lock was still there; `tryRemoveAllFiles` reports that as a failure rather than claiming the destination is clean. `open` also removes a lock it created when the verification that follows throws. Otherwise the lock outlives the failed attempt and fences the destination against every later one, which cannot match it either: a retry picks a fresh backup UUID, so the orphaned lock belongs to nobody. The rest is state that only ClickHouse Cloud reads. `BackupImpl` is where continuing an interrupted backup is implemented, so what it keeps for one belongs here: whether this attempt is a continuation, the timestamp text the earlier attempt wrote into `.backup`, the ownership check to run before publishing anything, and whether `.backup` is already published. All of it, the two helpers that reconcile an already-published manifest, and every place the shared implementation reads or reports it, are behind `CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, so this build behaves as it did: it writes its own timestamp and always publishes metadata. The parameters that fill the state in stay out, along with the code that reads them. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `BACKUP` now creates the lock file in its destination atomically, and removes it when the attempt that created it fails before writing anything. A failed backup no longer leaves behind a lock that no later backup can match, and concurrent backups writing to one destination are reported as such instead of failing with whatever the storage returned.

signal.title: Fix Arrow export of JSON, Dynamic, QBit and AggregateFunction
signal.text:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115023 Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/91170 The `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types_as_binary` fallback wrote a column with no first-class Arrow mapping by calling `IColumn::getDataAt` per row. That method exposes a column's contiguous in-memory bytes, which most of the types reaching the fallback do not have: - `ColumnObject` (`JSON`), `ColumnVariant` (hence `ColumnDynamic`) and `ColumnQBit` throw `Method getDataAt is not supported`, so `SELECT ... FORMAT Arrow` failed on them — after the schema message had already been written, leaving the client with a truncated stream; - `ColumnAggregateFunction::getDataAt` returns the `AggregateDataPtr` itself, so exporting an aggregate state silently wrote raw heap addresses instead of the state, both corrupting the data and disclosing server addresses. Before the fallback existed these types were rejected with a clear `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, so both are regressions introduced together with the setting: ``` -- 26.4, before #91170 SELECT '{"a":1}'::JSON FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 50. The type 'JSON' of a column 'j' is not supported for conversion into Arrow data format. (UNKNOWN_TYPE) SELECT sumState(number) FROM numbers(3) FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 50. The type 'AggregateFunction(sum, UInt64)' ... (UNKNOWN_TYPE) -- 26.5 .. 26.8 SELECT '{"a":1}'::JSON FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 48. Method getDataAt is not supported for Object(max_dynamic_paths=1024, max_dynamic_types=32). (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) SELECT sumState(number) FROM numbers(3) FORMAT Arrow; -- succeeds, writes 00D0A9C9D37F0000 ``` The fallback now serializes each value through `ISerialization`, whose `serializeText`/`serializeBinary` are pure virtual and therefore defined for every type, so the "do not fail a `SELECT *`" property that motivated the setting holds by construction instead of depending on an unrelated method's implementation status. The aggregate state written in binary mode is the `RowBinary` encoding and deserializes back into the original `AggregateFunction` type. `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types` (`throw` / `text` / `binary`) replaces the boolean, adding a `text` mode that writes what `CAST(col AS String)` would produce — useful for the BI clients that drive `SELECT *` over Arrow Flight SQL, and the workaround users had to apply by hand for `JSON`. Its default, `binary`, is the previous behavior, and its `SettingsChangesHistory` entry has identical previous and new values so `compatibility` never marks it changed. The boolean keeps working with full effect (`0` means `throw`, `1` means `binary`) and is only consulted while the new setting is left at its default, so an explicit mode wins whichever order the two are set in. Both writers — the native Arrow IPC one behind `FORMAT Arrow`/`ArrowStream` and the Apache-Arrow-library one behind Arrow Flight SQL — make the accept/reject decision in the schema converter, before the schema message is written, so a rejected type can no longer abort a stream whose schema the reader has already accepted. Both serialize the values with the query's own `FormatSettings`, so a setting the serialization depends on (`output_format_binary_write_json_as_string`, `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers`, …) produces the same payload whichever writer serves the query. An opaque column is tagged in both writers with the `clickhouse.opaque` Arrow extension name and the original ClickHouse type name in `ARROW:extension:metadata`, so a consumer can tell it apart from a genuine string or binary column. Per the Arrow extension-type convention a reader that does not know the extension name ignores the metadata and sees the plain storage type, so no existing consumer changes behavior. `StorageArrowFlight::ArrowFlightSink` built its converter settings from scratch and never consulted the setting, so it always used the struct default. It now resolves the mode from the query context like the other Arrow Flight call sites, which makes `INSERT INTO ... ENGINE = ArrowFlight` of an `AggregateFunction` column follow the setting; `throw` reproduces the previous behavior exactly. `JSON` and `Dynamic` cannot reach that sink, because the storage rejects a dynamic-structure column when the table is created and the table function takes its header from the remote schema. Verified against a local ClickHouse Arrow Flight server as well as `FORMAT Arrow`: `SELECT *` over a table with `JSON` and `AggregateFunction` columns returns them as `clickhouse.opaque`-tagged `binary` fields carrying the ClickHouse type name, with a neighbouring `String` column left untagged; `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types = 'text'` switches them to tagged `string` fields holding the text; and the payloads match the native writer byte for byte under the serialization settings above. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `SELECT ... FORMAT Arrow` failing with `Method getDataAt is not supported` for `JSON`, `Dynamic` and `QBit` columns, and silently exporting heap addresses instead of the aggregate state for `AggregateFunction` columns. Added the `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types` setting (`throw` / `text` / `binary`, default `binary`) which supersedes `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types_as_binary`.

signal.title: Push down volume-reducing functions in query plan
signal.text: Adds a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, so those steps carry the fixed-size result instead of the original `String` / `FixedString` argument. The rewrite is done with `ActionsDAG::split`: the function nodes form the first part, which becomes a new step below the child, and the second part becomes the parent step's `ActionsDAG` and reads the results as inputs. It only fires when the wide argument column really stops flowing through the child step — the column is removed from the child's output, and unless the child reads it itself it is not even produced below the child. `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` and `trySplitFilter` keep the pushed functions where they are, so the optimizations do not move the same nodes in opposite directions. For the shape from the issue below, `SELECT avg(length(s)) FROM test WHERE notEmpty(s)`, the filter still needs `s` to evaluate its condition, but `length(s)` is now computed before the filter, so the wide column is not copied for the surviving rows. Enabled by default; can be turned off with `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions = 0`. An earlier attempt at the same optimization was https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 by @talmawash, credited as a co-author. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82378 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, replacing the wide `String` / `FixedString` argument with the fixed-size result, so it is neither buffered by a sort nor copied by a filter. signal.title: Fix division by zero in `ReadFromMergeTree` when `StorageMerge` truncates the number of streams
signal.text: The `AST fuzzer (amd_debug)` raised `Integer divide by zero` on ```sql SELECT id FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t$') ORDER BY id DESC SETTINGS max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 1073741824, max_threads = 4 ``` The planner computes `max_streams = max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 2^32`, which passes the existing overflow check because it fits in `size_t`. `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` passed `UInt32(streams_num)` to `storage->read`, truncating `2^32` to zero. The child `ReadFromMergeTree` then divides by the requested number of streams in `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder`. `IStorage::read` takes `size_t num_streams`, so this change removes the narrowing cast and adds a regression test. Additionally, `StorageMerge` multiplied the requested number of streams by `max_streams_multiplier_for_merge_tables` with unchecked `Float64` to `size_t` conversions. Both sites now use a shared checked helper that throws `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` if the product does not fit in `size_t`. `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreams` and `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder` also now use a division-based comparison when clamping streams to data, avoiding overflow in `num_streams * min_marks_for_concurrent_read`. The previously added streaming-read guard and its test are removed because current `master` now bounds effective `MergeTree` stream counts before that code path. Found by the AST fuzzer on an unrelated PR: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113010&sha=59507af89c33f62942e855b50b3e66704cbcf2e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113010 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an arithmetic exception in debug and sanitizer builds when reading from a `Merge` table with a very large `max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`: the number of streams was truncated to 32 bits, so multiples of `2^32` became zero. Also throw `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` instead of invoking undefined behavior when multiplying stream counts for a `Merge` table exceeds `size_t`, and avoid an overflow when limiting `MergeTree` streams to the amount of data. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113382&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113382](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113382+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Tag functional tests averaging over 60s under MSan with `no-msan`
signal.text: MSan stateless jobs are the slowest functional-test jobs in CI and sit right at the edge of the 9000 s job timeout. In a recent run the private `Stateless tests (amd_msan, distributed cache, meta in keeper, s3 storage, sequential, 2/2)` job spent 8324 s of its 9000 s budget on tests and was then killed during teardown, even though all 526 tests had passed. MSan is ~5.8× slower than release on the same tests, and the cost is concentrated in a long tail: under MSan, 8 tests take over 180 s each, and the 30 slowest account for ~48% of a sequential shard's runtime. This tags every functional test whose mean duration under MSan exceeds 60 s with `no-msan`, except two tests that would otherwise lose all sanitizer coverage. ### How the set was chosen From `play.clickhouse.com`, over the public MSan stateless checks (`Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, parallel, N/M)` and `Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, sequential, N/2)`, excluding the flaky-check and selected-tests flavors): ```sql SELECT test_name, count() AS runs, avg(test_duration_ms)/1000 AS avg_s FROM checks WHERE check_name LIKE 'Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, %' AND check_name NOT LIKE '%flaky%' AND check_name NOT LIKE '%selected%' AND test_status = 'OK' AND check_start_time >= now() - INTERVAL 30 DAY GROUP BY test_name HAVING runs >= 20 AND avg_s > 60 ORDER BY avg_s DESC ``` 351 tests matched. 30 of them no longer exist in `master` (reverted, split into smaller tests, or removed), leaving 321. One of those, `04062_text_index_json_all_values_ghdata`, already carried `no-msan`; two more remain under MSan to retain their only sanitizer coverage, so 318 files change here. Only `OK` runs are counted, so timeouts and failures do not inflate the averages. ### Initial expected effect The following estimates were calculated before retaining the two sanitizer-coverage tests. | Flavor | MSan test time per commit | Removed | Share | |---|---|---|---| | parallel | 129025 s | 24766 s | 19.2% | | sequential | 11236 s | 4108 s | 36.6% | ### 25 slowest of the tagged tests | Test | Mean under MSan | Runs | |---|---|---| | `03988_cached_read_big_at` | 384.6 s | 9014 | | `03008_deduplication_insert_several_blocks_replicated` | 337.2 s | 9116 | | `03008_deduplication_several_mv_into_one_table_nonreplicated` | 308.8 s | 9118 | | `03008_deduplication_insert_several_blocks_nonreplicated` | 282.6 s | 9118 | | `04039_merge_tree_snapshot_teardown_race` | 275.2 s | 9347 | | `01195_formats_diagnostic_info` | 234.6 s | 9278 | | `02475_bson_each_row_format` | 206.1 s | 9264 | | `00626_replace_partition_from_table_zookeeper` | 202.5 s | 9323 | | `01019_alter_materialized_view_atomic` | 192.5 s | 9340 | | `04062_text_index_json_all_values_ghdata` | 190.4 s | 1806 | | `01721_join_implicit_cast_long` | 182.8 s | 9339 | | `00746_sql_fuzzy` | 180.5 s | 9340 | | `03755_large_primary_key_explain` | 180.2 s | 9337 | | `02943_variant_type_with_different_local_and_global_order` | 180.2 s | 9284 | | `02448_clone_replica_lost_part` | 177.4 s | 9263 | | `02372_analyzer_join` | 176.3 s | 9345 | | `04327_cluster_functions_huge_num_streams_no_crash` | 171.8 s | 9261 | | `01721_join_implicit_cast_long_oldanalyzer` | 168.9 s | 9346 | | `01079_bad_alters_zookeeper_long` | 166.8 s | 9322 | | `01747_system_session_log_long` | 165.9 s | 9014 | | `03208_array_of_json_read_subcolumns_1` | 165 s | 9339 | | `00429_long_http_bufferization` | 160.9 s | 9277 | | `04411_deep_nested_field_to_type` | 156.8 s | 9262 | | `01383_log_broken_table` | 156.4 s | 9340 | | `03326_protobuf_schemas_race` | 155.1 s | 9279 | (318 tests are tagged in total; the full list is the diff.) ### Trade-off A large share of these are the ZooKeeper, replication, mutation and race tests — precisely where MSan is most likely to find real uninitialized-memory bugs. They continue to run under ASan, UBSan and TSan, but this is a genuine reduction in MSan coverage rather than a pure win. An alternative that keeps the coverage is duration-aware sharding of the sequential jobs: the split is currently `crc32(test filename) % total_batches`, which gave one recent shard 8248 s against its sibling's 5514 s (1.50×), so balancing alone would have reclaimed ~23 min on the shard that timed out. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115050&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115050](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115050+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not treat an existing object as proof that a multipart upload completed
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114348 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113994 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed silent data loss when writing to a fixed S3 key that already holds an object, for example `INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3(...)` with `s3_truncate_on_insert = 1`. If the multipart upload was aborted between create and complete, for example by an `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule, `CompleteMultipartUpload` correctly returned `NoSuchUpload`, but the error was rewritten to success whenever any object existed at the key, so the INSERT was acknowledged while none of its rows were stored and the previous object kept being served. The error is now only absorbed when the object at the key is the one the upload would have produced. Closes #114348. ### Description Requested by @ zlareb1 in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114348#issuecomment-5255487765. `Client::CompleteMultipartUpload` absorbs `NoSuchUpload` if a `HeadObject` finds any object at the key. That check is from #56475, whose premise is a completion that succeeded and whose response was lost - i.e. the completion was replayed *and* the object is this upload's. Key existence tests neither, so a genuinely aborted upload against a key holding an unrelated object also passes, and the INSERT is acknowledged with none of its rows stored. `NO_SUCH_UPLOAD` is unretryable and excluded from `isTransientCompleteMultipartUploadError`, so this rewrite is the only thing between the abort and a silent success. MergeTree over S3 is unaffected: it writes random unique keys. The rewrite now requires the object to carry the ETag implied by the request's own part list, `md5(concat(binary md5 of each part))-<N>`. No extra request, no new state, and both callers (`WriteBufferFromS3`, `copyS3File`) are fixed at once. It fails closed: when the ETag does not match or is not derivable - SSE-KMS, a non-default checksum algorithm, S3 Express, a provider that computes it differently - the original error is returned, so a replay that used to be absorbed now errors. A failed INSERT is recoverable; a silently discarded one is not. A matching ETag proves the payload, not the create-time attributes: a completion may also carry `If-Match` / `If-None-Match`, and `CreateMultipartUpload` may carry metadata or a storage class, which this layer cannot observe. That residual is pre-existing, strictly less reachable here, and unset on the in-tree S3 multipart paths. #113994 addresses it in `WriteBufferFromS3`, which knows the writer identity. A new integration test fails on master (INSERT acknowledged, old object survives) and passes here, with a no-fault control. Two unit tests keep #56475 honest: a matching object is absorbed, a foreign one errors. cc @ scanhex12 @ kssenii @ CheSema <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114375&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114375](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114375+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Announce the connection endpoint once when the client asks for a password
signal.text: `clickhouse-client` printed `Connecting to ...` twice whenever it had to ask for a password: ``` $ clickhouse client --host clickhouse.new --secure --user alexey-milovidov ClickHouse client version 26.8.1.1. Connecting to clickhouse.new:9440 as user alexey-milovidov. Password for user (alexey-milovidov): Connecting to clickhouse.new:9440 as user alexey-milovidov. Connected to ClickHouse server version 26.8.1. ``` Neither `--password` nor `--ask-password` was given, so the client did not know whether the user has a password at all and connected without one. The server answered `REQUIRED_PASSWORD`, and the retry loop in `Client::main` set `ask-password` and called `connect` again, which prompted for the password and announced the very same endpoint a second time. Now an endpoint is announced only when it differs from the one announced last, and the announcement is forgotten after a successful connection, so a fallback to another port and a reconnect later in the session are still announced. Added `04909_client_password_prompt_announces_endpoint_once.expect`, which fails on the current `master` binary with `The endpoint was announced twice.` and passes with this change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `clickhouse-client` no longer prints the `Connecting to ...` message twice when it asks for a password interactively. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115081&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115081](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115081+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix logical error for RIGHT JOIN with parallel replicas
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113292 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108645 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the logical error `Can't determine table for parallel replicas` for a `RIGHT JOIN` whose right side has no table eligible for parallel replicas, and made such a `RIGHT JOIN` materialize a left side that is not a `MergeTree` instead of letting every replica read it independently. ### Description Master-only logical error thrown at `findParallelReplicasQuery.cpp:637`: release builds reject the query, debug and sanitizer builds abort, reddening Stress and fuzzer jobs. **Root cause.** For `JoinKind::Right` the side read with replicas is the right one, because `buildQueryTreeForShard` materializes the left table expression into a temporary table. `getSupportingParallelReplicasQueries` descended the left expression instead, so a query was accepted for its left side, the rewrite materialized that same side, and the lookup on the rewritten tree threw. `88b22b8fb66c115` (#108645) flipped the target while renaming `getRightTableExpression`; `26.2` through `26.7` still descend right, so the defect is confined to master. **The fix** descends the right expression again (`RIGHT SEMI`/`ANTI` were affected too), then corrects three places that had the materialized side wrong, each of which let every replica read its own copy of data it must not: - `rewriteJoinToGlobalJoin` decided locality from the right side for every kind; it now requires the materialized side of a `RIGHT JOIN` to be eligible for parallel replicas, not merely `MergeTree`. - That question was asked about the raw storage, so an eligible `View`/`MaterializedView` lost its local join; the wrapper is resolved to the table it reads first. - The global-join collector skipped each global join's right child, so a nested global join in the offloaded subtree never got a temporary table. The last two were reported by `clickhouse-gh[bot]`. No backport is requested: every release branch already decides locality from the right side while descending right, so that half is pre-existing there and no repro was measured on a release binary. **Validation.** New stateless test, untagged and parallel-safe. It fails on unmodified master with the logical error, and reverting any hunk reddens only that hunk's own assertions. At the current head it passes 30/30 sequentially and 12/12 at four-way concurrency, and is identical across the `join_use_nulls` and `compatibility` values Stress randomizes. The 127 `parallel_replicas` tests show no regression. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113515&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113515](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113515+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add assertions in IColumn::mutate to verify deep unique ownership of sub-columns
signal.text: Investigation for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/99920 This is a draft PR with diagnostic assertions to help find a COW violation bug where columns stored in `HashJoin` have their `allocatedBytes()` change because internal sub-columns are modified by someone who treats immutable columns as mutable. ## What was found The bug manifests as `data->allocated_size != debug_allocated_size` exception in debug builds. Investigation narrowed it down to: 1. **Removing the single-chunk optimization** in `Squashing.cpp:70-72` fixes the bug — this optimization passes chunks through without `IColumn::mutate`, so columns remain shared with Memory engine blocks 2. The **modification happens between** `addBlockToJoin` calls — during pipeline processing of the next chunk 3. The mutation is a **reallocation** (reserve/grow), not a data write — `protect()` (mprotect) doesn't catch it 4. The assertions in this PR (`IColumn::mutate` deep ownership check) **do NOT fire** — meaning the mutation happens outside the `IColumn::mutate` path entirely. Someone treats an immutable column as mutable without going through `mutate`. ## Reproducer The test `04049_fix_hashjoin_shared_column_allocated_size` reproduces the exception in debug builds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Refuse to materialize columns used in sort key expressions
signal.text: Changelog category: Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) Changelog entry: Fixed `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE COLUMN` for `MergeTree` tables: materializing a column required by a key expression (sorting key, partition key, projection sorting key, or the engine sign/version column) — directly or via a dependent `MATERIALIZED` column — is now refused instead of silently corrupting the sort order / partition assignment of existing parts. Dependent skip indices, projections, statistics and TTL bounds that read a recomputed column are rebuilt instead of being hardlinked with stale values. Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is not required (bug fix) ## What this PR does `ALTER TABLE MATERIALIZE COLUMN c2` was allowed when `c2` appeared inside a sort key expression like `ORDER BY metroHash64(c1, c2)`, but was correctly blocked for direct sort keys like `ORDER BY c2`. Materializing such a column recalculates its values (e.g., `MATERIALIZED now()` produces new timestamps), which invalidates the sort order of existing data parts. Subsequent merges or deletes then fail with: ``` Logical error: 'Sort order of blocks violated for column number 2' ``` ### Root cause The original check only consulted `getSortingKeyColumns()`, which returns the top-level column names in `ORDER BY`. For function-based keys like `ORDER BY metroHash64(c1, c2)`, the column names are `metroHash64(c1, c2)` — not `c1` or `c2`. So the check missed columns used as arguments to sort key functions. ### Fix `MATERIALIZE COLUMN` now mirrors the protections `UPDATE` already has, refusing the command (with `CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN`) when the materialized column — or a stored `MATERIALIZED` column computed from it (one level, matching `UPDATE`) — is required to evaluate: - the table sorting key expression (`getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey`, subcolumn-aware); - the partition key expression; - a projection's sorting key expression; - the engine merge-semantic column (`CollapsingMergeTree` sign / `ReplacingMergeTree` version). When the command is allowed, a dependent stored `MATERIALIZED` column is recomputed in an extra mutation stage, and any skip index / projection / statistics / TTL expression that reads a rewritten column is fed into the mutation stream so the derived object is rebuilt instead of hardlinked with stale values. ## Test plan - [x] Stateless test `04046_materialize_column_sort_key_expr.sql` covering: direct sort key column, sort-key function expression, subcolumn-parent sort key, projection sorting key, partition key (and subcolumn-parent partition key), skip-index/projection/statistics rebuild, dependent `MATERIALIZED` columns (recompute and key-feeding refusal), TTL recalculation, and the engine sign/version columns. A column not used in any key still materializes successfully (no over-rejection). - [ ] CI (full test suite) Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/93139 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99647&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/99647](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F99647+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Require a join subquery alias only when it removes a real ambiguity
signal.text: `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default) rejected every unaliased subquery, table function or union used in a multi-table join, even when the missing alias could not cause any ambiguity. That is stricter than necessary: an alias only serves to qualify a column, so it is only needed when the unaliased table expression exposes a column whose name also occurs in another table expression of the same join. `validateJoinTableExpressionWithoutAlias` now throws `ALIAS_REQUIRED` only on such a name collision (computed with the existing `getColumnsFromTableExpression` helper over the sibling table expressions), and otherwise allows the missing alias. Genuine ambiguities involving non-sibling table expressions are still caught later by the normal `AMBIGUOUS_IDENTIFIER` resolution, exactly as they are for ordinary tables. This lets standard queries such as TPC-DS q14 (whose `cross_items` derived table has no correlation name) run without setting `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 0`: ```sql SELECT i_item_sk FROM item, (SELECT iss.i_brand_id AS brand_id FROM store_sales, item AS iss ...) WHERE i_brand_id = brand_id; -- no shared column name -> no alias needed ``` Notes: - Validation in `resolveJoin`/`resolveCrossJoin` is moved to run after all table expressions of the join are resolved, so sibling columns are known when the collision is checked. - The change is purely permissive: it never turns a previously-succeeding query into an error. When the columns of any side cannot be determined it falls back to the old strict behavior. - Only the analyzer is affected; the deprecated non-analyzer path keeps the stricter behavior. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): With `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default), the analyzer now rejects an unaliased subquery or table function in a join only when the missing alias would make one of its columns unreachable, for example because the name collides with another joined table expression or is shadowed by an in-scope alias; otherwise the query is allowed. If the analyzer cannot determine the exposed names up front, it keeps the old strict behavior. Unambiguous queries, such as some standard TPC-DS queries, no longer require adding an alias. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109368&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109368](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109368+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Convert stateless tests that modify the server's data on disk to integration tests
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113978 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114056 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114057 Stateless tests are not allowed to modify the server's data on disk at all (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113978#pullrequestreview-4891978370): the stateless suite runs against arbitrary server configurations — object storage, shared merge tree, encrypted disks — where the local part layout either does not exist or does not mean what the test assumes, and modifying it corrupts shared state. This PR converts all stateless tests that do such manipulation into integration tests, grouped by scenario, and adds a style check that rejects new ones: **Extended existing modules:** - `test_broken_projections` ← `02254_projection_broken_part`, `04511_check_table_broken_projection_columns` - `test_broken_tmp_txn_version_startup` ← `04104_transaction_version_metadata_dummy_tid_load`, `04492_attach_as_replicated_clears_tmp_txn_version`, `04493_attach_part_clears_tmp_txn_version`, `04507_packed_part_stale_txn_version_guard` - `test_lost_part` ← `02369_lost_part_intersecting_merges`, `02370_lost_part_intersecting_merges`, `04215_replicated_missing_covered_part_on_start` **New modules:** - `test_corrupted_part_files` (files inside part directories damaged/removed; loading, fetching, and `CHECK TABLE` reactions) ← `02253_empty_part_checksums`, `02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start`, `02444_async_broken_outdated_part_loading`, `04151_unique_key_sst_rebuild_on_load`, `04235_corrupted_columns_substreams_detection`, `04323_text_index_marks_empty_part`, `04506_packed_part_fetch_checksum` - `test_mutations_with_tampered_parts` (mutations over parts with old-version emulation or corrupted index files) ← `04401_dynamic_mutation_old_part_no_substreams_file`, `04412_mutation_old_part_basic_map_partial`, `04426_mutate_repair_corrupted_missing_idx_checksums`, `04427_mutate_some_columns_drop_index_corrupted_idx`, `04428_mutate_corrupted_text_index_multistream`, `04431_mutate_corrupted_index_sibling_owns_file` - `test_attach_tampered_detached_parts` (detached part directories manipulated before `ATTACH` / `DROP DETACHED`) ← `04063_drop_detached_part_with_try_n_suffix`, `04246_materialize_index_force_recalc` (the canned `part_25.8.tar.gz` moves into the module), `04402_mutate_all_columns_preserve_legacy_idx_minmax`, `04403_mutate_preserve_legacy_idx_packed_minmax`, `04404_mutate_rebuild_legacy_idx_minmax`, `04425_mutate_mixed_legacy_idx_minmax` - `test_backups_from_disk` (backups placed or tampered with directly on the `backups` disk) ← `04054_backup_restore_validate_entry_paths`, `04495_backup_metadata_version_overflow`, `02864_restore_table_with_broken_part`, `03001_restore_from_old_backup_with_matview_inner_table_metadata`, `03214_backup_and_clear_old_temporary_directories`, `03231_old_backup_without_access_entities_dependents`. The canned backup zips move from `tests/queries/0_stateless/backups/` into the module, and `helpers/install_predefined_backup.sh` is replaced by a module helper. - `test_server_metadata_files` (direct manipulation of on-disk table metadata `.sql` and the `flags/` directory) ← `03001_matview_columns_after_modify_query`, `04329_create_or_replace_force_drop_flag`, `04545_attach_projection_part_offset_setting_disabled` The conversions are faithful: every `.reference` output became an exact assertion, the originals' explanatory comments are preserved, and `DETACH`/`ATTACH` stayed `DETACH`/`ATTACH` except where the original explicitly emulated a server restart (`02255`, `04215` — "on start" scenarios now use a real server restart). Notable finds along the way: - `02444_async_broken_outdated_part_loading` contained a quoting bug since its introduction: `rm -f "$path/*.bin"` never expanded the glob, so the "broken" outdated part was never actually broken. The converted test applies the corruption for real, and the assertions still hold. - `02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start` dropped a nonexistent table (`projection_broken_parts_1`) in cleanup instead of its own tables. Verified locally against a fresh master binary: all new tests pass under the integration runner, and the tampered-parts modules were additionally cross-checked against a pre-fix binary where the bug-detecting assertions fire as intended. The style check (`server_data_manipulation_in_stateless_tests` in `ci/jobs/check_style.py`, folded in from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114056) flags stateless `.sh` tests that fetch a server-side filesystem path from a system table (`system.parts`, `system.detached_parts`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.tables`, `system.disks`, `system.server_settings` with `name = 'path'`) and also run file-modifying shell commands (`rm`/`cp`/`mv`/`dd`/`truncate`/`ln`/`chmod`/`touch`/`mkdir`/`tar`, `sed -i`, output redirection into a variable-derived path, `clickhouse-disks write`/`remove`/...). With all offenders converted here, the exclusion list holds only one documented false positive (`04326_disks_app_read_checksums`, which writes an `mktemp` scratch file under `CLICKHOUSE_TMP`) and `04630_merge_over_stale_packed_tmp_dir`, whose conversion is pending in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114057. Verified: the check is clean on this branch and catches each converted test if its stateless original is restored. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114070&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114070](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114070+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
