signal.title: Fix the streaming-insert block wait not expiring under the query profiler
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109592 Related: https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/CONC-834 **Problem.** The file-descriptor poll timeout can silently never expire on a query thread. `ReadBufferFromFileDescriptor::poll` restarts the interrupted `poll` with the full original timeout after `EINTR`, resetting the deadline on every signal. Query threads receive periodic sampling-profiler timer signals (`query_profiler_real_time_period_ns`, default 1 s; the handler's `SA_RESTART` does not apply — per `signal(7)`, `poll` is never auto-restarted), so whenever the signal period does not exceed the timeout, the wait becomes unbounded while the fd stays silent. The user-visible path is the streaming-insert block wait: `IRowInputFormat::read` calls `poll` with the remaining `input_format_max_block_wait_ms` budget over a `StorageFile` fd/file or stdin buffer. With the profiler active, a stalled input source delays the partial-block flush indefinitely instead of flushing when the wait limit is reached. (All socket paths use `ReadBufferFromPocoSocket*::poll`, which is already deadline-aware, and are not affected.) **Root cause.** Same defect class as the MySQL `connect_timeout` fix in #109592 (mariadb-connector-c, upstream [CONC-834](https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/CONC-834)): an `EINTR` retry loop that passes the original timeout instead of the remainder. This was the last such site in `src/` — a sweep of all timed waits (`poll`/`epoll_wait`/`select`/`nanosleep`/`sigtimedwait`/io_uring/timerfd) found every other one deadline-aware (Poco sockets, `Epoll`, `KeeperTCPHandler`, `ShellCommandSource`, `base/sleep`). **Fix.** Re-poll with the remaining time computed **in microseconds from a single monotonic anchor**, reporting a timeout once the budget is exhausted. Per-retry whole-millisecond accounting (as in some existing call sites) would truncate a sub-millisecond retry interval to zero and make no progress under a sub-millisecond signal cadence, so the remainder is derived from the untouched anchor instead. The unit test (`gtest_fd_read_buffer_poll_under_signals.cpp`) waits on a pipe with no writer while a per-thread kernel timer (`timer_create` + `SIGEV_THREAD_ID`, the query profiler's own mechanism, so delivery deterministically targets the polling thread) interrupts the poll at two cadences: 10 ms (the classic deadline reset) and 0.5 ms (pins the microsecond-precision accounting). A watchdog thread disarms the timer after 3 s so a regressed build fails the elapsed assertion at ~3.2 s instead of hanging; the fixed poll returns in ~200 ms. Verified in both directions: the naive loop fails both cadences, a millisecond-accounting variant fails exactly the sub-millisecond one. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the block-wait timeout of streaming inserts (`input_format_max_block_wait_ms`) potentially never expiring while the query profiler is active: the file-descriptor poll restarted with the full timeout after every profiler signal, so a stalled input source could delay the partial-block flush indefinitely instead of flushing when the wait limit is reached. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109602&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109602](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109602+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix vacuous truth for x op ALL (empty subquery)
signal.text: `x op ALL (empty set)` should return TRUE per SQL standard (vacuous truth). ClickHouse was returning FALSE because the `= ALL` rewrite uses `singleValueOrNull`, which returns NULL for empty sets, making `x IN (NULL) = FALSE` incorrectly. The `min` / `max` rewrites used for the other comparison operators have the same problem, because they return the default value of the type for an empty set. Fixed in `modifyAST` by also selecting `count` from the right-hand side, so the empty case can be recognized. To keep the right-hand side evaluated exactly once - evaluating it twice is observable when it is non-deterministic - `count` and the aggregate are computed by a single `SELECT` returning a tuple, and the two values are taken apart with `tupleElement`: ``` x op ALL (S) --> tupleElement(SQ, 1) = 0 OR x op tupleElement(SQ, 2) where SQ = (SELECT (count(*), aggregate_function(*)) FROM S) ``` Both occurrences of `SQ` are textually identical, and scalar subqueries are cached by the hash of the subquery (`ExecuteScalarSubqueriesVisitor` for the old analyzer, `evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded` for the new one), so `S` is scanned once and both `tupleElement` calls observe the same evaluation. This preserves all existing behavior for a non-empty right-hand side and only fixes the empty-set case. `04759_all_subquery_single_evaluation` is a regression test that fails if the right-hand side is evaluated twice. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105957 ### Changelog category : - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description): Fixed `x op ALL (empty subquery)` incorrectly returning FALSE instead of TRUE (vacuous truth). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106373&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106373](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106373+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject invalid event numbers and durations in sequenceMatch patterns
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an `out_of_range` exception raised as an internal `Code: 1001` error when a `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` or `sequenceMatchEvents` pattern contains the event number `0`, for example `sequenceMatch('(?0)')`. Such a pattern is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. A temporal condition holding a lone sign, such as `sequenceMatch('(?1)(?t>+)(?2)')`, was silently treated as `(?t>0)` and is now rejected with `SYNTAX_ERROR`. ### Description Event numbers are 1-based, but the bound check validated only the upper bound, so `(?0)` passed it. The conversion to a 0-based condition index then underflowed `UInt64` to `SIZE_MAX`, and `std::bitset<32>::set()` rejected that with `std::out_of_range`. Thrown from the aggregate function constructor during analysis, it surfaced as an internal `Code: 1001` error and aborted the server in debug and sanitizer builds. Two further inputs reached the same state: an event number overflowing `UInt64`, and a sign with no digits, `(?+)`. In each case `tryReadIntText` fails after consuming a byte while its pointer overload discards the boolean, so the existing "Could not parse number" check does not fire and the output keeps its initialiser `0`. Adding the missing lower bound validates the parsed value and covers all three at once, error code and message unchanged. The sibling temporal branch shared that parse-success defect and is fixed here too, after review automation raised it: `(?t>+)` was accepted as `(?t>0)`. The duration is now read through the `ReadBuffer` overload so the boolean is available, and rejected when it is false. The position check is kept, because `tryReadIntText` also succeeds while consuming nothing for a leading non-digit, which is what rejects `(?t>)`. Only the sign form leaked; `(?t>-)` and an overflowing duration were already rejected, and `(?t>+5)` still equals `(?t>5)`. All three functions share this parser and were affected; all are covered by new assertions in `00222_sequence_aggregate_function_family`, which fail on an unfixed binary. One imprecision is left as is: an overflowing event number is reported as event number `0`. Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)`, `bitset set argument out of range` (STID 2508-34fb): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115019&sha=7be817c59e288cab7aa329a76ed1ba65b9d555e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29. Also seen on `Stress test (arm_tsan)`. Both carrier pull requests are bystanders; the defect reproduces on pristine master. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115056&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115056](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115056+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Share the speculatively built IN set between the part tasks of a mutation
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Restores set sharing between the part tasks of one mutation filtering on `IN (subquery)` over a primary key column. `enable_sharing_sets_for_mutations` is on by default, but the set built for primary key analysis stopped participating in the shared cache, so a table with N parts materialized the same set N times. ### Description `MutatePlainMergeTreeTask::prepare` installs one `PreparedSetsCache` per mutation so its part tasks materialize an `IN (subquery)` set once. The speculative build that feeds primary key analysis in `FutureSetFromSubquery::buildOrderedSetInplace` passed `nullptr` for that cache, and `CreatingSetsTransform` only consults a cache when it has one, so that build neither reused another part's set nor offered its own. The `nullptr` was justified by a hazard `findOrPromiseToBuild` only half handles: it drops a failed entry for a task arriving later, but not for a sibling already blocked in `SharedSet::get()`, which failed the whole mutation under `mutations_sync`. So sharing the build must make an abandoned build retryable without making a real failure retryable. Reaching `CreatingSetsTransform`'s destructor with the promise unfulfilled means the build was abandoned, so it now publishes a null set, the already existing retryable outcome; a real error is published by `CreatingSetsTransform::work`, which resets the promise, so it still reaches every waiter instead of being rerun once per part task. `04697_shared_set_error_not_inherited` pins the abandoned path with the `prepared_sets_build_ordered_set_inplace_fail` failpoint; `gtest_prepared_sets_cache` pins both halves. This passes the context's cache to the speculative build and reads the set back through `tmp_set_and_key->set`, since a cache hit rebinds that member. Measured on a four-part table: sets built per mutation goes from 6 to 2, cache hits from 2 to 6, and `02581_share_big_sets_between_mutation_tasks` from 10.0 s to 6.4 s on Debug; under coverage it had reached about 313 s against a 600 s cap ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111833&sha=9897b64077d80ba7454f1e53ce0ff6e345ab37fe&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20ParallelReplicas%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%29)). The sharing test asserts per part task, not per mutation, that no set key is materialized twice, that fewer part tasks build the set than there are part tasks, and that a part task which reused it still prunes; the cache lives only as long as the part tasks holding it, so how many share one materialization is a scheduling property. Reverting the read-back half reddens the pruning assertion; reverting the cache argument reddens all three. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112941&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112941](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112941+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Optimize `GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` queries by maintaining a bounded heap during aggregation to prune groups that cannot appear in the result, significantly reducing memory usage and execution time for high-cardinality grouping. Controlled by the `enable_group_by_top_k_optimization` setting. Based on the initial implementation by [Dmitriy Terenichev](https://github.com/Dmitry909) ([#78553](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/78553)). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/72610 Query shapes that benefit from this optimization: - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N` -- single key, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key LIMIT N` -- single key, no ORDER BY - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2, k3 ASC LIMIT N` -- 3+ keys, full match - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, ORDER BY is a prefix of GROUP BY - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 1 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 2 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 LIMIT N` -- composite keys, no ORDER BY - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL ORDER BY URL ASC LIMIT N` -- String keys - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL LIMIT N` -- String keys, no ORDER BY Not supported (optimization is skipped): - `ORDER BY agg()` (ORDER BY aggregate function, not a GROUP BY key) (handled by [another PR](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/98607)) - `WITH TOTALS`, `HAVING`, `GROUPING SETS`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP` - `LIMIT WITH TIES` - ~~Non-final aggregation (distributed partial aggregation)~~ - `max_rows_to_group_by` is set - `rows_before_limit_at_least` mode (exact count) - a COLLATE on any of the matched GROUP BY keys (a COLLATE on a later ORDER BY column past the full key prefix cannot affect which groups qualify and does not disable the optimization) - ORDER BY columns that are not a leading prefix of GROUP BY keys <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96630&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/96630](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F96630+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Feature: Enable overlay databases for server.
signal.text: Enables server-side `Overlay` databases. An `Overlay` database is a read-only facade that exposes the union of the tables of several underlying databases, resolving each table name through the listed sources in order (the first source that has the table wins). DDL on the facade is rejected — it has no storage of its own — while `SELECT` and pass-through `INSERT` resolve to the underlying source table. Reading or writing through the facade requires the corresponding grant on both the facade database and the underlying source, and the facade's row policies are combined with the source's. Previously an `Overlay` database existed only as the implicit default database of `clickhouse-local`. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/52764 <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow creating `Overlay` databases. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=86768&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/86768](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F86768+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Automatic LowCardinality serialization based on uniq statistics
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/85145 --> This PR adds automatic `LowCardinality` serialization for `MergeTree`, analogous to the existing automatic `Sparse` serialization. A `String` or `FixedString` column whose declared type is **not** `LowCardinality` can now be stored on disk in dictionary-encoded form when it has a `uniq` statistic with a low cardinality estimate. The encoding is transparent: the column keeps its declared data type, flows through the query pipeline as a (non-native) `ColumnLowCardinality`, and is materialized to a full column at the boundaries that require it. **Motivation:** save disk space and read I/O for low-cardinality string columns without requiring users to declare the column type as `LowCardinality(...)`. **How it works** - A new per-part serialization kind `LOW_CARDINALITY` (shown as `LowCardinality` in `system.parts_columns.serialization_kind`). - The decision is made at write time from the **existing** `uniq` statistic — there are **no changes to statistics serialization**. In `MergeTreeDataWriter`, a `String`/`FixedString` column whose `uniq` estimate does not exceed the new `MergeTree` setting `max_uniq_number_for_low_cardinality` (default `0` = disabled), and which was not already chosen for `Sparse`, is stored with `SerializationLowCardinality`. The column must therefore declare `STATISTICS(uniq)` and have `materialize_statistics_on_insert` enabled. - A new `is_native` flag on `ColumnLowCardinality` makes `getDataType` report the nested type, so the "column class matches data type" invariant holds while such a column flows through the pipeline. It is materialized to a full column in `removeSpecialRepresentations` (aggregation, joins, squashing, blocks), in the merge-input step of `IMergingAlgorithm`, in the sorting and sparse-removing transforms, and in `IFunction`. The `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` pass skips columns stored as non-native `LowCardinality`, since the dictionary encoding does not expose the data type's regular subcolumns. - The kind is independent of sparse serialization: `SerializationInfo` entries for eligible columns are created in the writer, in merges, in mutations and in the per-table serialization hints even when `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization = 1` disables `Sparse` entirely. **Notes** - Opt-in: disabled by default and requires an explicit `uniq` statistic, so existing tables are unaffected. Requires `allow_experimental_statistics`. - Reading a subcolumn of an encoded column (for example `s.size`) is not supported and reports `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`: the subcolumn's streams do not exist in a dictionary-encoded part. Making it read the full column and extract the subcolumn in memory needs a dedicated serialization and is left for a separate change. - Extracts and reimplements the automatic `LowCardinality` part of the draft #85145 against current `master`, without the statistics-serialization refactoring. That refactoring is still unmerged (#85145 and #109128 are open drafts). Validated locally with a server built from this branch: kind selection for `Wide` and `Compact` parts, `String` and `FixedString`, query correctness, functions, `GROUP BY`/`ORDER BY`/`DISTINCT`/`LIMIT BY`/window functions, joins, `IN` subqueries, `INSERT SELECT`, `UNION ALL`, `OPTIMIZE FINAL` (LowCardinality preserved through merges), mutations, `ALTER RENAME`/`MODIFY COLUMN`, `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, `PREWHERE`, input/output formats with and without `allow_special_serialization_kinds_in_output_formats`, and tables with mixed `Default` and `LowCardinality` active parts. The three tests also pass with `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization` forced to `0.0` and `1.0`, with `enable_block_offset_column`/`enable_block_number_column`, with compact parts, and over repeated fully randomized runs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added automatic `LowCardinality` serialization: a `String`/`FixedString` column that has a `uniq` statistic and low cardinality can be stored in dictionary-encoded form on disk while keeping its declared data type. Controlled by the new `MergeTree` setting `max_uniq_number_for_low_cardinality` (disabled by default). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107436&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107436](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107436+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114679&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114679](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114679+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Check the query cancellation while filling `system.parts` and its siblings
signal.text: The tables based on `StorageSystemPartsBase` (`system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`) build the whole result eagerly in `initializePipeline`, so a cancelled or timed out query kept building rows over every storage and part until the very end. In a stress test with ThreadFuzzer this took minutes and tripped the hung check: a `SELECT` over `system.parts_columns` (with a filter matching every active part on the server) stayed in the process list for 252 seconds with `is_cancelled = 1` and `max_execution_time = 10`. Check the query status per storage and per part, following the pattern of `system.zookeeper` and `system.remote_data_paths`. The check also covers the storage-discovery prepass in `StoragesInfoStream` (the eager enumeration of all databases and tables), the analogous prepass in `StoragesDroppedInfoStream` (so `system.dropped_tables_parts` is interruptible as well), the skip loop in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::next`, and the per-storage part enumeration itself: the `MergeTreeData` helpers (`getDataPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllDataPartsVector`, `getProjectionPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllProjectionPartsVector`) take an optional `need_stop` callback that is checked periodically while the parts snapshot is being built. The two column-oriented tables additionally check the query status inside their column-enumeration loops and their metadata prepass, so a very wide table does not create a long uninterruptible stretch inside a single storage. The return value of `checkTimeLimit` is honored, so with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'` the eager build stops at the soft deadline and returns the rows collected so far. The table-lock acquisition in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::tryLockTable` is interruptible as well: instead of a single wait inside `RWLockImpl::getLock` for the whole `lock_acquire_timeout`, the lock is acquired in 100 ms slices with a query-status poll between the attempts (the total timeout and the `DEADLOCK_AVOIDED` semantics are preserved), so a killed or soft-timed-out query does not sit in the lock wait while a concurrent DDL query holds the drop lock. The test `04869_system_parts_lock_wait_cancellation` pins this with a share lock held by a long `SELECT` and a `DROP TABLE` in an `Ordinary` database queued behind it. The test uses the new `slowdown_system_parts_enumeration` failpoint, which only affects the specially named test tables (so concurrently running tests are unaffected). It sleeps 500 ms on every enumerated part, so building the full result for a 20-part table takes at least 10 seconds, and it sleeps 1 second per `COLUMNS_CANCELLATION_CHECK_PERIOD` (128) enumerated columns of a part, so building the full `system.parts_columns` / `system.projection_parts_columns` result over a single part with 1,025 columns (and a projection over all of them) takes at least 8 seconds. The test asserts that queries with a 1 second deadline in the `break` mode finish well under that (the elapsed time is taken from `system.query_log`, because the startup of `clickhouse-client` alone takes seconds in the debug and sanitizer builds), which is only possible by stopping at the per-part and per-column cancellation checkpoints. Timed assertions are needed because a plain row-count assertion cannot distinguish a build with the fix from one without: in the `break` mode the executor drops the eagerly built result after the deadline in both cases. The test also asserts partial row counts under a pre-expired deadline for all five tables, including `system.dropped_tables_parts` over a deterministic dropped-table fixture. The pre-expired-deadline checks also run under the failpoint, so the fewer-rows assertion is deterministic even on a machine fast enough to build the whole result in under a millisecond. For tables with the `_snap` name marker, the failpoint additionally slows down the parts-snapshot walks inside `MergeTreeData` (500 ms per enumerated part) and makes them poll the stop callback on every element, and for tables with the `_meta` name marker it slows down the column-metadata prepass of the column-oriented tables (1 second per 128 enumerated metadata columns), so the timed checks also prove that the snapshot materialization and the prepass are interruptible: all six of these checks fail against a binary with the `need_stop` polls and the prepass checkpoints disabled. Caught by `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113722&sha=ceedb772f6aa36e221d25ce48f9af71f032a7b08&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113722 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries over `system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`, and `system.dropped_tables_parts` now react to cancellation and `max_execution_time` while the result is being built. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113909&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113909](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113909+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Command get xdbc type info
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115015 Generic Flight SQL clients rely on `CommandGetXdbcTypeInfo` to discover the data types supported by a server. It is used, for example, by Power BI's built-in ADBC Flight SQL path and by the Flight SQL JDBC driver's `DatabaseMetaData.getTypeInfo()`. Until now the command fell through to the `NotImplemented` catch-all in `commandSelectorImpl`, so those clients could not resolve column types. Adds a handler that builds the ODBC/JDBC type metadata table directly with the schema from `arrow::flight::sql::SqlSchema::GetXdbcTypeInfoSchema()`, so the 19-column result (including nullability) matches exactly what Flight SQL clients expect. The table covers 25 ClickHouse types: `Bool`, `UUID`, `Int8`-`UInt64`, the wide integers `Int128`/`Int256`/`UInt128`/`UInt256`, `Decimal`, `Float32`/`Float64`, `String`/`FixedString`, `Enum8`/`Enum16`, `Date`/`Date32`, and `DateTime`/`DateTime64`. Rows are ordered by `(data_type, type_name)` as the protocol requires, and the optional `data_type` filter is honored; an unknown code returns an empty table with the full schema. The metadata follows the semantics documented in `FlightSql.proto`: - Datetime rows report the generic `XDBC_DATETIME` (9) in `sql_data_type` and the concrete type in `datetime_subcode` (`XDBC_SUBCODE_DATE` = 1, `XDBC_SUBCODE_TIMESTAMP` = 3). - `create_params` is NULL for types without parameters and lists the parameter keywords otherwise (`FixedString` -> `length`, `Decimal` -> `precision,scale`, `DateTime` -> `timezone`, `DateTime64` -> `scale,timezone`). - Exact numeric types report their maximum precision in `column_size` and `num_prec_radix` = 10; approximate numeric types use `num_prec_radix` = 2. The direct-table approach (same pattern as `CommandGetSqlInfo`) was chosen over building the result from SQL because it lets the result schema match `SqlSchema::GetXdbcTypeInfoSchema()` exactly; Flight SQL clients compare the returned schema against that canonical schema. Also includes: - `FlightSQLClient.get_xdbc_type_info()` in the integration test client, with a hand-built protobuf descriptor for `CommandGetXdbcTypeInfo`, and two integration tests covering the unfiltered table, the ordering, the metadata values (`sql_data_type`, `datetime_subcode`, `create_params`, `num_prec_radix`), and the `data_type` filter (including the empty result for an unknown code). - A row in the Arrow Flight SQL documentation listing `CommandGetXdbcTypeInfo` as supported. The two integration scenarios were exercised end-to-end against a locally built server: the unfiltered call returns 25 rows in `(data_type, type_name)` order, and the `data_type` filter returns only the matching rows. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added support for `CommandGetXdbcTypeInfo` in the Arrow Flight SQL server, so generic Flight SQL clients can retrieve ODBC/JDBC type metadata for ClickHouse data types, including the optional `data_type` filter.

signal.title: Fix set index on an expression with a Nullable operand
signal.text: A `SELECT` filtered on an expression that matches a `set` skip index raises `LOGICAL_ERROR`: ```sql CREATE TABLE events (id UInt32, INDEX b_set intDiv(id, 1000) TYPE set(100) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO events SELECT number FROM numbers(5000); SELECT count() FROM events WHERE intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000)) = 3; -- Code: 49. Unexpected return type from equals. Expected Nullable(UInt8). Got UInt8. ``` `SELECT 1000` is Nullable(UInt16), while the underlying column type of the index is plain UInt32, so when MergeTreeIndexConditionSet rewrites the predicate it loses the Nullable type and just saves that it is a UInt. However the equals function still expects a Nullable, and this mismatch throws an error in `ExpressionActions.cpp:executeAction`. ============================================ No `Nullable` appears anywhere in the schema or the query. A scalar subquery is typed `Nullable` because it may return no rows, and that is enough. In practice this shows up when the divisor or bucket size comes from a lookup or settings table instead of a literal; the typing is identical. Explicit wrappers reach the same failure: `nullIf(1000, 0)`, `toNullable(1000)`. `MergeTreeIndexConditionSet` matched a query subexpression to an index key column by name only. Names are computed from constant-folded arguments and never include types, so `intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000))` renders exactly like the index expression `intDiv(id, 1000)` while carrying `Nullable(UInt32)`. The whole subtree was then replaced by the granule column while the enclosing `equals` was re-added with its already-resolved `IFunctionBase`, keeping the return type it was resolved with. `ExpressionActions::execute` binds inputs by name without checking types, so the granule supplied a non-`Nullable` column and the declared return type no longer matched what execution produced. `atomFromDAG` now binds the key column input to the type the granule block holds and restores the query-side type on top of it with `toNullable`, so the enclosing atom keeps the `IFunctionBase` it was resolved with. The atom function is not re-resolved from `FunctionFactory`, so there is no resolution failure to catch. A `chassert` pins the postcondition that the node handed back carries the type the query side expects. `toNullable` changes the type and not the data: the granule column's null map is all zeros, so `equals` produces no NULL, the `ifNull` that `traverseDAG` adds for a `Nullable` atom substitutes nothing, and the mask is bit-for-bit what the non-`Nullable` atom produces. Pruning is therefore unchanged rather than merely correct — `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` reports the same 5/50 granules for `t % nullIf(19, 0) = 16`, `t % toNullable(19) = 16`, `t % (SELECT 19) = 16` as for the plain `t % 19 = 16`. Two cases fall back to `UNKNOWN_FIELD`, which leaves the granule unpruned and sends the query through the regular filter path. A key column that is already an `INPUT` of the filter DAG, which cannot be re-typed, because a second input under the same name would be left unbound where `ExpressionActions::execute` maps each name to one block column. And a type difference that is not a `Nullable` the query side added: `toNullable` over the granule type has to reproduce the query-side type exactly, since dropping a `Nullable` the granule holds would substitute values for its NULLs. The regression test covers both granule filtering paths, since `secondary_indices_enable_bulk_filtering` selects between `getPossibleGranules` and `mayBeTrueOnGranule`, and each reaches the same actions independently. An index whose expression is itself `Nullable` is unaffected in either direction, because the types agree and nothing is re-typed; such an index prunes conservatively both before and after this change, because the granule genuinely stores NULLs and each maps to `UNKNOWN_FIELD`. Reproduces on the official release `26.8.1.727`. In builds with assertions enabled it aborts the server, which is how it surfaced in CI — 14 occurrences in 90 days across unrelated pull requests and every build configuration, through `tests/queries/0_stateless/01786_explain_merge_tree.sh` once the AST fuzzer wraps the modulus in a `Nullable` expression. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113233 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113234 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113233 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/89802 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `LOGICAL_ERROR` when reading a table with a `set` skip index defined on an expression and the query repeats that expression with a `Nullable` operand, for example `WHERE intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000)) = 3` over `INDEX b_set intDiv(id, 1000) TYPE set(100)`. A scalar subquery is enough to trigger it, since it is typed `Nullable`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113244&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113244](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113244+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1673` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` in `query_plan_convert_join_to_in` with `arrayJoin` JOIN key
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` exception in `INNER JOIN ... ON arrayJoin(...) = ...` queries when `query_plan_convert_join_to_in` is enabled and the SELECT references the source array column. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- Not applicable -- bug fix, no new feature or API change. --> --- ### Problem With `SET query_plan_convert_join_to_in = 1` (off by default), the optimizer rewrites a hash `INNER JOIN ON arrayJoin(L.col) = R.col` into `[Expression("Calculate join left keys"), Filter("IN"), DelayedCreatingSets, Expression("Join output actions")]`. If the SELECT projection (or any post-JOIN expression) references the source array column `L.col` itself, or `arrayJoin(L.col)` again, the rewritten plan throws ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column __table1.tags in block ... (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` at execution (and at `EXPLAIN actions = 1` planning time). Minimal repro: ```sql CREATE TABLE lt (id UInt64, tags Array(String)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE rt (tag_id String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tag_id; INSERT INTO lt VALUES (1, ['a','b','c']), (2, ['d','e']); INSERT INTO rt VALUES ('a'), ('d'); -- Throws NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK: SELECT lt.id, lt.tags FROM lt INNER JOIN rt ON arrayJoin(lt.tags) = rt.tag_id SETTINGS query_plan_convert_join_to_in = 1; -- Same with arrayJoin in the projection -- also throws: SELECT lt.id, arrayJoin(lt.tags) FROM lt INNER JOIN rt ON arrayJoin(lt.tags) = rt.tag_id SETTINGS query_plan_convert_join_to_in = 1; ``` ### Root cause `tryConvertJoinToIn` builds `left_pre_join_actions = JoinExpressionActions::getSubDAG(<left join keys>)`. The output set is only the JOIN-key expressions — `arrayJoin(__table1.tags)` and `__table1.id` in the repro — **not** the source `__table1.tags` array column. Later, `cloneSubDAGWithHeader(output_header, JoinExpressionActions::getSubDAG(join_output_actions))` clones the post-JOIN expressions onto a new DAG seeded from `output_header`. `cloneSubDAGWithHeader` calls `mergeInplace(..., remove_dangling_inputs=true)`, which remaps `INPUT` nodes by name to the corresponding inputs in `output_header`. When `join_output_actions` references `__table1.tags` (because SELECT did), the source `__table1.tags` INPUT in `second_dag` has no match in `output_header` — `mergeInplace`'s `remove_dangling_inputs` only removes input nodes that collide with `first`'s inputs, not input nodes that have no counterpart at all. The non-INPUT nodes that depend on it (the cloned ARRAY_JOIN node when SELECT had `arrayJoin(lt.tags)`, or the column reference itself when SELECT had `lt.tags`) survive, and the resulting `ExpressionStep` cannot find the column at execution. ### Fix Decline the conversion in `tryConvertJoinToIn` whenever any input of `join_output_actions` is not among the outputs that `left_pre_join_actions` forwards. The check runs immediately after `left_pre_join_actions` / `right_pre_join_actions` are computed and **before** any plan mutation (`makeExpressionNodeOnTopOf` etc.), so the bail-out is safe — the query then runs through the normal JOIN path and produces the correct result. ```cpp { auto join_output_actions_subdag = JoinExpressionActions::getSubDAG(join_output_actions); std::unordered_set<std::string_view> forwarded_columns; for (const auto * out : left_pre_join_actions.getOutputs()) forwarded_columns.insert(out->result_name); for (const auto * input : join_output_actions_subdag.getInputs()) if (!forwarded_columns.contains(input->result_name)) return 0; } ``` The check mirrors the established `appendInputsForUnusedColumns` style (`ActionsDAG.cpp:1453-1461`), which is the idiomatic "verify every input is present in a sample block" pattern in this codebase. ### Related fixes for the same root cause This is the third bug in 12 months rooted in `mergeInplace` / `clone` of an ARRAY_JOIN-bearing DAG being merged into a context whose stream header does not provide a required INPUT column. The prior two are: - #96989 (prevention strategy: blacklist `ARRAY_JOIN` in the pushdown eligibility check). - #97239 (bail-out strategy: detect ghost `ARRAY_JOIN` after the merge and abandon the optimization). - #104785 (post-hoc cleanup strategy: snapshot the merged-in `ARRAY_JOIN` pointers and drop them after the merge via a new `ActionsDAG::removeNodes` helper). This PR follows the bail-out pattern of #97239 — `tryConvertJoinToIn` is an optional optimization, so declining the rewrite is safe and the query falls back to the regular JOIN path. A more invasive follow-up could forward the missing left-side columns through `left_pre_join_actions` so the optimization stays on even in these cases; left for a separate PR once we have evidence that real workloads hit the bail-out frequently. The setting `query_plan_convert_join_to_in` is off by default, so the bug is reachable only when explicitly enabled. ### Regression test `tests/queries/0_stateless/03918_convert_join_to_in_arrayjoin_dangling.{sql,reference}` — co-located with #96989's `03918_arrayjoin_function_with_join_and_where`. Four queries: 1. `SELECT lt.id ... INNER JOIN ... ON arrayJoin(lt.tags) = rt.tag_id` — the optimization stays on, returns the correct rows (validates the fix's "no-regression" guarantee for the cases it does not bail out on). 2. `SELECT lt.id, lt.tags ...` — before fix: NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK; after fix: correct result via the fallback JOIN path. 3. `SELECT lt.id, arrayJoin(lt.tags) ...` — same shape as (2). 4. Control: same as (3) with `query_plan_convert_join_to_in = 0`. Confirms the fallback path returns the same answer the fix produces in (3). Repro-first verified: queries (2) and (3) were observed to fail with NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK on un-fixed upstream master (`7bd0fa28146`) before the reference was locked. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1674` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Block disabling the analyzer in the Stress test and fuzzers more tightly
signal.text: The Stress test and the AST fuzzer (and BuzzHouse, which installs the same profile) already constrain `enable_analyzer` to `<min>1</min>` so that neither a test nor a fuzzed query spends the run on the old interpreter. A constraint only rejects an *explicit* setting change though. `compatibility` set below 24.3 — the version where the analyzer became the default — rewrites every setting that is not marked `changed`, so it reverts `enable_analyzer` to 0 without an explicit change and the constraint never fires. With the Stress test profile as it is now: ``` SET compatibility = '23.2'; SELECT getSetting('enable_analyzer') --> false /?compatibility=23.2&query=SELECT getSetting('enable_analyzer') --> false ``` The AST fuzzer profile is immune because it also pins the value (`<enable_analyzer>1</enable_analyzer>`), which keeps the setting `changed` so that `applyCompatibilitySetting` skips it. The Stress test profile had no such pin and relied only on the client-side `enable_analyzer=1` that `stress.py` passes, while `stress.py` randomizes `compatibility` down to 20.1. This pins the value in the Stress test profile too, and documents in all four places why both halves are needed, so that neither is later removed as redundant. The comment in `ast_fuzzer_job.py` still described a `readonly` constraint that was replaced with `min` in 03782060870. The new test builds the same pinned and constrained profile in SQL and checks that: - every explicit way of disabling the analyzer is rejected (`SET`, an in-query `SETTINGS` clause, the `allow_experimental_analyzer` alias, the client command line, settings stored in a view); - a no-op `enable_analyzer = 1` sent together with `compatibility` is still accepted — a `CONST` constraint rejects it, which is why `min` is used; - a pre-24.3 `compatibility` does not revert the pinned value. Not addressed here: `SET <setting> = DEFAULT` is not checked against constraints at all (`resetSettingsToDefaultValue`), so `SET compatibility = '23.2'; SET enable_analyzer = DEFAULT` still gets through. That is a server-side bypass of settings constraints in general and is fixed separately. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115328&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115328](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115328+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1675` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add UUID2 data type with correct sorting
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110066 Introduces `UUID2`, a variant of the `UUID` data type with correct (lexicographic) sorting. ## Motivation For historical reasons, the `UUID` data type sorts by the *second half* of the value. This is unexpected and, in particular, hurts the performance of primary indexes built on `UUIDv7` columns, whose most significant bits are a timestamp: with sorting by the second half, primary-key analysis cannot prune granules by the timestamp. ## What this does `UUID2` stores the 128-bit value as a plain big-endian integer of the 16 canonical bytes, so that natural integer comparison of the underlying value matches the textual (lexicographic) order and the canonical byte order used by most other systems. It reuses the `UUID` column and `Field` representation (like `DateTime` reuses `UInt32`), so sorting is correct with no extra comparison code, and its binary/interchange serialization is the canonical big-endian byte order. - `UUID1` is an alias of the current `UUID` type. - A new setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) controls whether the bare name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` (`1`) or `UUID2` (`2`) at `CREATE`/`ALTER` time. The resolved concrete type is materialized into the stored table definition (including nested types such as `Array(UUID)`), so reads never depend on the session setting and existing tables are never rewritten. The default will be flipped to `2` in a later, separate change. - Conversions to/from `String`, `UInt128`, `FixedString(16)` and `UUID`, plus `toUUID2` / `toUUID2OrZero` / `toUUID2OrNull`. - Parity across functions (`hex`/`bin`, `reinterpretAs*`, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `UUIDToNum`, `empty`/`notEmpty`, `min`/`max`, hashing, `uniq`), formats (`RowBinary`, `Native`, `JSON`, `CSV`, `TSV`, `Arrow`, `Parquet`, `Avro`, `BSON`, `MsgPack`, `Protobuf`, `CapnProto`, `JSONExtract`) and storage (`generateRandom`, `bloom_filter` skip index). The `UUID` type is unchanged (verified: still sorts by second half, identical conversions, default `uuid_type_version = 1`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new data type `UUID2`, a variant of `UUID` that sorts by its textual (lexicographic) representation instead of by the second half of the value. signal.title: Fix MATERIALIZED column value depending on the selected columns while a mutation is pending
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103182 ## Problem While a mutation is pending, the value of a `MATERIALIZED` column can depend on which columns the query selects: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, x Int32, z Int32, m1 Int32 MATERIALIZED x + z, m2 Int32 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1; INSERT INTO t (id, x, z) VALUES (1, 10, 100); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; SET alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0, enable_lightweight_update = 1, apply_patch_parts = 1; ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; -- stays pending SET apply_mutations_on_fly = 0; UPDATE t SET z = 500 WHERE 1; -- lightweight update, creates a patch part SET apply_mutations_on_fly = 1; ``` ``` SELECT m2 FROM t; -- 511 (consistent with m1 = 510, the value in the patch) SELECT x, z, m1, m2 FROM t; -- 20 500 520 521 ``` Both reads see the same data, so both must return the same `m1` / `m2`. The expected result is `20 500 510 511`: `m1` in the patch part was computed from `x = 10`, the value visible when the lightweight update ran. The code being fixed was added to master in #103182 and is not part of any release, so no released version is affected. ## Root cause After an `UPDATE`, `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` emits one stage per dependency level to recompute the `MATERIALIZED` columns derived from the updated ones (`emit_materialized_recompute_stages`). Those stages were created with a plain `stages.emplace_back(context)`, leaving `Stage::mutation_version` unset, while the `UPDATE`'s own stage carries `command.mutation_version` (via `addStageIfNeeded`). On-fly reads derive the patch-visibility window from consecutive stages' versions (`AlterConversions::getMutationSteps`, `MergeTreeReadersChain`), so a version-less stage leaves that window unbounded above: a patch part created *after* the pending `UPDATE` becomes visible to the recompute stages, which then recompute `m1` from the patched `z` and override the value the patch carries itself. Whether that happens depends on which columns the read requests, hence the two different answers above. ## Solution Pass the command's version into the recompute stages, so they are fenced exactly like the stage of the command they belong to. The patch-materialization and `CLEAR COLUMN` call sites keep the current behaviour (`std::nullopt`): the stages they follow carry no version either, and choosing a version for them is a separate question, out of scope here. Regression test `04927_materialized_recompute_stage_mutation_version`, which on master returns `20 500 520 521` / `520` instead of `20 500 510 511` / `510`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115372&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115372](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115372+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support bearer-token authentication in BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP
signal.text: `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP` had no way to authenticate with a bearer token: callers spliced an `Authorization: Bearer` entry into the header list themselves and had to remember not to pass HTTP Basic credentials at the same time, because both occupy the same header. `create` now takes the credential directly, in three overloads: Basic credentials, a bearer token, or both — with a non-empty token taking precedence, so the either/or rule lives in one place instead of in every caller. `create` also appends the bearer header to a local copy of the header list rather than mutating the builder, so a builder can be reused without carrying over a stale token. Every bearer-token call site of the class is migrated to the new overloads: - `HTTPBasedCatalogUtils` and `UnityCatalog`: built the header by hand and passed never-used HTTP Basic credentials alongside; now call `create` with the token. - `RestCatalog`, `OneLakeCatalog`, `BigLakeCatalog`: `getAuthHeaders` now returns an `AuthHeaders` (a bearer token plus extra headers). The bearer goes to `create`; only genuine extra headers (a user-supplied `auth_header`, `x-goog-user-project`, `User-Agent`) stay in the header list. `OneLakeCatalog`'s pre-obtained token also moved from a spliced header to the bearer. - `PaimonRestCatalog`: the `bearer` token provider (the `dlf` request-signing branch keeps its own signed headers). Out of scope — different transport (plain Poco requests or S3-client headers), not `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP`: `OpenAIProvider`, `CloudJWTProvider`, ArrowFlight `AuthMiddleware`, GCS `diskSettings`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110313&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110313](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110313+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: [ClickHouse-58380] Implement Retries in distributed queries when server stopped during queries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Add settings `distributed_query_retries` and `distributed_query_retry_interval_ms` (disabled by default): when enabled, a query to a `Distributed` table or to the `remote` table function is retried after a network error (`NETWORK_ERROR`, `SOCKET_TIMEOUT`, `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF`, e.g. when the remote server is stopped while the query is running). The query is retried on another available replica and only if no result data has been received from the remote server yet, so the result never contains duplicated rows. Queries executed with parallel replicas and cluster function tasks are not retried. While a retry is still possible, the progress reported by the remote server is deferred until the first block of result data (or the completion of the query), so the work replayed by a retry is not double-counted in read limits and quotas. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- The settings documentation is autogenerated from the setting descriptions in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58380 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=66791&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/66791](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F66791+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not use a non-deterministic expression as a join key when rewriting a comma or `CROSS` join
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112965 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes wrong results for a comma or `CROSS` join whose `WHERE` clause compares columns of two tables using a non-deterministic expression such as `rand`. Such a query could return rows that do not satisfy its own `WHERE` clause, because `cross_to_inner_join_rewrite` (enabled by default) moved the expression into the join key position where it is re-evaluated. The `query_plan_merge_filter_into_join_condition` optimization can still move the same class of expression into a join key; that path is fixed separately by #112965. ### Description `SELECT ... FROM l, r WHERE rand(l.a) % 16 = r.a AND rand(l.a) % 16 = 3` can return rows where `r.a` is not `3`, with no error: the second conjunct stays in the `WHERE` and pins the key to `3`, yet `uniqExact(r.a)` reads `16`. `CrossToInnerJoinPass` **moves** an `equals` conjunct out of the `WHERE` into the join `ON`, rebuilding the `WHERE` from the conjuncts it did not take. In the key position it is evaluated per row of each joined side rather than once per cross-product row, so the key a row was hashed under is unrelated to the value the surviving conjunct checked. I add one guard where a condition is chosen as a join key: it is refused if its subtree holds a window function, a stateful function, one not deterministic in the scope of the query, or one fixed per executing node (`isServerConstant`, such as `hostName`). A refused condition stays in the `WHERE`, as `cross_to_inner_join_rewrite = 0` does; under `= 2` a query whose only equi condition is refused reports the pre-existing "no equi-join conditions found" error. The predicate is `isDeterministicInScopeOfQuery`, not `isDeterministic`, so `now`, `currentUser`, `randConstant` and `dictGet` keep their rewrite. Several functions of that class did not declare the property, so the guard could not see them: `queryID`, `FQDN`, `getServerPort`, `getClientHTTPHeader`, `showCertificate`, the `transaction*` and `filesystem*` families, `addressToSymbol` and `addressToLine`. They now declare it where they are defined, so the pass compares no function names. The `query_plan_merge_filter_into_join_condition` step moves the same class of predicate into a join key and is on by default, so until #112965 lands a default-settings query can still be rewritten by it. The tests pin `query_plan_enable_optimizations = 0` to measure this pass. Following review, two declarations I had added are reverted, because neither function belongs to the class the guard is for. `randConstant` is designed to hold one value for a whole query, like `now`, and the analyzer already delivers that by sharing one built `FunctionBase` between syntactically identical calls; the disagreement I had measured came from `getTreeHash` covering the alias, so only the aliased spelling misses that cache. And omitting `DETERMINISTIC` on a WebAssembly UDF says the value may differ between queries, not between two evaluations within one, so deriving query stability from it would have cost every unannotated - that is, most - WebAssembly UDF its `KeyCondition`, projection and read-in-order eligibility for no correctness gain. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112938&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112938](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112938+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures
signal.text: # Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures ## (Human) Introduction As someone who works with ClickHouse but also occasionally opens a pcap in Wireshark, I've always had a wish to be able to do some quick stats on a pcap using ClickHouse SQL. Especially for large files, I always thought it would also be nice to be able to persist them in a MergeTree, so they don't have to be re-scanned every time. So this is my first draft at making this a reality: adding PCAP as an (experimental) input format which can be read by Clickhouse directly (and consequently be ingested, as well). It currently only parses very basic stuff (mostly L2-L4), but this could be extended in the future (imagine having all Wireshark dissectors 😍 ) I realize this may be considered "unfinished" (in the sense: lacking features), but I wanted to open a PR and get feedback on the idea early on, to see if it was worth pursuing. Full transparency: this is basically 100% vibe-coded -- ideas and some design decisions are mine, but I didn't really write any code. Thanks Claude. In that spirit, here's the Claude-generated description including some notes that may be relevant to reviewers: ## AI-generated Overview Adds a `PCAP` input format that reads packet capture files (classic `pcap` and `pcapng`) and produces one row per packet with decoded L2–L4 fields — timestamp, lengths, link type, the ordered protocol chain, Ethernet/IPv4/IPv6/TCP/UDP header fields, the L4 payload, and the raw frame. Modelled structurally on the `DWARF` format. Parsing uses `libtins` for dissection and `libpcap` for reading the capture container, added as contrib submodules behind a new `USE_PCAP` flag (`libpcap` built offline-only with pre-generated BPF grammar/scanner; WPA2/ACK-tracking disabled to avoid OpenSSL and Boost.ICL). Includes documentation and a stateless test with small Wireshark sample captures. > Transparency note: this PR was vibe-coded with Claude (Anthropic `claude-opus-4-8`) in an agentic workflow, with human review and direction. The AI co-authorship is recorded via `Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits. ### Notes for reviewers - **New contrib submodules:** `libtins` (v4.5) and `libpcap` (1.10.5), gated behind `ENABLE_PCAP`/`USE_PCAP` (on by default with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES`). They use the upstream repositories directly (not ClickHouse forks). - **libpcap build:** built offline-only using the `null` capture backend (no live capture / remote / optional backends). Its BPF grammar/scanner are pre-generated with bison/flex and checked in under `contrib/libpcap-cmake/generated/` so the build needs no flex/bison. A hand-written `config.h` targets Linux/glibc. - **libtins build:** hand-written `config.h`; WPA2 decryption and ACK tracking are disabled to avoid pulling in OpenSSL and Boost.ICL for now. Deeper protocol dissection can be layered on later. - **Disabled-build safety:** the format is wrapped in `#if USE_PCAP` with empty registration stubs, so linking succeeds when the feature is off (e.g. fasttest builds with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES=0`). The stateless test is tagged `no-fasttest` for the same reason. - **Test fixtures license:** the capture files under `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_pcap/` are sample captures from the Wireshark test suite (GPL-2.0); provenance is recorded in that directory's `README.md`. Happy to swap them for self-authored synthetic captures if the GPL-2.0 provenance is a concern. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New input format `PCAP` for reading network packet captures (`pcap` and `pcapng`), producing one row per packet with decoded Ethernet/IP/TCP/UDP fields, the protocol chain, payload, and raw frame.

signal.title: Read all summed columns for SELECT FINAL from SummingMergeTree
signal.text: `SELECT ... FINAL` from a `SummingMergeTree` table returned wrong results when the query read only a subset of the columns of the summation. A merge removes a row when the values in **all** of the columns of the summation are zero after summing. The FINAL read applied the same rule, but only over the columns the query happened to read. Two ways to misbehave follow from that: - A query reading a subset of the summed columns removed every group whose visible columns summed to zero, even though an unread summed column made the row survive a real merge — rows silently disappeared. The most common victim is bare `count()`, which reads a single smallest column (plus the internally added sorting key): on a table `(c0 Int8, c1 Int32, c3 UInt64) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY c3` with two overlapping parts where `c0` sums to zero for some keys, `SELECT count() FROM t FINAL` returned 10 instead of 15, and `SELECT c0, c3 FROM t FINAL` lost the same 5 rows. - A query reading none of the summed columns (e.g. only the sorting key) never removed anything, keeping rows that a real merge deletes. The fix always includes all columns that a merge would aggregate into the FINAL read set (and into the set protected from plan-level column pruning), so the removal decision is taken over the same set of columns as in a real merge. This makes `SELECT ... FINAL` agree with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` followed by a plain `SELECT`. Note that queries over `SummingMergeTree FINAL` that previously read a subset of the summed columns now read all of them, which is the price of the correct result. Found by the nightly SQLancer `FinalMerge` oracle (`SELECT count() FROM t0 FINAL` returned 9947 before `OPTIMIZE TABLE t0 FINAL` and 9999 after it on the same data): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5c9f28ed5a2c585ad46bf74d6600cdcf3aa07a9e&name_0=NightlySQLancer&name_1=SQLancer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=SQLancer ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results of `SELECT ... FINAL` from `SummingMergeTree` when the query reads only a subset of the columns of the summation: the decision to remove a row whose sums are all zero is now taken over all columns of the summation, as in a real merge, instead of only the columns the query reads. Previously, rows could silently disappear from the result (for example, `SELECT count() FROM table FINAL`). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115032&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115032](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115032+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Switch the default compression to ZSTD(3) for table data and network
signal.text: Switch the default compression in ClickHouse from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`, for both on-disk table data and network communication. ### Motivation `LZ4` has been the default for a long time and optimizes for speed, but `ZSTD(3)` gives substantially better compression ratios at a still-modest CPU cost, reducing both storage footprint and network traffic out of the box. ClickHouse Cloud already uses a stronger default; this aligns the self-managed defaults. ### What changes - **On-disk table data.** `CompressionCodecFactory::getDefaultCodec` now returns `ZSTD(3)` instead of `LZ4`. For `MergeTree` column data the built-in default is *size-aware*: when a column specifies no codec and no `<compression>` server-config case matches, `CompressionCodecSelector::choose` uses the faster `LZ4` for parts smaller than 100 MB and `ZSTD(3)` for larger parts, so freshly inserted data starts as `LZ4` and the bigger parts produced by background merges switch to `ZSTD(3)`. The direct `getDefaultCodec` users — the `Log` family, part checksums, the HTTP `compress=1` output, the `StripeLog` data stream, and the persistent `Set`/`Join` files — are not size-aware and switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. External temporary (spill) files are unaffected: they keep their own `temporary_files_codec` default (`LZ4`). - **Network.** The defaults of `network_compression_method` (`LZ4` → `ZSTD`) and `network_zstd_compression_level` (`1` → `3`) are changed, so the native client/server and Distributed (server/server) protocol uses `ZSTD(3)` by default. The changes are recorded in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so the `compatibility` setting restores the previous behavior for these paths. The distributed-query streaming exchange (`StreamingExchangeSink`) does not read `network_compression_method` and always uses the server default codec; this is safe because each frame is self-describing (the receiver auto-detects the codec) and the exchange is a transient, same-version channel — `StreamingExchangeProtocol` rejects peers on a different protocol version, so a stream is never read back by a node expecting a different codec. - **Upgrade safety.** The append-only `Log`/`TinyLog`/`StripeLog` engines resolve the default codec at write time, so a table written before the upgrade (`LZ4`) and appended to after it (`ZSTD(3)`) ends up with mixed-codec blocks in one file. Their readers now pass `allow_different_codecs = true` (as the `MergeTree` reader already does) so such files still read back correctly. The legacy custom-frame Keeper snapshot format (`compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format = false`) is pinned to `LZ4` so it stays the documented format. Columns, tables, and connections that specify a codec or method explicitly are unaffected — with one exception: streams written through the built-in default codec directly, which ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config. The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files (written by `SetOrJoinSink` and `StorageJoin::mutate` through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with no codec), and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`, via `MergeTreeDataPartChecksums::write`) always follow the new default; see the changelog entry below for the per-path rollback. ### Validation Built locally and verified against the new binary: - A `MergeTree` table created with no explicit codec follows the size-aware default: small parts report `LZ4` and parts larger than 100 MB report `ZSTD(3)` as their `default_compression_codec` in `system.parts`. Direct `getDefaultCodec` streams (e.g. `StripeLog`) report `ZSTD(3)` regardless of size. - `system.settings` shows `network_compression_method = ZSTD` and `network_zstd_compression_level = 3`. - End-to-end `SELECT`/`INSERT` over the native protocol with default (now `ZSTD`) network compression work; all of `LZ4`/`lz4hc`/`zstd`/`none` still work and an invalid method still errors with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. - The `02995_new_settings_history` consistency check passes (both setting changes are recorded). - The on-disk byte-dump tests (`02047_log_family_*_data_file_dumps`) were regenerated for the new default: `Log`/`TinyLog` keep `LZ4`-pinned columns, while `StripeLog`'s shared `data.bin`/`index.mrk` reflect the `ZSTD(3)` default (it uses `getDefaultCodec` and ignores the per-column codec). Size-sensitive stateless and integration tests that assert compressed byte sizes were pinned back to `LZ4` (cache segment sizes, distributed-batch corruption offsets, full-disk thresholds, frozen-part checksums). The CI performance comparison does **not** measure this tradeoff: the harness pins the built-in default codec to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/config.d/compression.xml`) and `network_compression_method` to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/users.d/perf-comparison-tweaks-users.xml`) on *both* the reference and the tested server, deliberately, so the report measures query logic rather than drowning in expected codec regressions. It therefore serves only as a regression filter for the non-codec parts of this change; the storage/network-vs-CPU tradeoff of `LZ4` → `ZSTD(3)` itself is a well-known property of the two codecs and is not measured by this pull request's CI. Documentation updated accordingly, including the `Native` format and protocol specifications and the `<compression>` config examples. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The default compression method is changed from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. For client/server and server/server network communication it switches uniformly to `ZSTD(3)`. For on-disk table data, `MergeTree` column data now uses a size-aware built-in default — parts smaller than 100 MB use `LZ4` and larger parts use `ZSTD(3)` — while the direct built-in-default streams (the `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and part checksums) switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. This improves compression ratios and reduces storage and network usage out of the box, at a modest increase in CPU usage. None of the on-disk or HTTP paths are controlled by `compatibility`; the previous behavior can be restored per path as follows. For client/server and Distributed network compression, use the `compatibility` setting (or set `network_compression_method = 'LZ4'`). For `MergeTree` column data, set a column/table `CODEC(LZ4)` or configure the server `<compression>` default to `LZ4`. For the `Log`/`TinyLog` engines, set a column `CODEC(LZ4)` (their default does not consult the `<compression>` config). The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`) use the built-in default codec directly — they ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config — so they always use the new `ZSTD(3)` default and have no runtime rollback; reading stays correct because every compressed frame is self-describing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108786&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108786](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108786+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
