signal.title: Server shutdown hangs forever when a backup is blocked on unresponsive I/O
signal.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the situation A single `SIGTERM` never completes if a `BACKUP` is in flight and its I/O does not return. The server closes its listening sockets, then blocks in `BackupsWorker::wait()` — an unbounded `condition_variable::wait` with no timeout and no shutdown escape — and stays there indefinitely. Only a *second* signal (or `SIGKILL`) ends the process. **Both** shutdown branches reach the same wait, so no server setting avoids it: - `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 1` (default) → [`waitAllBackupsAndRestores()`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/programs/server/Server.cpp#L3743) → `waitAll()` (BackupsWorker.cpp:1496) → `wait()` (BackupsWorker.cpp:1475) - `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 0` → [`cancelAllBackupsAndRestores()`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/programs/server/Server.cpp#L3745) → `cancelAll(wait_ = true)` (BackupsWorker.cpp:1547) → the *same* `wait()` `cancelAll` requests cancellation and then waits for the operation to reach a final status. A thread parked in a socket read that never returns never observes the cancellation, so "cancel on shutdown" blocks exactly as long as "wait on shutdown" does. The blocking call is `status_changed.wait(lock, pred)` at [BackupsWorker.cpp:1479](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp#L1479). It has no `wait_for`, and its predicate consults only the operation status — never a shutdown-requested flag — so nothing can wake it while the operation is stuck. This is not hypothetical: it is how ClickHouse behaves under any supervisor that sends one `SIGTERM` and then force-kills — `systemd`, `docker stop`, and the integration-test framework's `stop_clickhouse()` (30s, then `SIGKILL`) all do this. The result is a server that is always hard-killed instead of shutting down, losing whatever a clean shutdown does. ### How to reproduce * ClickHouse version: **26.8.1.1384** (also observed on 26.8.1.1 in CI) * Non-default settings: none required (the default `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 1` is enough; the repro below also shows `0` fails the same way) Any destination that accepts a connection and never answers will do. A black-hole TCP listener standing in for S3 is the simplest: ```python # blackhole.py — accept connections, never reply import socket, sys srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1) srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", int(sys.argv[1]))); srv.listen(128) held = [] while True: conn, _ = srv.accept() held.append(conn) # hold it open, send nothing ``` ```bash python3 blackhole.py 18999 & clickhouse-server --config-file=config.xml & # plain single-node config clickhouse-client -q "CREATE TABLE t (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k" clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(100000)" # Start a backup that can never finish: the endpoint accepts and never responds, # and the timeouts are long enough that the request stays in flight. clickhouse-client -q " BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://127.0.0.1:18999/bucket/backup1', 'key', 'secret') SETTINGS async = 1" \ --s3_request_timeout_ms=3600000 --s3_connect_timeout_ms=3600000 --s3_retry_attempts=1000 clickhouse-client -q "SELECT status FROM system.backups" # CREATING_BACKUP kill -TERM $(pgrep -x clickhouse-server) # one graceful SIGTERM ``` **Expected:** the server shuts down, abandoning or cancelling the stuck backup. **Actual:** it never exits. Still running after 2 minutes (and indefinitely): ``` <Information> BaseDaemon: Received termination signal (Terminated) <Debug> Application: Received termination signal. <Information> Application: Closed all listening sockets. <Information> BackupsWorker: Waiting for running backups and restores to finish <Information> BackupsWorker: Waiting backup S3('http://127.0.0.1:18999/bucket/backup1', 'key', '[HIDDEN]') to complete ``` Main thread: ``` #9 std::condition_variable::wait<BackupsWorker::wait(...)::$_0> #10 DB::BackupsWorker::wait src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:1479 #11 DB::BackupsWorker::waitAll src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:1512 #12 DB::Context::waitAllBackupsAndRestores src/Interpreters/Context.cpp:4197 #13 DB::Server::main ... $_24 programs/server/Server.cpp:3649 #15 BasicScopeGuard<...>::~BasicScopeGuard base/base/scope_guard.h:50 ``` Only a second signal ends it: ``` <Information> BaseDaemon: Received second termination signal (Terminated). Immediately terminate. ``` #### `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 0` does not help Setting it and repeating the steps produces the same hang, one frame different: ``` <Information> BackupsWorker: Cancelling running backups and restores <Information> BackupsWorker: Cancelling backup S3('http://127.0.0.1:18999/bucket/backup2', 'key', '[HIDDEN]') ``` ``` #10 DB::BackupsWorker::wait src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:1479 #11 DB::BackupsWorker::cancelAll src/Backups/BackupsWorker.cpp:1567 #12 DB::Context::cancelAllBackupsAndRestores src/Interpreters/Context.cpp:4203 #13 DB::Server::main ... $_24 programs/server/Server.cpp:3651 ``` Still running after 60s. So there is currently **no configuration** under which a graceful shutdown completes while a backup is stuck in a non-responsive I/O call. ### How it was found A fuzzer run on a 3-node cluster, where `BACKUP ... ON CLUSTER` / `RESTORE ... ON CLUSTER` were issued while nodes and ZooKeeper were being killed and restarted. One node never shut down and had to be force-killed; its main thread was in the same `BackupsWorker::waitAll()` frame. The single-node repro above removes the cluster, Keeper, and the fuzzer, and reduces it to "one backup whose I/O does not return". ### Suggested direction Either would fix it; the first is the smaller change: 1. Give the shutdown path a bounded wait — `status_changed.wait_for(...)` with a deadline (a new `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores_timeout`, or reuse `shutdown_wait_unfinished`), and proceed with shutdown when it expires. 2. Make the predicate shutdown-aware, so `cancelAll` genuinely stops waiting once cancellation has been requested rather than waiting for a status the stuck thread cannot publish. `cancelAll(wait_ = true)` in particular looks like it wants to be bounded: the operation has already been told to cancel, and blocking forever for it to acknowledge defeats the purpose of the `= 0` setting.

signal.title: Size parallel replicas mark_segment_size by active replica count
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107805 --> Related: #107805 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallel replicas now size the automatic `parallel_replicas_mark_segment_size` by the number of active replicas, consistent with the reading coordinator, so registered-but-inactive replicas no longer skew segment sizing. ### Description Follow-up to #107805 (the optional `total_nodes_count` / `mark_segment_size` alignment noted in review). #107805 made the parallel replicas reading coordinator size itself by the number of *active* replicas (excluding registered-but-inactive ones), so mark segments are not assigned to replicas that never participate. The automatic `mark_segment_size` heuristic in `ReadFromMergeTree`, however, still derived its work-distribution denominator from `getAllNodeCount()` (the *registered* count via `ParallelReadingExtension::total_nodes_count`). When a replica was registered but inactive the two sizings disagreed. This sources `ParallelReadingExtension::total_nodes_count` from the active replica count through a shared `ClusterProxy::getActiveReplicasCountForParallelReplicas` helper that mirrors the coordinator's sizing exactly: the active count when liveness is known, the registered count when it is not (or when it does not line up with the cluster definition), and a zero-active safety net that falls back to the registered count. `total_nodes_count` feeds only `chooseSegmentSize`, whose result is clamped to `{128, 1024, 16384}` and is never used for indexing, so this cannot go out of range (replica numbering stays bounded by the registered count) and can only make segments smaller, which balances work no worse. The existing integration test `test_parallel_replicas_skip_inactive_replicas` is extended to assert the segment-sizing heuristic sees the active replica count (2), not the registered count (3), when one of three replicas is stopped. Verified the added assertion fails before this change and passes after; the `all_groups` sibling test is unaffected. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109377&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109377](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109377+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Restructure the Cascades optimizer code following the review of #86353
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86353 Restructures the Cascades optimizer code to address the review comments on #86353. No behavior changes: every plan-shape reference is byte-identical, and the Cascades gtests and the distributed-plan test suite pass unchanged. - `CascadesOptimizer` now owns the search engine: the memo, the rule registries, the task stack, costing, and plan extraction. The former `OptimizationEnvironment` fields become the new `OptimizerContext`, a plain per-query settings struct stored in the memo. - One rule per file: `LocalRead`, `ParallelRead`, `ReplicatedRead`, `TopN`, and `TwoStageTopN` each moved into their own source file. The helpers shared by the rules moved to `RuleUtils`, and the fixed model constants (task budget, fallback selectivities, row-width defaults) moved to `OptimizerDefaults.h`. The per-operator cost constants stay in `CostConfig` because a query can override them. - Implementation strategies are stateless, so they became per-type singletons (`strategySingleton<T>`), and expressions compare them by pointer instead of by name. - `EnforcerAxis` is renamed to `EnforcedProperty`. - Optimization tasks are owned by `std::unique_ptr` instead of `std::shared_ptr`. - Logical expressions in a group now get the same structural deduplication as physical ones, so a transformation that derives an already-known alternative does not grow the group. Covered by a new case in `gtest_cascades_group_dedup`. - Small cleanups from the review: the eligibility check in `Group::selectInputImplementation` is inlined into the selection lambda, `DistributionPassthrough` rejects an impossible variant before it copies the `GroupExpression`, and the repeated input-requirement construction in `DistributionEnforcer` is extracted into `inputAtSourceDistribution`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115293&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115293](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115293+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Avoid double compression in adaptive codec selection
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Adaptive compression used to have two phases: selection and compression. During selection, we compressed every candidate that cannot report its compressed size cheaply into a temporary buffer to measure it. If such a candidate won, the compression phase then compressed it again. This fuses selection into compression. We do a single pass in which candidates with cheap sizing are only measured, and the rest compress into `dest`, or into a scratch buffer when `dest` holds the best result so far. After the pass the winner reaches `dest` one of three ways: it is already there, it is copied from scratch, or, for a measured-only winner, it is compressed now, for the first and only time. With today's pool this halves the compression work whenever the default codec wins a block. Not for changelog because adaptive compression is released in 26.8 (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adaptive codec selection now compresses with each candidate codec at most once per block instead of measuring all candidates and then recompressing the winner. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113511&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113511](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113511+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1671` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Report the owner query_ids and hold count in RWLock re-entrancy errors
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110893 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): When an `RWLockImpl::getLock()` re-entrancy assertion fires (`RWLock is already locked in exclusive mode` / `Cannot acquire exclusive lock while RWLock is already locked`), the error message now names the other `query_id`s currently owning the lock and how many locks the requesting `query_id` already holds, to make such lock-ordering errors diagnosable. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110893 The two fast-path re-entrancy assertions in `RWLockImpl::getLock()` fire when the requesting `query_id` is already present in `owner_queries`, but their messages named nothing at all - so the only artifact of a rare lock-ordering error was the bare sentence. That is the case for the `CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... POPULATE` re-entrant deadlock seen under stress, which has no local reproducer. Both messages now report: - the **set of owner `query_id`s**, with a count next to any `query_id` held by more than one thread - i.e. who else is holding the lock, which is not recoverable from anything else in the log; - the **number of locks the requesting `query_id` already holds** - an owner count above one shows the re-entrancy is across sibling threads of the same query rather than a single nested acquisition; - the `query_id` itself. This is the lock key passed to `getLock()`, not the ambient `query_id`: callers pass `getInitialQueryId()` on some paths (`InterpreterSelectQuery`, `InterpreterInsertQuery`), `getCurrentQueryId()` on others, and `RWLockImpl::NO_QUERY` from background threads, so it is not redundant with the log-line prefix. The requester thread id is deliberately *not* printed: `OwnPatternFormatter` already prefixes every line with `[ thread_id ]`, and the holder TID - the one worth pivoting from into a thread dump - is not tracked. Locks taken with `NO_QUERY` never enter `owner_queries`, hence the wording "owner query_ids" rather than "owners". Behaviour-neutral: two error strings, plus `getOwnerQueryIdsDescription()` refactored to share the new `formatOwnerQueryIds()` helper. No new bookkeeping on the lock hot path; the public `getOwnerQueryIds()` API is unchanged. All 8 `Common.RWLock*` unit tests pass. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1672` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Adaptive lazy execution of short-circuit function arguments (continues #73776)
signal.text: This continues #73776 by @lgbo-ustc, whose branch was ~17 months behind `master` and could no longer be merged mechanically (27 conflicting files in the hottest central code). The author's commits are preserved; on top of them this reconciles the change with the current `master` and reworks the plumbing. Short-circuit evaluation decides *statically* which arguments of `and`, `or`, `if` and `multiIf` are executed lazily. Lazy execution is not free: the rows which are not needed are filtered out and the result is expanded back to the original size. When the filtered out part is small, or the argument itself is cheap, this overhead is larger than the work it saves. This adds an opt-in adaptive mode: the execution of every function is profiled (elapsed time and processed rows), and every 20000 rows the decision is revisited per action - lazy execution is turned off when the estimated cost of the full execution is lower than the measured cost of the lazy execution, and turned back on when the per-row cost of the action grows significantly. Actions whose function can throw an exception on invalid input values (for example `intDiv(1, 0)`) are never switched to eager execution, so the short-circuit protection is preserved. The mode is disabled by default and enabled with the new experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`. Changes on top of the original branch: * The flag no longer travels through `ExpressionStep`/`FilterStep` constructors, the query plan optimizations, the planner and the step serialization. It lives in `ExpressionActionsSettings` next to `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, which removes ~20 files from the change and all the ripple through `QueryPlan/Optimizations`. * `ExpressionActions::execute` and `executeOnColumns` stay `const`; the free `executeAction` became a member with three virtual hooks (`shouldExecuteLazily`, `executeFunction`, `finalizeBlockExecution`) which `AdaptiveExpressionActions` overrides. * The profile plumbing follows the current `IExecutableFunction` chain, including `executeWithoutReplicatedColumns`, which did not exist when the branch was written. * `is_no_except` is computed only when the setting is enabled, so nothing changes for the default path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`, which enables dynamic evaluation of whether a short-circuit function's argument should be lazily executed. The execution of the functions is profiled at runtime, and the lazy execution of an argument is disabled when it costs more than executing the argument on all the rows. signal.title: Add the `Cluster` database engine
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114411 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/59304 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110975 Implement the `Cluster` database engine, a follow-up to the `Remote` database engine (#110975). Each table is exposed as a `Distributed` proxy that forwards `SELECT` and `INSERT`, with the same local-shard visibility rules and remote-replica fallback as `Remote`. signal.title: Do not let SET <name> = DEFAULT bypass the settings constraints
signal.text: `SET <name> = DEFAULT` resets a setting rather than assigning to it, so it does not produce a `SettingChange` and never reached `SettingsConstraints`. Any constraint could therefore be escaped by resetting the setting instead of assigning to it: ```sql CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p SETTINGS max_query_size = 1000 MAX 1000; SET max_query_size = 2000; -- SETTING_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION, as expected SET max_query_size = DEFAULT; -- silently restored the default of 262144 ``` A `CONST` constraint was just as escapable, and so was readonly mode, which is enforced by the same check: ```sql SET readonly = 2; SET readonly = 0; -- READONLY, as expected SET readonly = DEFAULT; -- silently left readonly mode ``` This describes the reset as the change it effectively is — to the value declared in the source code, which is what `Context::resetSettingsToDefaultValue` restores — and runs the usual check on it before anything is applied, so that a violation leaves the whole statement without effect. The in-query `SETTINGS <name> = DEFAULT` form goes through the same interpreter and is covered too. A reset that does not change the value is still allowed, because the check drops changes whose new value equals the current one. Resetting a setting that was never touched therefore keeps working under a `CONST` constraint and in readonly mode — which is what CI profiles that pin a setting to its declared default rely on (`max_parser_backtracks` in `limit-recursion-settings.xml`, for example). Settings without a declared default are unaffected: a custom setting is dropped rather than reset and cannot carry a constraint, and an unknown name stays silently ignored. The client only mirrors the reset into its own settings when the server accepted the statement, so its view does not drift. One consequence worth calling out: a profile that caps `max_threads` below the machine's core count now rejects `SET max_threads = DEFAULT`, because the declared default resolves to `auto(<cores>)`. That is the intended reading of the constraint, but it means the CI profiles that cap `max_threads` at 128 would reject that reset on a machine with more than 128 cores. Verified locally against a build of this change: the four rejection paths above are rejected, the rejected statement leaves the value alone, and the no-op reset, custom-setting reset and unknown-setting reset all keep working. `04202_set_default_preserves_max_threads_auto` and `04078_settings_constraints_compatibility_const` still pass, and a sweep of every stateless test that uses `= DEFAULT` plus every test whose name mentions constraints/readonly/settings profiles produced no constraint or readonly error attributable to this change. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115328 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bypass of settings constraints: `SET <name> = DEFAULT` reset a setting without checking the constraints from the user's profile, so a `MIN`/`MAX`/`CONST` constraint could be escaped by resetting the setting instead of assigning to it, and a session could leave readonly mode with `SET readonly = DEFAULT`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115334&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115334](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115334+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix PostgreSQL-protocol authentication for users that also have an ssh_key
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/76839 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix authentication over the PostgreSQL wire protocol for users with several authentication methods: a user that also had an `ssh_key` method (or any other method that stores no password) was rejected with `Invalid user or password` even when the correct password for its `scram_sha256_password` method was supplied, and a wrong SCRAM salt was sent to the client when the SCRAM method was not the last one (e.g. for a user with `scram_sha256_password` followed by `sha256_password`). A user with multiple authentication methods, one of which is `ssh_key`, could not authenticate over the PostgreSQL protocol at all (in either order of the methods), while the same user authenticated fine over the native, MySQL, and HTTP protocols. Reproduced on 26.7.3.19 and current master. Anyone who adds a public SSH key to their user (e.g. for the SSH endpoint) silently loses PostgreSQL access with a misleading "wrong password" error. Two defects, both fixed (each order of methods hits at least one of them): 1. `checkScramSHA256Authentication` did not check the type of the authentication method it verifies the client proof against, and `IAccessStorage::authenticateImpl` calls it for every method of the user. For methods that store no password hash (e.g. `ssh_key`), the empty hash was passed to `hmacSHA256` as the HMAC key; `EVP_MAC_init` fails for a null key, so the check threw `OPENSSL_ERROR` (`Authentication failed: Code: 454. DB::Exception: EVP_MAC_init failed`) instead of returning false, aborting the whole authentication instead of trying the next method of the user. Now it returns false for non-SCRAM methods, the same way `checkMySQLAuthentication` handles non-MySQL-compatible methods. 2. `ScrambleSHA256Auth::authenticate` in the PostgreSQL handler sent the salt of the *last* authentication method of the user instead of the salt of the SCRAM method, so the client derived a salted password that could never match the stored verifier: an empty salt when `ssh_key` was last, or an unrelated random salt when e.g. `sha256_password` was. Now it sends the salt of the first `scram_sha256_password` method. Verified before/after with `psql` against a local server; added an integration test covering both method orders, the `scram_sha256_password` + `sha256_password` combination, and wrong-password rejection. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115084&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115084](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115084+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Assign merges for all partitions at once for OPTIMIZE FINAL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46770 For a non-replicated `MergeTree` table, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` without an explicit partition used to process partitions one by one: it selected and ran the merge for one partition, waited for it to finish, and only then moved on to the next one. On a table with many partitions this serialized all the work and only ever showed a single merge in `system.merges`. Now the per-partition merges are assigned and executed in parallel, so all partitions are merged at once. The degree of parallelism is bounded by the configured `background_pool_size` and reserves only currently available merge-executor capacity. This mirrors how `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::optimize` already assigns a merge per partition and then waits for all of them. Notes: - Tables inside an explicit transaction keep the sequential path, because parallel merges would otherwise share a single transaction object that is not made for concurrent use. - The wait for already-running merges inside `selectPartsToMerge` (the `OPTIMIZE FINAL` path) is now scoped to the current partition: merges in other partitions cannot prevent selecting all the parts of this one, and waiting for them would needlessly serialize the parallel assignment. Verified on a local build: on a table with 8 partitions, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` now runs 8 merges concurrently (observed via `system.merges`) instead of one at a time, and every partition is still correctly merged into a single part (checked for `MergeTree`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL DEDUPLICATE`, and `ReplacingMergeTree`, plus the `optimize_skip_merged_partitions` / `optimize_throw_if_noop` no-op paths and two concurrent `OPTIMIZE FINAL` queries). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a non-replicated `MergeTree` table now assigns and runs the merges for all partitions at once instead of processing them one partition at a time. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109004&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109004](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109004+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Read fresh in-memory metadata at the OPTIMIZE merge-selection read
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104822 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed data loss when a `RENAME COLUMN` runs concurrently with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a `MergeTree` table: the merged part could be written with the pre-rename column list, permanently filling the renamed column with its `DEFAULT`. ### Description `26.3`-only fix for issue 80648, authorized in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113929#issuecomment-5229587902. `StorageMergeTree::optimize` calls `merge` synchronously on the query thread, so the merge-selection metadata read runs with a live query context. `MergeTreeData` overrides `getInMemoryMetadataPtr` with a per-query cache that `InterpreterOptimizeQuery` has already populated with the pre-`ALTER` snapshot, so the read returns metadata predating the rename while selection pairs it with parts that already carry the mutation. `MergeTask` takes `storage_columns` from that snapshot and never re-reads, so the merged part keeps the old column list and the renamed column stays `DEFAULT`. Passing `bypass_metadata_cache=true` makes the read honour the invariant the comment above it already states. `scheduleDataProcessingJob` keeps its bare read: its only caller is the background pool, which has no query context, so it already bypasses. `26.4` and later declare the accessor as `(ContextPtr, bool)` with no default, forcing every caller to state a context, so the read is already fresh there. `25.8` has the same bare read but ships `enable_shared_storage_snapshot_in_query` defaulting to `false`. `26.3` is the only supported branch with both the defaulted parameter and that setting `true`, which is why the backport of 104822 compiled unchanged as `getInMemoryMetadataPtr()` and took the cache-consulting path. Validation on two interleaved, load-matched servers built from this tree, setting at its default: base reddens 16 of 7000 iterations against 0 for the fix (Fisher exact p = 3.0e-05); swapping the binaries onto each other's port and data directory keeps the effect with the binary (30/7000 against 0/7000); 80 runner runs of the unmodified `04238_alter_rename_column_merge_race` per arm give 3 base failures with the exact CI signature and 80/80 on the fix. None of the 211 merge and mutation tests with a verdict in both arms regressed.

signal.title: Resolve the 25.8 cherry-pick conflict of #112327
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112327 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114796 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a use-after-free when a `LEFT JOIN` to a dictionary with `join_algorithm = 'direct'` had a join key that is serialized `Sparse`. `getColumnVectorData` returned a `PaddedPODArray` reference into a column owned only by a function-local `ColumnPtr`, so the dictionary lookup read freed memory. ### Description Backport of #112327 to `25.8`. The robot cherry-pick #114796 is `CONFLICTING`, so the automation cannot carry it. The conflict is in one file. `getColumnVectorData` materializes its key column with `removeSpecialRepresentations` on master and with `recursiveRemoveSparse` here; `removeSpecialRepresentations` does not exist on this branch. The resolution keeps 25.8's call and takes the fix's predicate, so the resolved change is the same 8 insertions and 7 deletions as the merged commit. On this branch the copy therefore guards `Const` and `Sparse`; `ColumnReplicated` does not exist here and is dropped from the comment's carrier list. `25.8` is affected. On the official `25.8.30.17` binary the repro (a 2M-row sparse probe joined to a `FLAT()` dictionary) segfaults in 2 of 7 runs, and with jemalloc junk filling it fails 4 of 4 with `Invalid number of rows in Chunk ... expected 65409, got 0`. The same data written densely passes. Comparing returned values alone cannot see this, because freed but intact memory still yields the correct numbers. Verified in both directions with a clang-19 Debug build, this branch's pinned compiler, asserting build ids against the running server. Pristine `25.8` aborts on the first assertion of the ported test, at `PODArray::operator[]` inside `FlatDictionary::hasKeys` reached through `IDictionary::getByKeys` and `DirectKeyValueJoin::joinBlock` - the mechanism reported on master. With the fix the test passes and the repro returns the correct result in 3 of 3 runs. One branch adaptation in the test: `enable_lazy_columns_replication` does not exist on `25.8` and is rejected as an unknown setting, so it is dropped from the `ARRAY JOIN` statement. The statement and every assertion are kept.

signal.title: Report malformed Parquet thrift metadata as INCORRECT_DATA
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113006 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a Parquet file whose Thrift metadata is corrupt. Such a file now reports `INCORRECT_DATA` instead of the internal error code `STD_EXCEPTION` (`Code: 1001`), so a bad input file can be told apart from a server-side problem. ### Description Reading a Parquet file whose Thrift metadata is corrupt reported `Code: 1001 STD_EXCEPTION`. That is an internal-error code: it tells the user nothing about the input and cannot be classified programmatically as a bad-file error. `apache::thrift::TException` derives from `std::exception`, so it was caught by the generic clause in `deserializeThriftStruct` and converted through `CreateFromSTDTag`. Catching `TException` before that clause and mapping it to `INCORRECT_DATA` fixes it. All five Parquet metadata struct types deserialize through this one function, so the change covers every carrier. Split out of #113006 on reviewer request, where this rode along with an unrelated Arrow IPC change and shared no file with it. The regression test asserts the error code on a file whose metadata is corrupted after writing. Removing the new catch clause and rebuilding makes it fail, so the assertion is on the fix rather than on incidental behavior. Found by mutation fuzzing. Related: #113006

signal.title: Fix Iceberg OPTIMIZE MANIFEST when table metadata omits `refs`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112082 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... MANIFEST` failing with `Poco::NullPointerException: Null pointer` on Iceberg tables whose metadata file omits the spec-optional top-level `refs` object, which is common for tables created by other engines. Closes #112082. ### Description `refs` is optional in the Iceberg spec, so an external writer may produce a metadata file without it. `MetadataGenerator::generateManifestOnlySnapshot` seeded the missing `refs` with a raw `Poco::JSON::Object *`: ```cpp if (!metadata_object->has(Iceberg::f_refs)) metadata_object->set(Iceberg::f_refs, new Poco::JSON::Object); if (!metadata_object->getObject(Iceberg::f_refs)->has(Iceberg::f_main)) // <-- throws ``` `Poco::JSON::Object::set` stores the value's static type inside a `Dynamic::Var`, and `Object::getObject` matches strictly on `typeid(Object::Ptr)` (`base/poco/JSON/src/Object.cpp`), returning a null `Ptr` for any other type tag. The next `operator->` then throws `Poco::NullPointerException` from `SharedPtr::deref`, so `OPTIMIZE ... MANIFEST` failed on such a table: ``` Code: 1001. DB::Exception: Poco::NullPointerException: Null pointer. (STD_EXCEPTION) 1. base/poco/Foundation/include/Poco/SharedPtr.h:285 DB::MetadataGenerator::generateManifestOnlySnapshot(...) 2. src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Compaction.cpp:718 DB::Iceberg::writeConsolidatedManifestFile(...) 3. src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Compaction.cpp:1281 DB::Iceberg::compactIcebergManifests(...) 4. src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/IcebergMetadata.cpp:507 DB::IcebergMetadata::optimizeManifestFiles(...) 5. src/Interpreters/InterpreterOptimizeQuery.cpp:70 ``` The sibling builder `generateNextMetadata`, in the same file, already stores an `Object::Ptr`: it was corrected by #106896 for the insert path, and the manifest-only copy was missed. The fix makes the compaction seed identical to it, so `getObject` sees the expected type tag and the `refs.main` branch is written as intended. The same function already seeds `metadata_log` / `snapshot_log` as `Array::Ptr` for exactly this reason. A sweep of `set(..., new Poco::JSON::(Object|Array))` over `src/`, `programs/` and `base/` returns this one site and nothing else, so the change closes the class rather than one instance. `getObject` returning null was not relied on anywhere: no caller of the changed function inspects the pre-seed value, and the metadata written after the fix is what the code always intended to write. No setting, no serialization format and no on-disk compatibility is affected. #### Verification Reproduced deterministically with `clickhouse local` and plain `IcebergLocal`, no object storage and no external catalog: create a partitioned Iceberg table, insert 35 single-row batches, remove the top-level `refs` key from the newest metadata JSON, then run `OPTIMIZE TABLE t MANIFEST SETTINGS iceberg_manifest_min_count_to_compact=5`. - Before the fix: `Code: 1001 ... Poco::NullPointerException: Null pointer` with the stack above. - After the fix: the statement succeeds, `SELECT count()` returns 35, and the new metadata contains `"refs": {"main": {"snapshot-id": <new>, "type": "branch"}}` with `snapshot-id` equal to `current-snapshot-id`. Two controls isolate the failure to the compaction path: with `refs` present the same `OPTIMIZE ... MANIFEST` succeeds, and with `refs` removed a plain `INSERT` succeeds (that path goes through the already-fixed `generateNextMetadata`). That second control is also why the failure is not necessarily permanent: `generateNextMetadata` seeds `refs` correctly and the whole mutated metadata object is stringified into the next metadata version, so any successful write to the table leaves a metadata file that does contain `refs`, after which compaction works again. On a table that is only read after being written by another engine there is no such write, and manifest compaction stays unavailable. The regression test is a new case in the existing `IcebergMetadataGenerator` gtest suite, which already covers this family of "external engine omitted an optional metadata field" defects. It asserts `isObject(refs)` and a non-null `getObject(refs)` rather than merely the absence of a throw, so it also rejects re-introducing the raw-pointer spelling (`typeid(Object *)` satisfies neither check). Reverting only the changed line makes that case fail with `Null pointer` while the six pre-existing cases keep passing, since they exercise `generateNextMetadata`.

signal.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signal.text: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106136 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes silently missing rows when a query filters on `intDiv(constant, key)` or `divide(constant, key)`. Primary-key and partition analysis reports the wrong direction of monotonicity for a constant divided by a key column, so matching granules are pruned away and the query returns fewer rows with no error. Also fixes `intDiv` with an unsigned constant dividend whose high bit is set, stops claiming monotonicity when a `Decimal` operand makes the division compute in the decimal's native width, and stops key analysis from raising `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` for a valid query that divides an `IPv4`/`IPv6` constant by a key column. ### Description `FunctionBinaryArithmetic::getMonotonicityForRange` reports the direction of `c / x` incorrectly in its `const / variable` branch, so `KeyCondition::applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` inverts the transformed range exactly when it must not, the range matches no granule, and matching rows are dropped with no error and exit code 0. Reproduced at completely default settings (no `SETTINGS` clause), 20000-row `Int32`-keyed MergeTree: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(toInt32(-1000000), a) >= 11; -- keyed MergeTree: 0 ENGINE = Memory oracle: 10909 ``` #### Root cause For `f(x) = c / x` on an interval excluding 0, `d/dx (c/x) = -c/x²`, whose sign is `-sign(c)` for every `x != 0` — the `x²` denominator is positive on both sides of 0. So the direction is governed by `sign(c)` alone and is the *same* on the negative and the positive branch; only the values differ. The code instead treated the two arms as needing opposite polarity, which is the intuition that `1/x` "flips" across the branches. It does not: it is monotone on each branch separately, which is exactly why the strict range-sign guards are there. The two arms are now one return with a single `!is_constant_positive`, and the strict guards are kept verbatim. Fixing only that is not sufficient, and on its own would be *worse* than the current code for one shape. Three further defects live in the same branch: * **Unsigned constant dividend.** `intDiv` casts the dividend through `make_signed_t` whenever either operand is a signed integer (`DivisionUtils.h`), so an unsigned constant whose high bit is set divides as negative — `intDiv(toUInt8(200), x)` is `intDiv(toInt8(-56), x)` — while the raw `Field` still compares as positive. The boundary is `2^(8 * width - 1)` of the dividend's own width (verified for 8/16/32/64/128/256-bit dividends; the divisor width is irrelevant). This is reachable with no cast at all, because the literal `200` is `UInt8`. On a *negative* range the un-negated arm is accidentally correct for this shape, so adding the missing `!` alone would turn a correct answer into a wrong one. A new `intDivConstDividendReinterpretsNegative` helper corrects the effective sign; it deliberately does not reuse the existing `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative`, whose width early-out has the opposite polarity here. * **`Decimal` operand.** With a `Decimal` on either operand and no `Float` operand, the division computes in the decimal's native width (`DecimalBinaryOperation` casts both operands to `NativeResultType` and substitutes the integral operation even for `divide`). The divisor is then truncated, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), x)` is periodic in `x` with period `2^32` and not even monotonic. Nothing is claimed for that combination, mirroring the rejection the sibling `variable / constant` branch already performs. A `Decimal`/`Float` pair is exempt: it is converted to `Float64` before the operation, never truncates, and is itself a carrier of the direction defect, so those shapes are fixed rather than rejected. The rejection is deliberately keyed on the operand types and not on the constant's value, so it also covers a *zero* dividend and therefore runs ahead of the `constant == 0` fast path. That ordering is load-bearing: the truncation moves where the quotient is defined, so a range that strictly excludes 0 can still contain a point where the function is undefined, which is exactly what the zero-constant guard assumes away. With `Decimal32` the divisor truncates to `Int32`, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), key)` over an `Int64` key range around `2^32` raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`; letting the zero guard win would claim monotonicity, prune the raising row away, and return a silent answer instead. Pinned by `c5iv`. * **Non-numeric operand (pre-existing exception on a valid query).** `IPv4`/`IPv6` are substituted with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so their declared width does not describe the arithmetic, and their raw `Field` cannot be compared with a numeric zero. Two existing comparisons against zero therefore raise `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD "Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long"` during key analysis today: one in the single-value fast path (reached when a granule's min equals its max) and one in the zero-constant guard (reached otherwise). Both roles are affected — `intDiv(toIPv4('192.168.0.1'), numeric_key)` and `intDiv(1, ipv4_key)` — and one of them fires even when the key range spans 0. A numeric gate hoisted above the fast path removes both; after it each query returns the correct rows with no pruning. Placing the gate inside the `const / variable` block would cover only the second site, which the new test pins at two granularities. Scope note: "both roles" here means the IP value as the dividend constant and as the key column, both with the constant on the left. The mirror shape, an IP constant as the *divisor* (`intDiv(numeric_key, toIPv4(...))`), still raises the same exception, as do `plus`/`minus`/`multiply` with an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand. Both are pre-existing (measured byte-identical on `origin/master`) and are tracked separately rather than widened into this PR, since a correct fix for them also has to touch the `multiply` arm and the shared fast path. #### Behaviour changes to be aware of * **Two pre-existing key-analysis exceptions disappear.** As above, a non-numeric operand now reports non-monotonic instead of raising, so the query succeeds unpruned. This is a scope extension beyond "fix the direction", included because those same comparisons against zero are the mechanism being corrected and an exception on a valid query is a bug either way. * **Pruning is lost for `Decimal` shapes with no `Float` operand.** Measured with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: | shape | before | after | |---|---|---| | `Decimal32(0)` key, `intDiv(toInt32(-1000), a) = -25`, positive range | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 4/4` | | `UInt64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), a) = 250` | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 3/4` | | `Int64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), a) = 5`, range around `2^32` | `Granules: 0/2` | `Granules: 2/2` | The first two queries return the same rows before and after — the index simply stops filtering. The third is the zero-dividend case: it must stop pruning, because the pruned plan silently returned `0` for a query that correctly raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`. This mirrors the decision already shipped for the `variable / constant` branch, where the same truncation applies. `Decimal`/`Float` pairs keep pruning and are additionally fixed. No committed reference in the repository changes. * **Everything else keeps pruning.** Strictly-positive ranges with a signed constant, both-unsigned operands, `Float` divisors, and unsigned key ranges crossing the divisor's own `2^(8W-1)` are all unaffected. That last group is worth naming: the *values* jump across the wrap while the *order* is preserved, which satisfies the non-strict definition of `Monotonicity`, so rejecting them would delete pruning that is correct today. The new test pins them, with plan-level assertions. #### Testing `04651_intdiv_const_variable_monotonicity` and its three siblings `..._decimal_float`, `..._controls` and `..._ip` compare a keyed MergeTree against an identical `ENGINE = Memory` table on the same data, so each of their 86 count rows prints `1` when index-based pruning agrees with the full-scan ground truth. The probes are split by family across four files, sharing one case numbering, so that no single file outgrows the CI per-test time limit: the cost is fixture DDL for the 26 tables of the (type, range, granularity) matrix, which cannot be trimmed without dropping coverage. Together they cover both range signs for both functions and both constant signs, unsigned dividends at several widths, `Decimal` in either role plus the `Decimal`/`Float` exemption, `Float64`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable` keys, ranges that span zero or have zero as an endpoint, the unsigned wrap shapes, and the `IPv4`/`IPv6` cases at two granularities. Twelve further rows assert with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the surviving shapes still prune (so the fix cannot silently degrade into "no pruning at all") and that the zero-dividend `Decimal` shape stops pruning — 98 asserted rows in total. On a master-HEAD binary the tests fail: 34 rows print `0` and `..._ip` aborts with `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`. On this branch they pass, including 50/50 runs with randomized settings. Each of the four edits was mutation-tested individually — reverting the negation, the sign correction, the `Decimal` rejection, the `Float` exemption, the numeric gate, the gate's hoisted position and its role restriction each make specific named rows fail. `index_granularity` decides whether the range handed to `getMonotonicityForRange` is strictly negative, strictly positive or spans zero, so it is pinned per DDL and the test carries `no-random-merge-tree-settings` with that reason stated inline in each of the four files. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112156&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112156](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112156+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix wrong results for intDiv by an effective -1 in key analysis
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/90461 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/90461 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes wrong results for queries where a `MergeTree` primary key expression is wrapped in `intDiv` with an effective divisor of `-1`. `intDiv(x, -1)` maps the signed minimum of the computation width onto itself instead of onto the maximum, so it is not monotonic on any range containing that minimum, but it was reported as monotonic. Primary-key analysis therefore pruned a granule that did hold a matching row, and `ORDER BY intDiv(x, -1)` returned mis-sorted rows through the read-in-order optimization. Both now return correct results. ### Description `intDiv(x, -1)` is mathematically `-x`, which is not representable at the signed minimum of the computation width: `TYPE_MIN / -1` overflows and folds back onto `TYPE_MIN`, while `TYPE_MIN + 1` maps to `TYPE_MAX`. The function is therefore neither non-decreasing nor non-increasing on any range containing that minimum. `FunctionBinaryArithmeticWithConstants::getMonotonicityForRange` already models two other `intDiv` wraps (`intDivRangeCrossesSignedWrap` for an unsigned dividend, `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative` for an unsigned divisor) but never modelled this **result** wrap, so it reported the function monotonic there. `multiply` already carries the equivalent guard in its `check_overflow` lambda (`/// TYPE_MIN / -1 is UB for native signed types.`); `intDiv` simply lacked it. Two user-visible, silent, default-reachable symptoms (no error, `RC=0`): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO t VALUES (-9223372036854775808), (-9223372036854775807), (-5), (5); -- primary-key pruning drops the matching row SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(a, toInt64(-1)) = toInt64(-9223372036854775808); -- before: 0 after: 1 (ENGINE = Memory, which runs no key analysis, returns 1) -- ORDER BY returns mis-sorted rows via read-in-order SELECT intDiv(a, toInt64(-1)) FROM t ORDER BY intDiv(a, toInt64(-1)); -- before: -5, 5, MAX, MIN after: MIN, -5, 5, MAX ``` The fix adds three helpers next to the existing ones and two guards in each of the two branches that decide `intDiv`'s monotonicity: - `intDivWrapsInsteadOfThrowing` — is this operand pair one that divides by an effective `-1` **and** takes the FPE-suppressing vectorized path? The wrap is produced only by `DivideIntegralByConstantImpl::vectorConstant`, which short-circuits `b == -1` and deliberately avoids `throwIfDivisionLeadsToFPE`. With a signed dividend those registered specializations are an `Int32`/`Int64` dividend with a native signed divisor. Every other **scalar** operand pair throws `ILLEGAL_DIVISION` instead — at runtime as well as during analysis, verified on `ENGINE = Memory` — so it is not a monotonicity problem and is deliberately left alone here. - `intDivCompoundDividendWrapsInsteadOfThrowing` — the same wrap one type wrapper up. An `Array`/`Tuple` dividend divided by a scalar constant is evaluated element-wise, so an element type that wraps carries the same defect, while `getMonotonicityForRange` sees only the outer type and the scalar predicate above cannot detect it. Nesting is followed recursively, and a tuple is a carrier as soon as any one of its elements is. Measured carriers: `Array(Int64)`, `Array(Int32)`, `Array(Array(Int64))`, `Array(LowCardinality(Int64))`, `Tuple(Int64, Int64)` and the mixed `Tuple(Int64, Int8)` — each returned the wrong `count()` and a mis-sorted `ORDER BY` before this change. A compound dividend with a Float, `Int128` or high-bit-unsigned divisor throws `ILLEGAL_DIVISION` and is not a carrier. Because the endpoints are `Array`/`Tuple` Fields whose element-wise containment of the wrap point is not cheaply modelled, a compound carrier is reported non-monotonic unconditionally, mirroring the Decimal-divisor case immediately above. - `intDivRangeContainsResultWrapPoint` — does the analysed range contain that minimum? Decided **per side**, so a range like `[0, +Inf)` genuinely excludes it and keeps being pruned. A range containing the wrap point now reports `{false, true, false, false}` (non-monotonic, no pruning), exactly as `multiply` does on overflow. A range excluding it stays monotonic on that range, but `is_always_monotonic` becomes `false`: it means "monotonic on the whole input range", and the whole domain of a signed type always contains its minimum. #### Cost, stated explicitly The unbounded-endpoint verdict is what `ReadInOrderOptimizer` reads, and it has no range to narrow with, so `ORDER BY intDiv(x, -1)` loses the read-in-order optimization **even when the minimum is absent from the data** (measured: such a query uses `InReverseOrder` today and `Default` after this change). That is unavoidable at this layer — the whole column may contain the minimum and the unbounded probe cannot know — and it is the same trade `intDivRangeCrossesSignedWrap` already makes for unbounded unsigned ranges. It is a deliberate correctness-over-optimization choice, not a free fix. Ordinary `intDiv` pruning is unaffected, and the test asserts that: a positive divisor, a divisor that is not effectively `-1`, unsigned/unsigned, a Float divisor, a half-bounded range excluding the minimum, and a single-point range at the minimum all keep pruning exactly as before, with the granule counts pinned — ten `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` assertions in all, including two that pin an `Array` dividend with a positive divisor and an `Array(UInt8)` dividend, so the new compound guard is provably keyed on the element type and the constant rather than on "is compound". #### Deliberately out of scope - **`Code 153` throws at other widths.** No verdict this function can return fixes them. If the analysed range excludes the minimum a correct guard must report the range monotonic (otherwise valid pruning is lost), and `KeyCondition::applyFunction` then evaluates the chain over the **entire** index column, so an out-of-range minimum still in that column still throws. If the analysed range contains the minimum at a throwing width, the query throws at runtime too (the `ENGINE = Memory` oracle exits with the same error), so it was never analysis-injected. Same reason `single_point` partition pruning is untouched: `applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` short-circuits monotonicity when `single_point`, so nothing inside `getMonotonicityForRange` can reach it. - **The two sibling `intDiv` predicates read the outer dividend type too.** `intDivRangeCrossesSignedWrap` gates on `isUInt(arg_type)` and `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative` on `isInt(arg_type) && isUInt(divisor_type)`, so an `Array`/`Tuple` dividend fails both exactly as it failed the scalar wrap predicate before this change. They model different mechanisms (a step function at `2^(w-1)` for an unsigned dividend, and a direction flip for a high-bit-unsigned divisor), so extending them is a separate concern with its own root cause and its own test matrix, and is tracked separately rather than bundled here. - **Two further defects found while investigating this one**, each with its own root cause and therefore its own PR rather than being bundled here: the `const / variable` branch reports the inverted direction on a strictly-negative range (wrong results for `intDiv` *and* `divide`, no wrap involved), and `throwIfDivisionLeadsToFPE` compares a floating-point dividend against `numeric_limits<Float>::min()`, which is the smallest *positive* value, so `intDiv(2.2250738585072014e-308, -1.0)` throws spuriously.

signal.title: Do not construct remote-I/O fibers on AArch64 with MemorySanitizer
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110124 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Stress test (arm_msan)` fails roughly once a week with `Segmentation fault (STID: 4348-2010)` in the `RemoteQueryExecutorReadContext` fiber during teardown. CIDB over the last 100 days: 16 hits, **all** on `Stress test (arm_msan)` (15 distinct pull requests plus one master hit on 2026-06-10, sha `7bd1b86ef3ef`), and zero hits on every other check, architecture and sanitizer. Each hit kills the server mid-run and discards the remainder of that job's coverage. **Root cause.** On AArch64 with `-fsanitize=memory`, clang materialises the thread pointer (`mrs xN, TPIDR_EL0`) into a callee-saved register and keeps it live across a call. When that call switches to another OS thread's stack, the cached value still names the *old* thread, so the next MemorySanitizer shadow-TLS access dereferences an address that is unmapped in the current thread. ClickHouse resumes suspended remote-I/O fibers on threads other than the suspending one, and destroys them while suspended (`force_unwind`) on the caller's thread, which is why every hit is a shutdown or timeout teardown. Disassembling the exact failing binary (`clickhouse-common-static_26.8.1.1_arm64.deb` from a `build_arm_msan` job, `readelf -n` Build ID `b337b381a47106833eee64c02435cbed21e2b920`, matching the `build id:` line in `fatal.log`), in `boost::context::fiber::resume() &&`: ``` 357d4da4: mrs x22, TPIDR_EL0 ; thread pointer, read once in the prologue 357d4dc0: ldr x25, [x22, x23] ; pre-switch shadow read (correct thread) 357d4e10: bl fiber_activation_record::resume() ; contains ::swapcontext() 357d4e54: b.eq 0x357d4ed4 ; force_unwind -> cold throw block 357d4ee0: str xzr, [x22, x23] ; faults: x22 is the stale thread pointer ``` `x22` is provably not reloaded on that path: its only writes in the function are that prologue `mrs` and an epilogue `ldp x22, x21, [sp,#0x40]` which sits on the fall-through *return* path that the `b.eq` skips. The offsets resolve against the binary's own symbol table to `__msan_param_tls`, `__msan_retval_tls` and `__msan_va_arg_tls` — MemorySanitizer's own shadow area, no user data. This is arch-exclusive for a mechanical reason. On x86-64 MSan TLS is `%fs`-relative and resolved by the CPU per access, so there is no register to go stale; compiling the same translation unit `--target=x86_64-linux-gnu` produces 30 `fs:` accesses and **0** `mrs`. AArch64 has no segment register, so the thread pointer must live in a general-purpose register, and once there it is hoistable. AddressSanitizer is immune (per-context `fake_stack` save and restore) and ThreadSanitizer switches fibers explicitly. That matches the CIDB distribution exactly. **What this pull request does.** It compiles out the fiber-backed remote-I/O paths on AArch64 with MemorySanitizer, at the five places where the code *already* makes a build-conditional asynchronous-versus-synchronous choice, driven by one capability macro in a new `src/Common/RemoteAsyncCapability.h`: | Site | Existing guard, and its synchronous counterpart | |---|---| | `RemoteQueryExecutor::readAsync` | `#if defined(OS_LINUX) \|\| defined(OS_DARWIN)`, `#else return read();` | | `RemoteQueryExecutor::sendQueryAsync` | same, `#else sendQuery(); return -1;` | | the hedged branch building `HedgedConnections` | `#if defined(OS_LINUX)`, falls through to `MultiplexedConnections` | | `ConnectionPoolWithFailover::tryGetEntry`'s asynchronous block | `#if defined(OS_LINUX)` plus `if (async_callback)`, synchronous `ConnectionEstablisher` beside it | | `distributedIndexAnalysis`'s connection and read **selectors** | plain `if (use_hedged_requests)` / `if (use_async_reading)` with the synchronous variants beside them | No mechanism is invented; each of the five conditions is widened, and every `#else` branch already runs today on non-Linux builds. `processParallelReplicaPacketIfAny` is guarded too because it dereferences `read_context` unconditionally and `read_context` is never created without the asynchronous path. Note for the last row: the selectors are gated, **not** `establishConnectionsAsync`/`executeRemoteAnalysisAsync`'s own `#if`s, whose `#else` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR "Hedged connections are not supported on this platform"`. Gating the implementations would have converted a crash into an exception. Settings values are deliberately left untouched. The guard is at build level rather than in `applySettingsQuirks` because a settings-level scheme is bypassable: `Context::setSettings`, `setSettingWithLock` and `resetSettingsToDefaultValue` never call it, and `InterpreterSetQuery::executeForCurrentContext` applies changes and *then* resets defaults, so `SETTINGS async_socket_for_remote = DEFAULT` restores the compiled default after any quirk ran. One of the six fiber construction sites (`ConnectionPoolWithFailover.cpp`) is gated on `async_callback` rather than on any setting, so no settings-level scheme could ever have covered it. Gating at build level makes the property structural: no setting value, `SET`, profile, `DEFAULT` reset or test randomizer can produce a fiber in this build. **Verification.** The change is verified at object level, because the crash needs an aarch64 plus MemorySanitizer build and cannot be reproduced by any functional test. - The mechanism is witnessed directly: a checker over the generated assembly of the unmodified boost header reports 3 stale-thread-pointer uses at exactly the instructions that fault in CI, and 0 for a control build. - `CH_FIBERS_SUPPORTED` and `CH_REMOTE_ASYNC_IO` were asserted with the real build flags across 7 configurations: both 0 for aarch64 with MemorySanitizer, both 1 for x86 with MemorySanitizer, and for AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and release builds on aarch64, and release on x86. - On aarch64 with MemorySanitizer, all four fiber constructor references disappear from the objects (2+1+1 to 0+0+0) and are **retained** in every other configuration. - Reverting any one of the six guards individually makes the constructor it dominates reappear, so no guard is decorative. - For every configuration where `CH_REMOTE_ASYNC_IO` is 1, the generated code is identical to master across 24 translation-unit-by-configuration combinations, with a control proving the comparison can detect a real difference. Release behaviour is unchanged. - The synchronous fallbacks were exercised end to end on a real binary with the predicate forced on locally: correct results, no hangs, `SuspendSendingQueryToShard` stays 0, and the four tests that set these settings explicitly pass. - The new header costs **0** preprocessed lines in all six affected translation units (`base/defines.h` is already in their closures). Because both macros are always defined as 0 or 1, a dropped include is a build failure under `-Werror,-Wundef` rather than a silently disarmed guard. - Every translation unit that touches fibers compiles clean for `aarch64-linux-gnu -fsanitize=memory` with the real build flags and `-Weverything -Werror`: `RemoteQueryExecutor`, `ConnectionPoolWithFailover`, `distributedIndexAnalysis`, `HedgedConnectionsFactory`, `RemoteQueryExecutorReadContext`, `checkStackSize`, `PacketReceiver`, `ConnectionEstablisher`, `HedgedConnections`, `AsyncTaskExecutor`, `RemoteSource` — 11 of 11, zero diagnostics. Compiling out a code path can strand a private member, so this is checked rather than assumed: `packet_in_progress` needs the `[[maybe_unused]]` this pull request adds (dropping it is a hard `-Wunused-private-field` error on that configuration), while `read_packet_type_separately` needs none, because its constructor initializer is a function call and clang counts that as a use. The second case is an incidental suppression rather than a designed one: if that initializer is ever simplified to a literal, this configuration stops building. Because the base rate is roughly one hit per week fleet-wide, **a single green `Stress test (arm_msan)` run on this pull request is not proof**. The durable check is the CIDB signature count over three or more weeks against the 16 hits in the preceding 100 days. **Costs, disclosed.** Two, and neither is hidden. First, the arm_msan lane stops exercising fiber code; it takes the same synchronous paths that non-Linux builds always take. That is a real coverage loss on one lane, traded against that lane crashing weekly and discarding the rest of the run. Second, on this configuration a multi-shard read at low `max_threads` is serialized. Measured on a real binary, `SELECT sleep(1.5) FROM remote('127.{1..10}', system.one)` at `--max_threads 1 --max_distributed_connections 10` takes 15.15 s instead of 1.65 s. `01602_max_distributed_connections` and `01514_distributed_cancel_query_on_error` would fail if that lane ran stateless tests. It does not. `arm_msan` has exactly one job in the whole configuration — `Stress test (arm_msan)` — and on it the stress runner records only its own script status: `run_func_test` collects each worker's return code into a local list it uses solely as a completion counter, and its caller discards the return value. Neither test is in that job's smoke check or hung check. The arm_msan *binary* does reach stateless tests through one other door, `Bugfix validation (functional tests, aarch64)`, which runs each ARM build type in turn — but that job runs only the tests a pull request itself changes, this one changes none, and it is `allow_failure` regardless. `01602` costs 600 s of one stress worker's time budget when it does run (its two retry loops each spend 30 attempts at `timeout 10`, reaching the runner's per-test cap), and no individual query can reach the hung-check threshold because each is killed at 10 s. The cause of that serialization is a **pre-existing defect on master**, not something this change introduces. The planner raises stream parallelism to compensate for blocking remote reads, but it keys that on the *setting* rather than on whether the read will actually block: ``` bool is_sync_remote = table_expression_data.isRemote() && !settings[Setting::async_socket_for_remote]; ``` `readAsync` is already `#if defined(OS_LINUX) || defined(OS_DARWIN)` with `#else return read();`, and the planner is platform-blind, so on a FreeBSD, SunOS or Android build of master today `readAsync` returns synchronously while `async_socket_for_remote` is still true and no compensation engages. The control measurement confirms the mechanism: with `async_socket_for_remote = 0` the same query takes 1.60 s on **both** binaries, so synchronous remote reads are not slow — synchronous reads while the setting claims asynchronous are. That residual is being fixed separately and is not a prerequisite for this change. It is kept out of this pull request deliberately: three successively larger designs for it were reviewed and rejected, and the shape that survives requires defining thread-accounting composition semantics for unions, joins, selectors and completed pipelines, which is a change with its own design questions and its own review surface. I will link the follow-up pull request here when it opens. If you would rather see that one first, say so and I will reorder. Finally, the underlying compiler behaviour is not fixed here. `swapcontext` changing the thread pointer is outside LLVM's model, and the right long-term home is upstream. This change makes the crash unreachable in the one configuration where it can occur. My merged #110152 does not cover this. That pull request fixes a *different* aarch64 MemorySanitizer fiber defect (padding shadow), and its content is compiled into the binary that produced this crash — inside `contrib/boost`, `git merge-base --is-ancestor 24df31b3e5c13c e24b1b25e334` is true — and the signature fired anyway. Both are needed.

signal.title: Fix signed integer overflow in Keeper coordination timeouts
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106961 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes signed integer overflow when a Keeper coordination timeout such as `operation_timeout_ms`, `session_timeout_ms` or `startup_timeout` is set to a very large value. Converting the millisecond count to nanoseconds, and adding it to the current time to form a deadline, could both overflow, so the wait expired immediately instead of waiting for the configured time, and the server aborted in builds with the undefined behaviour sanitizer. ### Description Found while sweeping the Keeper half of #106961, scoped out of it because coordination timeouts need a different bound from query-execution waits ([scope-out comment](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106961#issuecomment-5050311603)). #### What goes wrong A millisecond timeout reaches a `std::chrono` expression whose common type is `nanoseconds`, represented as `Int64`. Two operations there overflow, both undefined behaviour: the `count() * 1000000` conversion in `__chrono/duration.h`, and the deadline addition `steady_clock::now() + d` reached from `condition_variable::wait_for` and `std::future::wait_for`. A configured value in `[9223372036855, 9223372036854775]` is stored faithfully and still overflows the conversion. The wrapped deadline lies in the past, so a wait configured to be long gives up immediately. Under `-fno-sanitize-recover=all`, set for sanitizer builds, it aborts the server instead: `signed integer overflow` at `__chrono/duration.h:93`, [example report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108468&sha=90aff18153638c03d5c74142a927349b3c3405b4&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29), symbolizing into `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::popImpl` at one of the lines changed here. #### What I changed Saturation at the unsafe conversion, in the callee owning the timeout, bounded at `(INT64_MAX / 2) / 1000000`, about 146 years. No setting is capped: `e90238828006b0` ("Allow to use bigger timeouts for zookeeper") fixes this bug class by widening the conversion and leaving the value alone. Half the range, because each site then adds `steady_clock::now`, so a bound that only just fits the conversion still wraps after days of uptime; `AtomicStopwatch::secondsToNanoseconds` does the same. Twenty sites: waits and `steady_clock` comparisons in `KeeperServer`, `KeeperContext`, `KeeperDispatcher` and both request dispatchers; three via `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::tryPop`/`tryPush`, fixed inside the queue; two at the `open_client_req_stream` boundary into NuRaft. The three boundaries keep deliberately different rules, detailed below. #### Tests 14 unit tests in `src/Common/tests/gtest_saturated_wait_duration.cpp` and `src/Coordination/tests/gtest_keeper_saturated_wait.cpp`; these timeouts have no SQL surface. The oracle is behavioural: the wait's predicate is satisfied shortly after the wait begins, so an unfixed build fails instantly on its wrapped deadline. That discriminates on every build type and covers `UINT64_MAX`, which produces no sanitizer report at all. Each production change was confirmed load-bearing by reverting it alone. #### Not in this PR - `contrib/NuRaft/src/asio_service.cxx` does the same conversion for its other callers; being a submodule it needs a separate pull request against the fork first. - #106961 adds `DB::saturatedMilliseconds` with a one year policy bound and touches the same two `ConcurrentBoundedQueue` lines. The helpers can converge once it merges; a one year cap would be wrong here. - `src/Coordination/Changelog.cpp` builds five `milliseconds` values from three raw `UInt64` changelog settings, one of which (`log_readahead_serve_wait_timeout_ms`) reaches a `wait_until`. Same conversion, different setting family, file untouched here, and I have not measured a consequence there. <details> <summary>The three boundary rules, and which waits are actually unsafe</summary> - **Waits** get the half-range bound, two-sided, non-positive clamped to zero, which is what `wait_for` does with a non-positive duration anyway, so no shutdown path can newly block. The two dispatchers already read this setting into different types on `master`, `int64_t` in `KeeperRequestDispatcher` and `uint64_t` in `KeeperRequestDispatcherOld`, so a negative count saturates to zero on the signed sites and to the bound on the unsigned ones. Those declarations are untouched; on `master` both are undefined behaviour instead. - **`min_session_timeout`/`max_session_timeout` in `KeeperTCPHandler`** only get their `* 1000` made safe, at the full `Poco::Timespan::TimeDiff` range. This is not a wait: it is copied into the replicated request, stored in `session_and_timeout` and the expiry queue, and compared at full microsecond value, so clamping it would change expiry policy. The wait on this path is bounded inside `getSessionID`. The handshake reply is a protocol `int32`, so a `session_timeout_ms` above `INT32_MAX` already diverges between server and client on `master`, identically; widening that field is separate. - **The NuRaft boundary** saturates only the upper end, converting to unsigned first exactly as the `uint64_t` parameter does today. NuRaft arms its timers only when the count is nonzero, so mapping a negative count to zero would silently disable the timer, which is worse than the overflow. `condition_variable::wait_for` without a predicate is already safe, going through `__safe_nanosecond_cast`; the undefined behaviour is only in the predicate overload, which every one of these sites uses. `std::future::wait_for` is unsafe regardless, being `wait_until(now() + rel)` with no checked cast. `sleep_for` is safe, so the two Keeper `sleep_for` sites are untouched, and `KeeperServer.cpp`'s `operation_timeout_ms * 2` never enters `std::chrono`. Both test files also build against the merge-base tree, because `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` overlays them there without the fix and reports a compile failure as inconclusive. Cases naming the new helper, and the two reaching the private `interruptibleSleep`, compile only where the header exists; the rest are unconditional. </details>
