signal.title: Keep the stack when an async signal arrives during an MSan report
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110102 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Bumped `contrib/llvm-project` so MemorySanitizer reports keep their stack trace when an asynchronous signal is delivered while the report is being printed. Affects MSan CI builds only. ### Description MSan check types intermittently produce a failure artifact with no stack at all. The entire report, in every artifact (`sanitizer.log.<pid>` is 60 bytes; `stderr.log`, `clickhouse-server.err.log` and `fatal.log` contain nothing more), is: ``` ==117==WARNING: MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value MemorySanitizer: nested bug in the same thread, aborting. LLVM ERROR: IO failure on output stream: Broken pipe ``` CIDB buckets all of them under one synthetic test name, `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value (STID: None)`. This is an observability defect that hides an unknown number of distinct uninitialized reads: 23 hits in the last 30 days across `AST fuzzer (amd_msan)`, `Stress test (arm_msan)`, `Stress test (amd_msan)`, `Stress test (azure, amd_msan)`, `Stateless tests (amd_msan, flaky check)` and `Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge)`, on 22 distinct commits, and not one has a usable stack. Root cause. `ScopedErrorReportLock::Lock` records the reporting thread in `reporting_thread_` and clears it only in `Unlock`. Printing a report is slow: `stack->Print` and `ReportErrorSummary` round-trip to the out-of-process `llvm-symbolizer`, so the reporting thread sits blocked on a pipe for milliseconds. `QueryProfiler` arms a per-thread `timer_create` on every query thread (`SIGEV_THREAD_ID` with `SIGUSR1` for the real profiler, `SIGUSR2` for the CPU profiler), so an asynchronous signal regularly lands inside that window. If its handler touches uninitialized memory, the second report re-enters the lock, takes the same-thread branch, and calls `internal__exit` without printing anything. The first report is lost, and the pipe to the abandoned symbolizer child produces the trailing `LLVM ERROR` line. The fix blocks asynchronous signals for the duration of the report in `PrintWarningWithOrigin`, the single funnel every UMR report goes through. On Linux `BlockSignals` keeps the synchronous signals (`SIGSEGV`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGILL`, `SIGTRAP`, `SIGABRT`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGPIPE`), `SIGSYS` and glibc's `SIGSETXID` unblocked, so a genuine crash while reporting still aborts as before, and it never unblocks a signal the caller had deliberately blocked. Those exemptions are themselves Linux-only, so the change is gated on `SANITIZER_LINUX`; on FreeBSD, which also builds the in-tree compiler-rt, behaviour is unchanged. **This fixes none of the uninitialized reads. It makes them diagnosable.** Once merged, these failures should start arriving with a real stack and a real STID, and can then be triaged individually. Library change: ClickHouse/llvm-project#118 (**open**). This PR pins `contrib/llvm-project` at that PR's head commit so ClickHouse CI can validate it end to end; the pin will be re-pointed to the merge commit on `ClickHouse/release-22.x` before this PR is merged. Verification, on ClickHouse's own rebuilt `clang_rt_msan` (the in-tree runtime is what actually ships: `cmake/compiler_rt_link.cmake` whole-archives `libclang_rt_msan{,_cxx}.a` and passes `-fno-sanitize-link-runtime`), using the new lit test, which raises the signal from inside the report via `__sanitizer_on_print` so that it always lands while the report lock is held: | runtime | `nested bug` aborts | stack frames | |---|---|---| | without the change | 50/50 | 0 | | with the change | 0/50 | 1600 (full stack + origin chain + `SUMMARY`) | Removing only the added line and rebuilding returns it to 50/50 aborts with 0 frames, so the guard is exercised. A synchronous `SIGSEGV` or `SIGABRT` raised inside the report window still produces a deadly-signal report and still aborts. Latest occurrence: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111930&sha=cd52dcce7cf17a6a72e0a0dda6220472bbd1f7d6&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29 The new lit test `compiler-rt/test/msan/Linux/nested_report_async_signal.cpp` lives in the fork PR. ClickHouse CI does not build or run compiler-rt's lit suite, so that test guards the fork and is runnable by hand. What this PR's own CI can and cannot show, stated plainly so nobody spends time on the wrong signal: the signature is rare per run (23 hits over 7659 `AST fuzzer (amd_msan)` and 8613 `Stress test (amd_msan)` runs in 30 days, so under 0.15% of runs), so a green MSan run here is **not** evidence the guard works, and a red one is a pre-existing uninitialized read that should now arrive with a stack. What this PR's CI does prove is that the bumped runtime builds and that MSan jobs behave normally with the mask in place. The guard itself is proven by the 50-run both-directions measurement above, on ClickHouse's own runtime, with the one-line mutation as the control. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110102

signal.title: Fix logical error 'Bad cast to ColumnVariant' in set operations
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110745 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a logical error `Bad cast from type DB::ColumnVector<long> to DB::ColumnVariant` that you could hit on a nested `EXCEPT` or `INTERSECT` chain over large unsuffixed integer literals combined with a correlated scalar subquery. Such a query now runs instead of failing, because the query planner and the analyzer no longer infer different supertypes for the same union column. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110745 (same function, disjoint trigger, see below) Reported by the AST fuzzer, but reachable from an ordinary `SELECT` at default settings: ```sql SELECT * FROM (((SELECT 9223372036854775806 AS n) EXCEPT ALL SELECT 10 AS n) EXCEPT ALL SELECT -9223372036854775807 AS n) WHERE (n = (SELECT n)); ``` CI report where I saw it: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110567&sha=f1bb40ed1844641f81efce3a2266f95abfb4e515&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 Terminology note: this is a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception, handled normally in release builds; it aborts only in debug and sanitizer builds. #### Root cause `DataTypeUInt64` carries a per-instance `canUnsignedBeSigned` flag. `FieldToDataType` sets it for a `UInt64` literal that also fits `Int64`, and `convertUInt64toInt64IfPossible` consumes it so that `getLeastSupertype` can return a plain `Int64` instead of a `Variant`. `DataTypeNumber::equals` compares only `typeid`, so a flagged and an unflagged `UInt64` are indistinguishable to every `equals()`-based check. `addConvertingToCommonHeaderActionsIfNeeded` is the function whose contract is "make every union branch match the computed common header", and it skipped such a branch twice over. `blocksHaveEqualStructure` reported equality, and even when the converting DAG was built, `makeConvertingActions` omitted the CAST because the types compare `equals()`-equal. The branch therefore published its own flagged type as the union output type. The enclosing union then folded that flagged `UInt64` together with an `Int64` branch, `convertUInt64toInt64IfPossible` fired, and the plan header collapsed to `Int64`, while the analyzer, whose nested fold went through a freshly constructed unflagged instance, had already declared `Variant(Int64, UInt64)` for the same node. Every consumer built off the declared type then disagreed with the column actually flowing through the plan. `IFunctionOverloadResolver::build` installs `FunctionBaseVariantAdaptor` whenever a declared argument type is `Variant`, so `ExecutableFunctionVariantAdaptor::executeImpl` cast a `ColumnVector`/`ColumnNullable` to `ColumnVariant` and threw. That also explains why the two occurrences of this signature reported different incoming column types: the defect is a type/column divergence, so whichever wrapper the real column happens to carry is what gets reported. The same class of flag loss is already worked around at the consumption site twice in `src/Functions/if.cpp` (issues #105649 and #70017). This fixes it one layer up, so every consumer above a union sees a consistent type rather than each function needing its own guard. #### The fix Force the conversion when a branch column and its common-header target compare `equals()`-equal but the branch carries the flag and the target does not, and force the CAST that `makeConvertingActions` would skip. Two properties are deliberate: - The predicate is one directional. A flagged common target is constructible through the `all_equal` shortcut in `getLeastSupertype`, so a union mixing flagged and unflagged branches resolves to a different type depending on branch order and is correct today. Adding a flag is never necessary, so the predicate never fires in that direction. Both orders are pinned as controls in the test. - It refuses a container that would strip one leaf's flag and add another's, because `addCast` converts a whole column and cannot flip one tuple element without flipping the sibling. `DataTypeTuple::equals` is element-wise and equally flag-blind, so such a pair compares equal today and is left untouched. Also pinned as a control. #### Relationship to #110745 #110745 restructures the same function into the same two-part shape (a `needs_conversion` flag replacing the bare skip, plus a forced cast after `makeConvertingActions`) for a different trigger: aggregate-state types that share a state representation but differ by type NAME. It cannot cover this bug, because both of its halves key on `type->getName()`, and `DataTypeNumberBase` derives its name from a static `family_name` that never encodes the flag. `toTypeName(9223372036854775806)` and `toTypeName(9223372036854775806::UInt64)` both print `UInt64`, so a name comparison skips the flagged pair exactly as `equals()` does. The two are disjoint triggers on the same lines. I wrote this fix to compose with that shape rather than re-derive it, and verified the composition: merging #110745 into this branch needs one mechanical resolution in the shared predicate, and on the combined binary both regression tests pass (this PR's `04647_union_common_header_supertype_flag` and #110745's `04545_lift_up_union_agg_state_type_mismatch`). #### Observed but not addressed The order dependence of a mixed flagged/unflagged fold, caused by `getLeastSupertype`'s `all_equal` shortcut returning `types[0]` verbatim, is a real wart, but it does not abort and changing it would move result types of currently working queries. Out of scope here. #### Verification - Fails on the base binary with the CI signature and a stack matching the CI report through `ActionsDAG::updateHeader`; passes with the fix. Driven statement by statement against the base binary, since the base aborts on the first offending statement and would mask the rest. - Each half of the fix mutation tested with its own discriminating query: reverting only the widened skip predicate brings back the abort for the `materialize()`-on-every-branch form, and reverting only the forced cast brings back the abort for the literal form. Neither mutation moves the negative controls. - The two deliberate restrictions above are each pinned by a `Conversion before UNION` plan-step count in the test, because a type name cannot see the flag and no asserted value changes with the predicate. Mutation tested: widening the predicate to "strips or adds" moves three of those counts, dropping only the mixed-direction refusal moves one, and neither mutation moves any other asserted byte. Every expected count was measured and then checked against a prediction written before the mutation builds. - 50 randomized runs of the new test, all green. - Type-wrapper matrix covered: bare, `Nullable`, `LowCardinality`, `Array`, `Tuple`, `Map`, all aborting on base and passing with the fix. - Union over aggregating branches through `remote()` checked to be unchanged, including at `serialize_query_plan = 1`. That check pins `prefer_localhost_replica = 0`, because the runner randomizes it and at value 1 a plain `MergeTree` shard is planned entirely locally, so no secondary-query plan would be built at all: measured 4 secondary queries with the pin against 0 without it, with identical results either way. - Sweep of the 354 stateless tests matching `union`, `except`, `intersect`, `variant` on the fixed and the base binary: failure sets identical apart from three tests independently confirmed flaky on the base binary.

signal.title: Convert 02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start from stateless to integration
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111922 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112000 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111922 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112000 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111053 CI report for the latest occurrence: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=86431&sha=3098f66a962dacb32386896928b706daa39908b0&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade%20check%20%28amd_release%29 Follows the directive on #111922 that functional tests must not fabricate or intervene with data parts outside the ClickHouse API surface, using the same conversion pattern as #112000. `tests/queries/0_stateless/02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start.sh` reads part paths out of `system.parts` and runs `rm -f "$path/data.bin"` on two server-written ReplicatedMergeTree parts. It is killed mid-run often enough that its own `detach`/`attach` recovery never executes, and the upgrade stage keeps the damaged table on disk: `--upgrade-check` implies `--fake-drop`, so every `DROP TABLE` of a table that stores data on disk is a no-op, and the odd stress workers run with `--database=test_N`, which disables `clickhouse-test`'s per-test database cleanup. After the upgrade restart the new binary finds the part, reports it broken and detaches it, which reddens `Upgrade check` with three `<Error>` lines: ``` <Error> test_1.rmt1 (...): Part .../all_0_0_0/ is broken and needs manual correction. Reason: Code: 107. DB::Exception: store/.../all_0_0_0/data.bin doesn't exist: columns: columns format version: 1 <Error> test_1.rmt1: while loading part all_0_0_0 on path store/.../all_0_0_0: <same> <Error> test_1.rmt1: Detaching broken part .../all_0_0_0 (size: 788.00 B). If it happened after update, it is likely because of backward incompatibility. You need to resolve this manually ``` The server is behaving correctly. 4 `Upgrade check (amd_release)` failures over 90 days, on 4 unrelated PRs, all on the same `test_1.rmt1` / `all_0_0_0` / 784-788 B fixture. The message text is also what a genuine backward-incompatible part-format regression would look like, so allow-listing it would mask the class this job exists to catch. Two changes: - `tests/integration/test_broken_parts_chain_on_start` replaces the stateless test. It owns its server and its restart, so the fixture cannot leak into a shared-database run. Coverage is stronger than the original: a kill + restart exercises the real on-start load path instead of `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, and the post-restart state is asserted explicitly (both parts detached as `broken-on-start_*`, the replica recovers all 3 rows, `lost_part_count` stays 0) where the original swallowed the `attach` error. - `tests/docker_scripts/upgrade_runner.sh` skips the test by name in the upgrade stage. This is needed because that stage runs the frozen previous-release checkout, so deleting the test on master cannot affect what runs there; a skip tag would be read from the previous-release file too. The comment records when the skip can be removed. `02254_projection_broken_part` removes `ab.proj/data.bin` the same way and has not produced this signature; it is converted separately rather than bundled here.

signal.title: Fix the CI failure reporter discarding the error message
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111892 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111708 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111873 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111934 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111892 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111708 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111873 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111934 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `FuzzerLogParser.parse_failure` trims the matched log record to "all lines before the next log line", but the scan started at index 0, i.e. it also tested the matched line itself. Several `error_patterns` alternatives are written with a leading `.*`, so `rg -o` keeps the record's own `] {query_id} <Level>` prefix; the next-record guard then fires at index 0, `error_lines[:0]` is empty and the failure is reported with an empty `Error:` section. This is what the `Server unresponsive: memory limit exceeded` leaf has been doing. Its 33 CIDB rows over 90 days span 23 pull requests and 9 master runs, and every one of them has an empty `Error:` section - 31 as the byte-identical 57-character envelope below, the other 2 as the same thing without the `Log files:` line that only the stress job prepends: ``` Log files: clickhouse-server.err.log, stderr.log Error: ``` while the job's own `clickhouse-server.err.log` holds the message, the limit, the RSS and the allocation site. For master run `b0ab0f245a7ce9eb8c32bbb0f68d3c1359dcfac4` (`Stress test (arm_release)`), the record the parser matched and then dropped is: ``` 2026.07.23 12:49:49.312341 [ 3574 ] {0166dacb-...::201403_1_29_1} <Error> virtual bool DB::MergePlainMergeTreeTask::executeStep(): Exception is in merge_task.: Code: 241. DB::Exception: (total) memory limit exceeded: would use 43.50 GiB (attempt to allocate chunk of 0.00 B), current RSS: 47.10 GiB, maximum: 47.07 GiB. (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) ``` plus eight frames naming `MemoryTracker::allocImpl` under `MergeTreeReadTask::createReaders`. Driving the real parser over that artifact: `error_output` is 0 characters on master and 1911 characters (message + allocation site, still bounded by the existing `head -n10`) with this change. `error_patterns` has 7 entries holding 12 top-level alternatives. One case per alternative was driven through the real parser in both directions (the two marked `†` follow from the leading-`.*` structure, sharing an entry with a measured sibling). Five of the seven entries lose their message this way and are repaired here; an entry can appear on both sides of the table, e.g. `Assertion` has one affected and two unaffected alternatives. | `error_patterns` entry | alternative | `Error:` on master | with this change | |---|---|---|---| | Memory limit exceeded | `.*\(total\) memory limit exceeded.*` | empty | message + allocation site | | Assertion | `.*_LIBCPP_ASSERT.*` | empty | message | | Signal | `.*Child process was terminated by signal 9.*` | empty | message | | Sanitizer | `.*[a-zA-Z]+Sanitizer: CHECK failed:.*` | empty | report | | Runtime error | `.*is located.*` | empty | message | | Runtime error | `.*runtime error: .*` † | empty | message | | Logical error | `Logical error.*` | correct | byte-identical | | SegFault | `Segmentation fault.*` | correct | byte-identical | | Signal | `Received signal.*` | correct | byte-identical | | Assertion | `Assertion.*failed` | correct | byte-identical | | Assertion | `Failed assertion.*` † | correct | byte-identical | | Sanitizer | `(SUMMARY\|ERROR\|WARNING): ...Sanitizer:.*` | correct | byte-identical | The alternatives that were already correct are exactly the ones without a leading `.*`: `rg -o` strips the prefix for them, so their line 0 never satisfied the guard. The guard itself is right; only its start index was wrong, and a loop looking for the *next* log record must not examine the record it started from. Job status is unaffected: `stress_job.py`'s `is_oom` override is computed independently of this parser, so this only restores the content of the leaf. Five regression tests are added in `ci/tests/test_log_parser.py`, one per repaired entry, each asserting the message is present in the `Error:` section specifically (the same text can also appear in the separate `Stack trace:` section, so an assertion over the whole info would pass even with the message dropped) and that the capture still stops at the next log record. Reverting the one-line change fails exactly those five and leaves the three pre-existing tests green. `ci/jobs/scripts/log_parser.py` is also touched by #111708, #111873 and #111934, all on other parts of the file. Each was merged onto this branch: all three merge with no conflict and the combined `ci/tests/test_log_parser.py` passes (16, 12 and 8 tests respectively). #111873 re-anchors the signal pattern, which incidentally removes the leading `.*` from one of the six alternatives above; the loop bound is still wrong for the other five, so the two changes are independent and compose in either merge order.

signal.title: Fix wrong result and LOGICAL_ERROR for a matcher inside a lambda with join_use_nulls / group_by_use_nulls
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107951 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107951 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results and a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Cannot capture column ... because it has incompatible type`) when a matcher such as `b.*`, `*`, `COLUMNS('...')` or `b.* EXCEPT c` appears inside a lambda body. A matcher expanded inside a lambda kept its pre-join column types, so `join_use_nulls = 1` did not turn columns from the NULL side of a `LEFT`/`FULL`/`RIGHT` JOIN into `Nullable` (unmatched rows produced a value computed over defaults instead of `NULL`), and `group_by_use_nulls = 1` with `WITH ROLLUP` / `WITH CUBE` / `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS` failed with `NOT_AN_AGGREGATE`. A matcher expanded inside a lambda now carries the same types it would have if the columns were written out explicitly, and a lambda inside `PREWHERE` is no longer promoted to `Nullable` by `join_use_nulls`. Also fixed wrong results for a matcher inside a lambda when `analyzer_compatibility_join_using_top_level_identifier = 1` makes a `JOIN ... USING` key resolve to a `SELECT` projection alias: the matcher selected the merged `USING` key instead of the right table's column. ### Description `QueryAnalyzer::resolveMatcher` applies both nullability promotions by reading state off the scope it is handed: `join_use_nulls` iterates `scope.registered_table_expression_nodes`, and `group_by_use_nulls` looks matched columns up in `scope.nullable_group_by_keys`. Both containers are populated only on the query scope that owns the join tree, and `IdentifierResolveScope`'s constructor does not copy either to a child scope. A lambda body is resolved in a fresh child scope, so inside a lambda both promotion blocks were dead code and the matched columns kept their pre-promotion types. Column discovery still worked because it reaches through with `scope.getNearestQueryScope()` - that asymmetry was the bug. The single-identifier path promotes from the join kind and side it computed while walking the join tree, which is why `b.x` worked inside a lambda while `b.*` did not. Four bugs are fixed: 1. `join_use_nulls = 1` plus a matcher in a lambda over the NULL side of a `LEFT`/`FULL` JOIN. This is a wrong-results bug that additionally aborts in debug and sanitizer builds: ```sql SELECT arrayMap(z -> sipHash64(b.*), [1]) FROM t1 LEFT JOIN t2 AS b ON t1.a = b.x SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1; ``` The unmatched row must produce `[NULL]` of type `Array(Nullable(UInt64))`, matching the explicit-column form `sipHash64(b.x, b.y)`. Shapes that did not abort silently returned a hash computed over default values instead of `NULL`. The same promotion is missing for a `JOIN ... USING` on same-typed keys, where an unqualified matcher inside a lambda over a `RIGHT` or `FULL` join aborted with `Cannot capture column 2 ... got Tuple(UInt8, Nullable(UInt64)), but Tuple(UInt8, UInt64) is expected`, and is fixed by the same change: ```sql SELECT arrayMap(z -> tuple(* EXCEPT w), [1]) FROM p1 RIGHT JOIN p2 USING (a) SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1; ``` 2. `group_by_use_nulls = 1` plus a matcher in a lambda with `WITH ROLLUP`, `WITH CUBE` or `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS` failed with `Code: 215 NOT_AN_AGGREGATE`, because the non-promoted matcher column no longer matched the promoted GROUP BY key: ```sql SELECT x, y, arrayMap(z -> sipHash64(t3.*), [1]) FROM t3 GROUP BY x, y WITH ROLLUP SETTINGS group_by_use_nulls = 1; ``` 3. An expression containing a lambda in `PREWHERE` combined with a JOIN and `join_use_nulls = 1` aborted, with or without a matcher: ```sql SELECT count() FROM m1 RIGHT JOIN m2 AS b ON m1.a = b.x PREWHERE arrayMap(z -> sipHash64(m1.a), [1])[1] > 0 SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1; ``` 4. A matcher in a lambda selected the wrong column when `analyzer_compatibility_join_using_top_level_identifier = 1` made a `JOIN ... USING` key resolve to a `SELECT` projection alias. `resolveUnqualifiedMatcher` suppresses the synthetic merged `USING` key when the key is absent from a table expression's own columns, but that membership check read `table_expression_node_to_data` off the scope it was handed, and like the two containers above the map is populated only on the join-owning scope. Inside a lambda the lookup missed, the suppression never fired, and the matcher matched the merged key while the same matcher at the top level did not: ```sql SELECT a + 1 AS id, arrayMap(z -> tuple(* EXCEPT a), [1]) AS matcher FROM (SELECT 1 AS a UNION ALL SELECT 9 AS a) AS q1 FULL JOIN (SELECT 2 AS id) AS q2 USING (id) SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1, analyzer_compatibility_join_using_top_level_identifier = 1; -- unmatched row returned [(10)]; the top-level matcher returns NULL ``` Unlike the first three this one is independent of any `Nullable` promotion: it reproduces with `join_use_nulls = 0` as well, where the unmatched row returned `[(10)]` instead of `[(0)]`. Reported by the automated reviewer on this pull request. Classifying which side of a join a matched column comes from also has to see through an `ARRAY JOIN`: `isFromJoinTree` descended into `JOIN` and `CROSS JOIN` children only, so a column sourced below an `ArrayJoinNode` could not be assigned a side and its promotion was skipped. A matcher in a lambda then disagreed with the same matcher at the top level: ```sql SELECT toTypeName(arrayMap(z -> tuple(b1.*), [1])) FROM b1 ARRAY JOIN b1.arr RIGHT JOIN b2 ON b1.k = b2.k SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1; -- Array(Tuple(UInt64, Array(UInt64))), while `SELECT b1.*` reports k as Nullable(UInt64) ``` Both promotion blocks in `resolveMatcher` now read their state from the nearest scope that owns it, bounded at the enclosing QUERY/UNION scope so a lambda in an inner subquery cannot adopt an outer query's join tree or GROUP BY keys. The owning scope is also passed to `convertJoinedColumnTypeToNullIfNeeded`, because it records the type change in `scope.join_columns_with_changed_types` and the `PREWHERE` rollback reads that map only from the query scope. `group_by_use_nulls` promotion must not apply to pre-aggregation values, and the block's aggregate guard read the immediate scope only. Since `ExpressionsStack` is per-scope, an aggregate enclosing a lambda sits on a parent scope's stack, so the guard is now the same cross-scope scan `resolveExpressionNode` already uses. `join_use_nulls` nullability is a property of the join output, so it deliberately has no such guard, and `sum(arrayMap(z -> sipHash64(b.*), [1])[1])` is promoted. `PREWHERE` is evaluated storage-side, before the join, so its expressions must keep pre-join types. `resolveQuery` enforced that by re-resolving `PREWHERE` and undoing promotions with `ReplaceColumnsVisitor`, whose `needChildVisit` does not descend into `LAMBDA`, so the rollback could not reach a lambda body. Rather than deepen the rollback, `join_use_nulls` is now cleared on the query scope while `PREWHERE` is resolved, so the promotion never happens there. This is the same mechanism already used at the USING-column alias site. A subquery nested inside `PREWHERE` re-reads the setting from its own context, so its own join is unaffected, and case 3 above is fixed by the same change. One related failure is deliberately left out of scope, because it is a different root cause that this change does not touch. A `JOIN ... USING` on differently typed keys retypes the matched column to the supertype in `createProjectionForUsing`, and that retype is independent of `join_use_nulls`: `need_nullable` only decides whether the type is wrapped in `Nullable`, while `setColumnType` runs either way. So an unqualified matcher in a `PREWHERE` lambda still adopts the `USING` supertype: ```sql -- p1.a is UInt8, p2.a is Int64 SELECT count() FROM p1 LEFT JOIN p2 USING (a) PREWHERE arrayMap(z -> tuple(* EXCEPT w), [1])[1].1 >= 0 SETTINGS join_use_nulls = 1; -- Unexpected return type from tuple. Expected Tuple(Int64, UInt64). Got Tuple(UInt8, UInt64) ``` This fails identically before and after this change, with `join_use_nulls = 0` and on `INNER JOIN` as well. The retype cannot simply be skipped, because its entry in `join_columns_with_changed_types` is what redirects the `USING` column to the left table in `PREWHERE`; a proper fix needs the `PREWHERE` rollback to descend into lambda bodies and to re-resolve the lambda's cached signature, which is a larger change than this one. Test: `tests/queries/0_stateless/04647_matcher_in_lambda_join_use_nulls.sql`. Every case asserts values against the equivalent explicit-column query rather than only the absence of an abort, and covers the matcher flavours (`*`, `b.*`, `COLUMNS`, `EXCEPT`, unaliased table name, nested lambdas), the join kinds, `LowCardinality` and `Array` column types, `USING` joins (including the `RIGHT`/`FULL` corner above, with and without `PREWHERE`), aggregate and window contexts, `PREWHERE` versus `WHERE`, a subquery nested in `PREWHERE`, and the projection-alias `USING` key of case 4 under both `join_use_nulls` values with a control that keeps the merged key matching when the compatibility setting is off, and a nullable side that is a subquery containing `ARRAY JOIN`, and both an `ARRAY JOIN` wrapped in a subquery and one directly on the join tree, whose columns are reached only by descending through the `ARRAY JOIN` when classifying the join side. Found by the AST fuzzer inside the stress test. CI reports: `Stress test (arm_debug)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110127&sha=40ea0f0e62eb09b0e480d458e33b45e54585e517&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_debug%29 `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110105&sha=f53e6fc6ff04e64324e20729e7eb7d3401627894&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29 `Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107582&sha=09ae616ec6fa5ae5f217d9acb4bcd15bec0a5ddd&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29 The signature is reported under two stack-trace ids, `STID 3293-4e7f` on arm builds and `STID 3293-46fa` on amd builds. They are the same defect: the ClickHouse frames are identical, differing only in two frames that arm inlines away, the aborting query is byte-identical, and over 40 days every 4e7f hit is arm and every 46fa hit is amd with no crossover. Combined, 9 hits across 9 unrelated pull requests in 40 days and never on master.

signal.title: Do not evaluate a potentially throwing PREWHERE condition ahead of its guard
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111879 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107988 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `CANNOT_INSERT_NULL_IN_ORDINARY_COLUMN` when a `PREWHERE` guard predicate and a throwing expression, such as a `CAST`, read subcolumns of the same column, for example a `JSON` or `Map` column. Such a query used to fail because the throwing expression was evaluated on rows the guard had rejected. Closes #111879. ### Description Closes #111879. Regression from #107988, present in 26.3 through 26.7. All conditions of one PREWHERE read step are evaluated on the same unfiltered block, and the step filter is applied only afterwards, so a guard condition cannot protect a later condition placed in the same step. Since #107988, `MergeTreeWhereOptimizer` groups conditions by their physical storage column, so a guard such as `payload.longitude IS NOT NULL` and a throwing predicate over `payload.latitude` arrive adjacent and `tryBuildPrewhereSteps` merges them into one step. The throwing expression then runs on the rows the guard rejects. Adding more `IS NOT NULL` guards does not help, because they are hoisted into the same step. The in-tree comment claimed adjacent-only merging was safe precisely because the WHERE optimizer makes such conditions adjacent. #111879 is the counterexample: that adjacency is what creates the unsafe merge. Commit 757261341d4b7 already reverted non-adjacent merging for the same hazard ("would pull the throwing conversion before the `value > 0` filter"); this change closes the adjacent case. Fix, in `tryBuildPrewhereSteps`: - Propagate a `may_throw` flag through the existing `fillRequiredColumns` DFS, using `IFunctionBase::isSuitableForShortCircuitArgumentsExecution` (the same predicate the short-circuit machinery uses, and what `IExecutableFunction::canThrow` delegates to). It is a heuristic for "throws or is expensive" rather than an exact can-throw oracle, so it is imprecise in both directions: it reports true for merely expensive functions, and false for a few that throw only while parsing row values, such as `addDays(String, ...)`. There is no exact oracle in the tree today; `IFunctionAdaptors.h` carries a TODO for a dedicated `canThrow`, and adding one would mean auditing every function class, so this change covers the functions the existing predicate already flags. - A condition that may throw always starts a new read step, so every condition already in the group is evaluated before it. - Force `need_filter = true` on the step immediately preceding such a boundary. A boundary alone is not sufficient: a non-final step's `need_filter` is just `query_plan_merge_filters` (and is hard-coded false for the Parquet reader), and `ReadResult::optimize` applies a step filter on its own only when fewer than 60% of the rows pass. Without this, a guard that keeps most rows, or `query_plan_merge_filters = 0`, would leave the throwing step reading rejected rows. - Flatten nested conjunctions before grouping. The splitter used to take the children of the top-level `and` verbatim, so an inner `and` counted as one atomic condition and its guard and throwing predicate stayed together. `optimizePrewhere` builds exactly that shape, `and(existing_prewhere, and(guard, throwing))`, when it merges a moved `WHERE` into an existing `PREWHERE` under `optimize_prewhere_after_pushdown`. The flattening is a plain recursion that appends children left to right, because both the boundary logic and the evaluation order promised for a user written `PREWHERE` depend on the original order; `ActionsDAG::extractConjunctionAtoms` walks with a stack and reverses sibling order, so it is not reused. Conditions that cannot throw are still grouped, so the redundant-read optimization from #107988 is preserved for the shapes it targets. `arrayElement`, `tupleElement` and the comparison functions all report false, so the query shapes in `tests/performance/map_subcolumns_prewhere.xml` keep their read-step counts (16 Map keys in explicit PREWHERE: 1 step; Map keys interleaved with another column: 2 steps; 6 Map keys via WHERE: 1 step). The cost of the predicate's imprecision is that conjunctions of merely expensive functions now split where master grouped them. Measured on the wide shape from that performance test, 16 conjuncts over 2 million rows: | PREWHERE conjuncts | Steps before | Steps after | Rows read by prewhere readers | Wall clock | |---|---|---|---|---| | `tags['kN'] != ''` x16 | 1 | 1 | 2.0M to 2.0M | unchanged within run-to-run noise | | `startsWith(tags['kN'], '1')` x16 | 1 | 16 | 2.0M to 19.2M | 172 ms to 857 ms | | `tags['kN'] LIKE '1%'` x16 | 1 | 16 | 2.0M to 19.2M | 166 ms to 871 ms | The step and row counts are deterministic; the timings are 3-run averages on a busy machine, so treat the ~5x as an order of magnitude rather than a precise figure. Selected marks stay at 245 in every case, so no extra granules are read; the cost is re-deserialization per step plus the forced filter materialization. A dedicated `canThrow` oracle would remove it and let `startsWith` and `LIKE` group again. I kept that out of this change because it means auditing every function class, and correctness comes first. Both regressed shapes are added to `tests/performance/map_subcolumns_prewhere.xml`, next to the `!= ''` shape from #107988 that stays in a single step, so the Performance Comparison check reports this cost instead of it living only in this description, and a future change to the boundary predicate shows up as a measured difference. The regression test covers the JSON repro from the issue, the same shape with both coordinates guarded, `allow_reorder_prewhere_conditions = 0`, `query_plan_merge_filters = 0`, a guard that keeps 90% of the rows, Map subcolumns via both WHERE and a user written PREWHERE, a guard and a throwing condition on different physical columns, a nested conjunction from a WHERE merged into an existing PREWHERE, and an assertion that non-throwing Map conditions are still rewritten to subcolumns. A companion `.sh` test asserts the grouping itself through the `RowsReadByPrewhereReaders` profile event, which is the only observable that distinguishes one grouped step from several split ones; it also asserts that flattening a nested conjunction of conditions that cannot throw still leaves them in a single step. The flat `WHERE` form of the different-columns case is deliberately not asserted. `MergeTreeWhereOptimizer` orders the conditions it moves by estimated column size, so a throwing condition can legitimately become the first step, with nothing before it to filter. That is equally true on master, so a flat `WHERE` carries no evaluation order contract. A user written `PREWHERE` does, and that is the form the test pins.

signal.title: Reject importing foreign persisted block identities in cross-table partition adoption
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108715 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108715 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Block offsets ... are not sorted within block number ...` in `applyPatchJoin`, an abort under debug/sanitizer builds) and the corresponding silent wrong-row patching in release builds, caused by lightweight updates on a table that adopted parts from another table via `REPLACE`/`ATTACH`/`MOVE PARTITION FROM`, `CREATE TABLE ... CLONE AS`, `FETCH PARTITION`/`FETCH PART`, or `MOVE PART TO SHARD`. Such adoption now throws `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` when a source part physically stores the `_block_number` or `_block_offset` column, because those persisted identities belong to the source table's block-number allocator and collide with the destination's. `FETCH` is rejected for any source path, including the table's own, because it clones the part into `detached/` for a later `ATTACH`. Also fixed a failing `FETCH PARTITION` leaving the parts it had already fetched in `detached/`, which made them attachable and made a retry of the same statement fail differently, with `PARTITION_ALREADY_EXISTS`. ### Description Found by `Stress test (arm_tsan)` on the unrelated PR #108715: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108715&sha=870fe2bdb1cfda4dbd20fd6fff4f788e074f0736&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 . Signature: `Logical error: 'Block offsets (0, 0) are not sorted within block number 1'` at `src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:578`, thrown while a background `MutateTask` applies patch parts. The same error was seen earlier on #97261 (2026-02-18). #108715 does not touch patch parts, mutations, or the reader chain, so this is a separate, pre-existing bug and I am fixing it in this separate PR. Root cause. With `enable_block_number_column` / `enable_block_offset_column` enabled, `_block_number` and `_block_offset` are persisted physical columns materialized at merge time (level >= 1 parts; zero-level inserts omit them). The patch-parts design requires `(_block_number, _block_offset)` to be a unique row identity (`PatchPartInfo.h`), and Join-mode patch application keys rows by exactly this pair. Cross-table partition adoption (`REPLACE`/`ATTACH`/`MOVE PARTITION FROM`, `CLONE AS`, cross-shard/foreign `FETCH`) clones parts by hardlink and renames them to fresh destination block numbers, but carries the source's persisted identity column data unchanged. Every table numbers blocks from 1, so the imported identities collide with the destination's own. A later merge gathers the duplicates into one part; applying a lightweight-update patch in Join mode then meets the same `(block_number, block_offset)` twice and hits the sorted/unique assertion in `applyPatchJoin` under debug/sanitizer builds. In a release build there is no abort but the join applies the patch value to every row carrying that identity, including rows attached after the update, so the update retroactively corrupts rows it must never touch. Fix. A new helper `MergeTreeData::assertNoPersistedBlockIdentityInAdoptedParts` throws `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` when any part being adopted physically contains `_block_number` or `_block_offset`. It is called at every sanctioned cross-table adoption door: `replacePartitionFrom` and `movePartitionToTable` (both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree`, on the initiator before the log entry), the `to_detached` path of `fetchPart` (user `FETCH PARTITION/PART`, including a same-table fetch that clones an active part into `detached/`), and `movePartitionToShard`. `CREATE TABLE ... CLONE AS` is covered through its lowering to `ATTACH PARTITION ALL FROM`. The check is content-based, not settings-based, because destination settings are mutable and a part without the persisted files serves only name-derived (native-consistent) virtual values. Self-`REPLACE` is exempt: it removes the originals it clones, so the identities stay native and unique; self-`ATTACH` is not exempt because it keeps the originals and duplicates their identities immediately. This mirrors the layer and error code of #107386, which closed the sibling patch-orphaning hole in the same functions. Second fix, found in review of the above. A failing `FETCH PARTITION` left partial state behind. `fetchPartition` fetches the parts of a partition concurrently and rethrows only after every worker has finished, so in a partition holding both a merged identity-bearing part and a later level-0 part, the level-0 worker renames its part into `detached/` before the merged one is rejected. The statement failed, yet that part stayed in `detached/` where an `ATTACH PART` could pick it up, and a retry of the identical statement then failed earlier and with a different error, `PARTITION_ALREADY_EXISTS` from `checkIfDetachedPartitionExists`. `fetchPartition` now records the parts it renamed into `detached/` itself and, unless the whole partition was fetched, removes exactly those on the way out. Ownership comes from the rename, not from the name: with `to_detached` a `true` result from `fetchPart` means that call performed the rename under that exact name, whereas the entry check is explicitly racy and a part detached concurrently would have taken a `_tryN` name instead. Each part is renamed out of the way and removed individually, as `DROP DETACHED PARTITION` does, so failing on one part neither rolls back nor skips the others, and a failure after the rename leaves at worst an inert directory (a `deleting_` prefix is never a candidate for `ATTACH`). That staging name carries a unique suffix, so a leftover from an earlier attempt can never collide with, and thereby block, a later one. This non-atomicity predates the new guard, since any mid-fetch failure reached it, but the guard is the first common way to hit it. Residual on that second fix, disclosed rather than papered over, with a correction to what I wrote earlier about it. Cleanup identifies its parts by name. That is sound against the ordinary case, where a part detached concurrently takes a `_tryN` name because ours still occupies the canonical one, but not against a session that first drops our just-fetched `detached/` part and then detaches the still-active part of the same name inside the failure window: the replacement lands under the canonical name too (`forcefullyMovePartToDetachedAndRemoveFromMemory` defaults to an empty prefix, `MergeTreeData.h:971`), and cleanup would remove it. Correction: I previously justified deferring this by saying the remediation changes the `to_detached` contract of `fetchPart`, "a function also used by background replication". That reason is wrong. `fetchPart` has three callers, and background replication passes `to_detached=false` (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:2791`); only user `FETCH PART`/`FETCH PARTITION` (`:8175`, `:8334`) reach the `to_detached` branch that owns the canonical rename, as the comment at `:5715` says. The real reasons it is separate work: the query-unique name must be threaded through both producers, the download path (`Fetcher::fetchSelectedPart` already takes `tmp_prefix`, `DataPartsExchange.cpp:421`) and the clone path (`cloneAndLoadDataPart(..., "tmp_clone_", ...)`, `:5602`); the final rename is deliberately destructive (`renameTo(..., remove_new_dir_if_exists=true)` at `:5726`, and `DataPartStorageOnDiskBase::rename` removes an existing destination directory at `:685`), so deferring it to the end of the statement relocates that clobber rather than removing it; and renaming to the canonical name only at the end changes what a concurrent reader of `system.detached_parts`, and `checkIfDetachedPartitionExists` for a concurrent fetch of the same partition, observes mid-statement. So it is a behaviour-affecting change to a shared function, which I would rather not fold into a PR about the block-identity guard; it now has its own tracking work and the fixing PR will be linked from the review thread. The current behaviour is still strictly better than the previous unconditional residue on every failure. Separately, the test covers successful cleanup and retryability but not a removal failure partway through: there is no failpoint for detached-part removal, so that path is not reachable from a stateless test. Compatibility. This deliberately restricts cross-table `REPLACE`/`ATTACH`/`MOVE`/`FETCH`/`CLONE AS` between tables that have `enable_block_number_column` or `enable_block_offset_column` enabled, once the source parts are merged. It is the same silent-corruption-to-explicit-rejection policy #107386 established. The escape hatch is `INSERT INTO dst SELECT ... FROM src`, which assigns fresh block identities. A feature-preserving alternative for the future is to re-stamp or strip the identity columns during the clone; that is an owner-scale redesign of part adoption (it degrades to a data rewrite for compact parts and touches replicated REPLACE checksum determinism), so I am not attempting it here. Not fixed here (separate root cause). The block-number allocator is initialized from active part NAMES only (`increment.set(getMaxBlockNumber())`), so persisted CONTENT identities can exceed it and be re-issued by later inserts without any cross-table import: `RESTORE` (plain and Replicated), `DETACH` max-block parts then restart then `INSERT` then `ATTACH`, and non-empty restores. These have different triggers, a different repro, and a different fix surface (allocator initialization / restore semantics, owned by the backup and patch-parts owners), and no narrow in-PR measure is sound (an attach/restore-time allocator bump cannot repair identities already re-issued at insert time, and rejecting `RESTORE` would break disaster recovery of every lightweight-update table). I propose a follow-up issue for it. The sibling assertion `PatchJoinCache::Entry::addBlock` (#107501, the patch-side producer) is a separate question and is not touched here. Tests. New `03100_lwu_54_attach_foreign_block_ids` (MergeTree) and `03100_lwu_55_attach_foreign_block_ids_replicated` (ReplicatedMergeTree, including every `FETCH PARTITION` case) together cover the rejected `ATTACH`/`REPLACE`/`MOVE`/`CLONE AS`/`FETCH` cases, both single-column sources (one persisting only `_block_offset`, one persisting only `_block_number`, so each half of the check is exercised on its own: the two settings are independent), the allowed cases (column-less source, self-`REPLACE`), a mixed partition (one merged identity-bearing part plus a later level-0 part) whose rejected `FETCH PARTITION` must leave behind only a part detached before it ran and must fail the same way when retried, and a correctness postlude verifying a lightweight update after an allowed `REPLACE` patches exactly the intended rows. `MOVE PART TO SHARD` is covered by code review only: besides being experimental and default-off, it currently cannot be exercised from a test on a debug build, because `ASTAlterQuery` does not print the `SHARD` keyword, so the query fails the format/parse-back consistency check in `executeQueryImpl` before reaching any storage code. That formatter gap is pre-existing and unrelated to this change. Five existing tests whose merged sources newly hit the guard under randomized settings had `enable_block_number_column`/`enable_block_offset_column` pinned off (`00975_move_partition_merge_tree`, `02998_projection_after_attach_partition`, `03008_s3_plain_rewritable`, `03008_s3_plain_rewritable_alter_partition`, `03008_azure_plain_rewritable_alter_partition`). The adoption coverage is split across the two files, and four of those five carry `no-flaky-check`, because the flaky check runs each changed test 50 times with the thread fuzzer enabled and fails any single run over 180s: the fuzzer adds a per-statement cost that dominates here (the combined adoption test measured 0.4s without it and 130s with it, on 93 individually trivial statements), and the four object-storage and 10M-row tests already cost 14-21s each without it. No assertion or fixture changes: the split preserves all 68 non-boilerplate statements, all 12 expected-error markers and all 14 reference lines in order, and the halves measure 60s and 62s under the fuzzer. `no-flaky-check` rather than `long` because it narrows only the flaky check and leaves the Fast test and coverage jobs untouched.

signal.title: Fix lost parentheses for an INTERSECT/EXCEPT child of a UNION chain
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107582 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a bug where a stored query combining `UNION` with a parenthesized `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` group lost its parentheses when serialized, so `X UNION ALL (Y EXCEPT Z)` was read back as `(X UNION ALL Y) EXCEPT Z`. Views returned wrong results after a server restart, and a materialized view could end up with metadata the server refuses to load, which prevented it from starting. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107582 `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery::formatQueryImpl` did not parenthesize a child that is an `ASTSelectIntersectExceptQuery`. Two reasons, both needed to hit the bug: - `SelectIntersectExceptQueryVisitor` rewrites the group into an `ASTSelectIntersectExceptQuery` and consumes its entry from `list_of_modes`, so the existing mode-based `is_except` test cannot see it any more. - The remaining guard only recognizes `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery`, and `ASTSelectIntersectExceptQuery` is not one: it derives from `ASTSelectQuery`, a separate branch under `IAST`, so that test cannot match it. `need_parens` stayed false and the child was emitted bare, so the operator precedence flipped on re-parse. The child's own formatter parenthesizes its left operand, which is what produced the misleading `(X UNION ALL Y) EXCEPT Z`: the parentheses did not disappear, they moved. This is a silent wrong-results bug for any stored query of that shape. Reduced repro, results differ across a metadata round-trip before this change: ```sql CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT 1 AS x UNION ALL (SELECT 2 EXCEPT SELECT 1); SELECT * FROM v ORDER BY x; -- 1, 2 DETACH TABLE v; ATTACH TABLE v; SELECT * FROM v ORDER BY x; -- 2 (before this change) ``` The fix mirrors 0ea9937c019f1, which added the symmetric guard to `ASTSelectIntersectExceptQuery::formatImpl` for `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` children. This one covers the other direction. The `list_of_selects->children.size() > 1` guard matters: a standalone `EXCEPT`/`INTERSECT` is also wrapped in a one-child `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` (`NormalizeSelectWithUnionQueryMatcher` only lifts up `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` children), and it has no sibling to rebind to, so wrapping it would add parentheses everywhere without preventing any ambiguity. How it surfaced: a fuzzer-created materialized view in a stress test, reported by @ alexey-milovidov on #107582. Its stored definition was rewritten into a shape `checkAllowedQueries` rejects, so metadata load failed with `Code: 397 ... MATERIALIZED VIEW support query with multiple simple UNION [ALL] only: While processing ATTACH MATERIALIZED VIEW test_7.v2__fuzz_9` and the server could not start. Unrelated to the `HiveText` output changes in that PR. Check: `Stress test (amd_debug)` Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107582&sha=fbe1fa6aad606580e4ccf85b967e794f6e3d4958&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_debug%29 Reproduced locally end to end: the persisted `.sql` holds the flipped text, and reloading that metadata fails with the same `Code: 397`. With this change the stored text matches what was submitted and the metadata loads. Two things I deliberately left out of this PR: - `checkAllowedQueries` (`SelectQueryDescription.cpp:88`) has `return` where it means `continue`, so it stops at a UNION branch with no `FROM` and never inspects the later branches. That is why this definition was accepted at DDL time. Fixing it as-is would make servers that boot today fail to boot after an upgrade, since that validator also runs on metadata load, so it needs its own compatibility work. - Databases that already hold a flipped definition still fail to load. This change stops new corruption; repairing existing metadata needs an explicit policy for failed materialized-view loading in `DatabaseOrdinary::loadTableFromMetadata`. Note the `#ifndef NDEBUG` `Inconsistent AST formatting` self-check could not have caught this: it runs at `executeQuery.cpp:1278`, before the visitors at 1555-1563 that produce the offending shape. Existing references changed only on the case this fix targets, and only by gaining parentheses; rows are unchanged. One line in `04295_105916_intersect_except_format_union_parens`, and one `explain syntax` block in each of `02004_intersect_except_operators.oldanalyzer.reference` and `02004_intersect_except_distinct_operators.oldanalyzer.reference`, which the old-analyzer jobs read in preference to the plain files. All three were regenerated, and each one fails against a pristine master binary with the inverse diff.

signal.title: Validate the database engine of a non-APPEND refreshable materialized view on ATTACH and RESTORE
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111370 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109454 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a logical error (server abort in debug and sanitizer builds) when a non-APPEND refreshable materialized view was created in a non-Atomic/Replicated database via a full-definition `ATTACH`, or via a `RESTORE` of a view that had a UUID into such a database. `CREATE` already rejected this combination; `ATTACH` and `RESTORE` bypassed the check and produced a view with a Nil UUID whose refresh tripped a `DatabaseCatalog::tryGetByUUID` assertion in the Replicated-DDL parent-table lookup. Backups of views that never had a UUID stay restorable, and their refresh now fails cleanly instead of aborting. ### Description A non-APPEND refreshable materialized view is only supported in `Atomic` and `Replicated` databases: its refresh swaps the inner table through an atomic `EXCHANGE`, and it needs a real UUID for parent-table tracking when the target lives in a `Replicated` database. `CREATE` enforces this in `validateMaterializedViewColumnsAndEngine`, but that call is gated on `mode <= LoadingStrictnessLevel::CREATE`, so two fresh-definition paths bypassed it: - a full-definition `ATTACH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... REFRESH ... TO ...` (runs at `LoadingStrictnessLevel::ATTACH`), and - a `RESTORE ... AS <other_db>.<view>` that lands the view in a non-Atomic/Replicated database (runs at `SECONDARY_CREATE` with `is_restore_from_backup`). In a `Memory` database the view gets a Nil StorageID UUID. When its refresh fires and issues `CREATE OR REPLACE` for the temp inner table into a `Replicated`-database target, the Nil UUID is written into `DDLLogEntry.parent_table_uuid`, and `DatabaseReplicatedDDLWorker::checkParentTableExists(Nil)` calls `DatabaseCatalog::tryGetByUUID(Nil)`, hitting `chassert(uuid != UUIDHelpers::Nil && ...)`. In release builds the assertion is compiled out and the refresh instead fails permanently with a misleading `TABLE_IS_DROPPED "Parent table doesn't exist"`. Fix: - Hoist the non-APPEND-RMV database-engine check out of `validateMaterializedViewColumnsAndEngine` into `createTable`, gated on `is_fresh_definition = mode <= CREATE || (mode == ATTACH && !attach_short_syntax) || (is_restore_from_backup && create.has_uuid)`. This mirrors the existing `is_fresh_definition` predicate in `registerStorageMergeTree.cpp`: stored definitions (short `ATTACH`, `ATTACH DATABASE`, restart) were validated when introduced and keep loading; plain Replicated-DDL replay stays exempt (its database is `Replicated` anyway); fresh full-definition `ATTACH` is user input and is validated like `CREATE`. The exception text is unchanged. - Add a fail-close Nil guard in `checkParentTableExists`: a Nil UUID never identifies a table, so return false (mirrors the existing Nil guard in `getRMVCoordinationInfo` in the same file). This keeps metadata written by older binaries loadable and makes its refresh fail cleanly instead of aborting debug/sanitizer servers. A `RESTORE` is only validated when the backed-up definition carried a UUID (`create.has_uuid`, which reflects the backup's own metadata: `RESTORE` overwrites `uuid` with a freshly generated one before the interpreter runs, but never `has_uuid`). A view that had a UUID lived in a database that holds UUIDs, so landing it in one that does not is the UUID-losing case that must be rejected. A backup of a view that never had a UUID (for example one moved to an `Ordinary` database by an earlier `RENAME`) is a definition that already lived without one: rejecting it would make such backups unrestorable on newer servers while the same metadata still loads on restart and on a short `ATTACH`, so it stays restorable under any name and the Nil guard keeps its refresh failing cleanly. Found by BuzzHouse: - `Logical error: 'uuid != UUIDHelpers::Nil && getFirstLevelIdx(uuid) < uuid_map.size()'`, BuzzHouse (arm_asan_ubsan): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111370&sha=3c509b961097528327cfb981dbef8957a5f9237a&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29 - same assertion, BuzzHouse (amd_msan): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109454&sha=5cf32f88e08f93010cf061d9bee9e626fd959d1f&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29 Both sighting PRs are unrelated to this code path (a datetime-function change and an unrelated change); the failure is a latent engine bug, not caused by either PR.

signal.title: Fix TTL merge slot leak when a selected merge is dropped before execution
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96130 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes background TTL merges stopping server-wide when a selected TTL merge is dropped before it starts executing (for example, when its table is dropped or detached while the merge is still queued in the background pool). Each such merge leaked a slot booked against `max_number_of_merges_with_ttl_in_pool`; once the counter reached the limit, no further TTL merges were scheduled until the server was restarted. ### Description A non-replicated TTL merge books a slot in the global counter for `max_number_of_merges_with_ttl_in_pool` at merge selection time (to close the assign-vs-execute race), and the booking is handed over to the `MergeList` entry only when the merge starts executing. If the selected merge is abandoned before that handover, the slot was leaked. Two abandonment paths were compensated; several were not, most notably the pending-queue removal that `DROP`/`DETACH TABLE` performs on a merge still waiting in the background pool. Each leak permanently decrements the number of TTL merges the server can run; once it reaches the per-table limit (default 2), `merge_with_ttl_allowed` is false for every default-limit table and background TTL merges stop server-wide until restart, while regular merges keep running. The fix makes the booking a scope guard owned by the selected-merge entry, released automatically on any path that abandons the merge before its `MergeList` entry exists, and disarmed once that entry takes over the accounting. This replaces the two ad-hoc per-path compensations with a single mechanism covering every abandonment path. The same book-to-insert gap in the replicated path (`MergeFromLogEntryTask`) is guarded symmetrically. A debug/sanitizer assertion guards the counter against underflow. The flaky test `04321_table_readonly_background_merges` surfaced this: its writable control table relies on a background TTL merge, which never ran once the global counter had leaked to the limit earlier in the run (test `02293_part_log_has_merge_reason`, the only test setting the limit to 100, was unaffected, which pinpointed the counter). Report where it was observed: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96130&sha=0aa6569f3e6563c982227857effd5d2d19c97527&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20azure%2C%20parallel%29 Regression test `04641_ttl_merge_slot_leak_unscheduled` reproduces the leak deterministically via the `mt_skip_scheduling_merge_once` failpoint (which drops a selected merge exactly once, the same accounting gap the table-drop hits) with the limit set to 1, and verifies that a later background TTL merge still runs after the dropped selection, and that a second TTL merge cycle runs afterwards (either a leaked or an over-released slot makes the second cycle time out, so the test discriminates both accounting errors in all build types).

signal.title: Fix signed integer overflow in the DateLUTImpl sunday-first week helpers
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107366 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `toStartOfWeek` and `toLastDayOfWeek` with a Sunday-first week mode returning a wrapped day number for a `Date32` value outside the representable calendar, for example after `toDate32('1970-01-01') + INTERVAL 2147483647 DAY`. The week boundary is now computed at the calendar boundary, consistently with the Monday-first week modes. The wrapping was also a signed integer overflow (undefined behavior). ### Description UBSan reported this in `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)` on an unrelated PR, from an AST-fuzzer query: ``` src/Common/DateLUTImpl.h:1316:11: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 6 cannot be represented in type 'int' ``` Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107366&sha=2f1747ab6b4ba58638193a2da4a7c3f0fc8415e1&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 The two `week_mode` overloads `toFirstDayNumOfWeek(v, week_mode)` and `toLastDayNumOfWeek(v, week_mode)` are the only week helpers in `DateLUTImpl.h` that lack the out-of-LUT-range escape branch all their siblings have. `toDayOfWeek(v)` internally takes the escape and returns the weekday of the clamped day, but the arithmetic that follows runs on the raw unclamped day number, so `v += 6` is undefined behaviour for an `ExtendedDayNum` at `INT32_MAX`. A `Date32` reaches such a value through wrapping `addDays`. This PR fixes two bugs with that one root cause: the reported `INT32_MAX` overflow in `toLastDayNumOfWeek`, and its `INT32_MIN` mirror in `toFirstDayNumOfWeek` (`DateLUTImpl.h:1302`, `-2147483647 - 6`). I added the escape branch to both overloads, mirroring the monday-first siblings, so the day number is clamped into the representable calendar before any arithmetic. `day_of_week % 7` maps Sunday (7) to 0 because these overloads start the week on Sunday. As with the monday-first overloads, the resulting week boundary may lie a few days past the calendar boundary; I kept that regime so the two paths agree for the same input. The in-range code is unchanged: `isOutOfLUTRange` passing bounds the day number to `[-25567, 120273]`, where the arithmetic cannot overflow, so every representable date keeps its current result. The bug is observable without a sanitizer, which is why the changelog category is `Bug Fix` rather than the `CI Fix or Improvement` used for the sibling overflows in this file. Before the fix `toLastDayOfWeek(toDate32('1970-01-01') + INTERVAL 2147483647 DAY, 0)` returned the wrapped day number `-2147483648`, and the first and last day of the same week were `-4294967290` days apart instead of 6. I found no open issue for this. The same UBSan signature fired in 5 unrelated pull requests over the last 45 days and never on master.

signal.title: Fix data loss when a merge expires a column whose only data lives in patch parts
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109356#discussion_r3649281761 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes data loss when a merge consumes a patch part (lightweight `UPDATE`) for a column that is physically absent from all source data parts. Such a column was dropped by the merge while the merged part still claimed the patch version, permanently losing the updated values. ### Description A no-default column whose only live values live in a patch part (from a lightweight `UPDATE`, never materialized into a data part) was silently lost when a merge consumed that patch. `MergeTask::ExecuteAndFinalizeHorizontalPart::prepare` builds the set of columns present in a merge from the source data parts only (`future_part->parts`). A column that exists only in `future_part->patch_parts` is therefore treated as absent and, having no default expression, is marked expired and erased from the merge column set. The merged part still bumps its mutation version to cover the patch (`FutureMergedMutatedPart::assign`), so the patch stops applying on read and the updated values are gone. Reads return NULL where a value existed before the merge. The fix keeps such a column alive: before the expired-columns decision, it collects the columns updated by the selected patch parts under their current (post-rename) names and excludes them from expiry. Patches store the pre-rename physical name, so the name is translated through each patch's own alter conversions exactly as `AlterConversions::addPatchPart` does on the read path. Once the column stays in the merge set, the existing read pipeline gathers and materializes the patch value into the merged part; no further changes are needed. The guard only runs for merges that carry patch parts, so merges without patches are unchanged. This is a pre-existing bug on master (not introduced by #109356): in this scenario the column is absent from every source data part, so #109356's rename keep-alive (which requires the pre-rename name to be present in a source part) does not apply. Verified by reproducing byte-identical loss on a control build with #109356's guard neutralized. Two manifestations are covered by new tests: - `04628_lwu_patch_only_column_expired_on_merge` (SQL, horizontal and vertical merge): `ADD COLUMN` with no default, lightweight `UPDATE`, then `OPTIMIZE FINAL` loses the value without the fix. - `04629_lwu_patch_only_rename_merge_race` (shell, failpoint): same as above with a pending `RENAME COLUMN` the merge straddles; the renamed column reads back NULL without the fix. Both tests fail on master and pass with the fix. Note on #109356: that PR is open and touches the same block in `MergeTask.cpp` (both move the mutations snapshot creation up). The two keep-alive sets are independent and compose by union in the same condition; whichever lands second resolves a trivial conflict.

signal.title: Do not consume a source block number for row-less chunks in insert deduplication
signal.text: <!-- No related open issue found (searched: deduplication_hashes.size, dedup LOGICAL_ERROR, source block number). Surfaced by CI Stress test (amd_msan): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111754&sha=79ec7ed9daf6348f4d886d723048dbacf5a4324a&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes nondeterministic insert deduplication block ids when a row-less chunk interleaves with data chunks during an `INSERT SELECT` (for example under parallel replicas). Such an insert can miss deduplication and produce duplicate rows on retry, and asserts `deduplication_hashes.size() == 1` in debug and sanitizer builds. ### Description `AddDeduplicationInfoTransform` numbered every arriving chunk with an incrementing source block number, including row-less chunks (0 rows, with columns; these reach the transform because `ISimpleTransform` only skips chunks that have neither rows nor columns). A row-less chunk contributes no deduplication token (`setUserToken` with count 0 is a no-op) and is later dropped by squashing, so numbering it only leaves a gap in the source block numbers. That gap breaks the contiguity check in `TokenDefinition::canBeExtended` (source number ranges must be adjacent), so squashing merges the two surrounding data blocks with `do_concat` instead of extending a single token. The squashed single part then carries several deduplication tokens, `getDeduplicationHashes` returns several hashes for one part, and `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink` asserts `deduplication_hashes.size() == 1`. In release builds the assert is compiled out and the part commits with two block ids whose values depend on where the row-less chunk interleaved (thread-timing dependent), so an identical retried insert computes different ids, misses deduplication, and duplicates rows. Fix: do not consume a source block number for row-less chunks. Source numbers then stay contiguous arrival indices of data chunks, a squashed block keeps a single deduplication token and hash, and the assert holds. The regression test is a unit test (`gtest_dedup_source_block_number`) rather than an SQL test: the interleaved row-less chunk only forms under real multi-host parallel-replicas timing, so no local single-node SQL shape delivers one to the transform (verified across six query shapes and eighty iterations). The test drives `AddDeduplicationInfoTransform` directly and fails without this fix (two tokens) and passes with it (one token). Surfaced as `Logical error: 'deduplication_hashes.size() == 1'` by the `Stress test (amd_msan)` check on an unrelated docs-only PR: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111754&sha=79ec7ed9daf6348f4d886d723048dbacf5a4324a&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29
